I_S ≈ (h/3)(k/3) ΣᵢΣⱼ wᵢ^S wⱼ^S sin(xᵢ+yⱼ)
= hk/9 times the tensor weighted sum.
Substitution gives
boxed: I_S≈0.773938300531.


INDEPENDENT EXACT CHECK
Integrate analytically:
∫₀¹ sin(x+y) dx = cos y − cos(1+y).
Then
I_exact=∫₀¹[cos y−cos(1+y)]dy
=sin1−(sin2−sin1)
=2sin1−sin2
≈0.773644542790.


ERRORS
Trapezoidal signed error:
I_T−I_exact≈−0.020134370133.
Absolute error≈0.02013437.
Simpson signed error:
I_S−I_exact≈+0.000293757741.
Absolute error≈2.94×10⁻⁴.
The Simpson result is much closer on this mesh.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Use the printed h and k separately; the mesh is not square in step size.
2. Apply the one-dimensional quadrature weights in both directions by tensor product.
3. Simpson 1/3 requires an even number of subintervals in each direction; here x has 2 and y has 4, so it is admissible.
4. Keep the hk scaling separate from the integer Simpson weights.
5. Compare against the exact integral only as an independent audit.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Using h=0.5 in both x and y directions.
• Forgetting corner/edge half-weights in the double trapezoidal rule.
• Applying only one Simpson weight vector instead of a tensor product of x and y weights.
• Forgetting the Simpson factor hk/9.
• Using Simpson 1/3 with an odd number of subintervals.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
For h=0.5, x=[0,0.5,1]; for k=0.25, y=[0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1]. Tensor-product composite trapezoidal quadrature gives boxed I_T≈0.75351017. Tensor-product Simpson 1/3 with weights [1,4,1] in x and [1,4,2,4,1] in y gives boxed I_S≈0.77393830. Exact I=2sin1−sin2≈0.77364454, so Simpson is much closer for the specified mesh.

questions.question: Derive Newton–Cotes formula and write its different forms.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Dr. Hem Raj Pandey’s course lecture notes §3.1 “Newton-Cote (Quadrature) formula”, printed pp.42–44, directly derive the general equal-step quadrature expression by integrating Newton’s forward interpolation polynomial. The same course derivation then specializes it to the Trapezoidal rule, Simpson’s 1/3 rule and Simpson’s 3/8 rule. This therefore qualifies as DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION.


SOURCE-QUALITY NOTE
The course page for the n=2 specialization contains a visible typesetting/arithmetic inconsistency: after integration it displays h/2(y₀+4y₁+y₂), while the immediately following panel formula and the composite formula correctly use h/3. The mathematically correct Simpson 1/3 coefficient is h/3. The v1.2 Study View uses the checked h/3 form; the source inconsistency remains documented here rather than being silently copied.


INTUITION
Newton–Cotes formulas replace f(x) over equally spaced points by an interpolation polynomial, then integrate that polynomial exactly. Different choices of the polynomial degree produce familiar quadrature rules.


CORE SETUP
Divide [a,b] into n equal subintervals:


xᵢ=x₀+ih,  i=0,1,…,n,
h=(b−a)/n,
x₀=a,  xₙ=b,
yᵢ=f(xᵢ).


Introduce
x=x₀+ph,  so dx=h dp.
When x=x₀, p=0; when x=x₀+nh, p=n.


WHY THIS CHANGE OF VARIABLE?
It converts the physical integration interval into the dimensionless interpolation coordinate p used by Newton’s forward formula.


STEP 1 — NEWTON FORWARD INTERPOLANT
For equally spaced data,


f(x₀+ph)
= y₀
+ pΔy₀
+ p(p−1)/2! · Δ²y₀
+ p(p−1)(p−2)/3! · Δ³y₀
+ … .


STEP 2 — INTEGRATE THE INTERPOLANT
Therefore,


∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx
≈ h∫₀ⁿ [y₀+pΔy₀+p(p−1)/2! Δ²y₀+p(p−1)(p−2)/3! Δ³y₀+…]dp.


Equivalently, the general Newton–Cotes expression can be written compactly as


∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx
≈ h Σᵣ₌₀ⁿ {Δʳy₀/r!} ∫₀ⁿ p(p−1)…(p−r+1) dp.


Integrating the first terms gives


∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx
≈ h[ n y₀
+ n²/2 · Δy₀
+ n²(2n−3)/12 · Δ²y₀
+ n²(n−2)²/24 · Δ³y₀
+ … ].


This is the Newton–Cotes general quadrature formula in forward-difference form.


WHY DOES THIS WORK?
The interpolation polynomial agrees with the tabulated function values at the selected nodes. Integrating the polynomial converts interpolation weights into quadrature weights.


DIFFERENT FORMS


1. TRAPEZOIDAL RULE — n=1 FOR EACH PANEL
For one interval [x₀,x₁], only the linear interpolant is required:


∫ₓ₀ˣ¹ f(x)dx
≈ h∫₀¹ (y₀+pΔy₀)dp
= h[y₀+1/2 Δy₀]
= h/2 (y₀+y₁).


Applying this panel by panel gives the composite trapezoidal rule:


∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx
≈ h/2[(y₀+yₙ)+2(y₁+y₂+…+yₙ₋₁)].


Restriction: any positive integer number of equal subintervals may be used.
Polynomial exactness: degree 1.
Composite error order: O(h²) for sufficiently smooth f.


2. SIMPSON’S 1/3 RULE — n=2 FOR EACH PANEL
Use a quadratic interpolant over two equal subintervals:


∫ₓ₀ˣ² f(x)dx
≈ h∫₀² [y₀+pΔy₀+p(p−1)/2 Δ²y₀]dp.


The integrals are
∫₀²1dp=2,
∫₀²pdp=2,
∫₀²p(p−1)/2 dp=1/3.


Hence


∫ₓ₀ˣ² f(x)dx
≈ h[2y₀+2Δy₀+1/3 Δ²y₀]
= h/3(y₀+4y₁+y₂).


Repeating over successive pairs gives


∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx
≈ h/3[(y₀+yₙ)
+4(y₁+y₃+…+yₙ₋₁)
+2(y₂+y₄+…+yₙ₋₂)].


Restriction: total number of subintervals n must be even.
Polynomial exactness: degree 3.
Composite error order: O(h⁴) for sufficiently smooth f.


WHY THE 1-4-2-4-…-1 PATTERN?
Adjacent two-interval Simpson panels share their interior endpoints. The shared even-index nodes receive weight 2, while the odd-index midpoints of each panel retain weight 4.


3. SIMPSON’S 3/8 RULE — n=3 FOR EACH PANEL
Use a cubic interpolant over three equal subintervals:


∫ₓ₀ˣ³ f(x)dx
≈ 3h/8 (y₀+3y₁+3y₂+y₃).


Repeating over groups of three subintervals gives


∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx
≈ 3h/8[(y₀+yₙ)
+3(y₁+y₂+y₄+y₅+…)
+2(y₃+y₆+y₉+…+yₙ₋₃)].


Restriction: total number of subintervals n must be a multiple of 3.
Polynomial exactness: degree 3.
Composite error order: O(h⁴) for sufficiently smooth f.


WHY THE 1-3-3-2-3-3-…-1 PATTERN?
Every internal node whose index is not divisible by 3 belongs to one cubic panel and receives weight 3. Junction nodes between adjacent panels are shared, producing weight 2.


PATTERN SUMMARY
Newton–Cotes derivation:
1. equally spaced nodes;
2. write Newton forward interpolation polynomial;
3. set x=x₀+ph and dx=h dp;
4. integrate from p=0 to p=n;
5. choose panel degree to obtain a named quadrature rule.


Named forms in the course derivation:
- degree-1 panel → Trapezoidal;
- degree-2 panel → Simpson 1/3;
- degree-3 panel → Simpson 3/8.


MATH QA
PASS — change of variable x=x₀+ph gives dx=h dp and limits 0→n.
PASS — first integrated coefficients independently checked: n, n²/2, n²(2n−3)/12, n²(n−2)²/24.
PASS — n=1 reduces to h/2(y₀+y₁).
PASS — n=2 independently integrates to h/3(y₀+4y₁+y₂), correcting the source’s isolated h/2 typo.
PASS — n=3 gives 3h/8(y₀+3y₁+3y₂+y₃).
PASS — composite weight patterns and panel-count restrictions are internally consistent.


COMMON MISTAKES
- writing the final rules without showing that they come from integrating the interpolation polynomial;
- forgetting h when converting dx to h dp;
- using Simpson 1/3 with an odd number of subintervals;
- using Simpson 3/8 when the subinterval count is not a multiple of 3;
- copying the isolated h/2 typo from the course-note n=2 line instead of the checked h/3 coefficient;
- mixing the local panel n used to derive a rule with the total composite subinterval count.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Let xᵢ=x₀+ih, h=(b−a)/n and yᵢ=f(xᵢ). Put x=x₀+ph, dx=h dp. Using Newton’s forward interpolation formula,


f(x₀+ph)=y₀+pΔy₀+p(p−1)Δ²y₀/2!+p(p−1)(p−2)Δ³y₀/3!+… .


Hence


∫ₐᵇf(x)dx
≈h∫₀ⁿf(x₀+ph)dp
=hΣᵣ [Δʳy₀/r!]∫₀ⁿp(p−1)…(p−r+1)dp,


which is the Newton–Cotes quadrature formula.


Special cases:


Trapezoidal:
∫ₐᵇf dx≈h/2[(y₀+yₙ)+2Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ⁻¹yᵢ].


Simpson 1/3, n even:
∫ₐᵇf dx≈h/3[(y₀+yₙ)+4Σ odd yᵢ+2Σ even-interior yᵢ].


Simpson 3/8, n multiple of 3:
∫ₐᵇf dx≈3h/8[(y₀+yₙ)+3Σ non-multiples-of-3 yᵢ+2Σ interior multiples-of-3 yᵢ].

questions.question: Derive Newton–Cotes formula. Explain Simpson’s 1/3 rule and Simpson’s 3/8 rule. Which is more accurate and why?
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Frozen status: SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. Exact occurrence: P2-PROV-2022-SPRING-ASSESSMENT-Q5, printed 5, 10 marks. NMA-SRC-LECTURE-HRP-001 covers Newton–Cotes formulas, Simpson rules and quadrature errors within PDF pp.48–69; the registered notebook supplies detailed numerical-integration support. The exact assessment wording is not established as a verbatim instructor worked derivation, so provenance remains COURSE_METHOD_MATCHED. The frozen answer requires derivation by integrating the equal-step interpolant, panel weights/restrictions and comparison of Simpson error constants.


NEWTON–COTES DERIVATION
Take n+1 equally spaced points
xᵢ=x₀+ih,  i=0,1,…,n,
with h=(xₙ−x₀)/n.
Approximate f(x) by its Lagrange interpolation polynomial
Pₙ(x)=Σ(i=0 to n) fᵢ Lᵢ(x),
where
Lᵢ(x)=Π(j≠i)(x−xⱼ)/(xᵢ−xⱼ).
Integrate the interpolant over [x₀,xₙ]:
∫(x₀ to xₙ) f(x)dx ≈ Σ fᵢ ∫(x₀ to xₙ)Lᵢ(x)dx.
Put x=x₀+th, dx=h dt, with t∈[0,n]. Then
boxed: ∫(x₀ to xₙ)f(x)dx ≈ h Σ(i=0 to n) Cᵢ fᵢ,
where
Cᵢ=∫₀ⁿ Π(j≠i)(t−j)/(i−j) dt.
These Cᵢ are the closed Newton–Cotes weights. Different n give trapezoidal, Simpson and higher-order Newton–Cotes rules.


SIMPSON 1/3 RULE
Set n=2 over x₀,x₁,x₂ with equal spacing h. Integration of the quadratic interpolant gives weights 1,4,1:
boxed: ∫(x₀ to x₂)f(x)dx ≈ h/3 [f₀+4f₁+f₂].
Composite form over an even number N of subintervals:
∫(a to b)f(x)dx ≈ h/3[f₀+4Σ f_odd+2Σ f_even+f_N].
Restriction: N must be even.
Leading composite error for sufficiently smooth f:
E₁/₃=−(b−a)h⁴ f⁽⁴⁾(ξ)/180.
Thus the composite method is fourth-order globally, O(h⁴).


SIMPSON 3/8 RULE
Set n=3 over four equally spaced points x₀,x₁,x₂,x₃. Integration of the cubic interpolant gives weights 1,3,3,1:
boxed: ∫(x₀ to x₃)f(x)dx ≈ 3h/8 [f₀+3f₁+3f₂+f₃].
Composite form requires the number N of subintervals to be a multiple of 3, with coefficient 2 at interior indices divisible by 3 and coefficient 3 at the other interior indices.
Leading composite error:
E₃/₈=−(b−a)h⁴ f⁽⁴⁾(ξ)/80.
This is also globally O(h⁴).


WHICH IS MORE ACCURATE?
For the same step size h, interval length and comparable fourth derivative, both rules have the same O(h⁴) convergence order, but Simpson 1/3 has the smaller leading error constant:
1/180 < 1/80.
Therefore, under the same smoothness and grid-spacing assumptions,
boxed: Simpson 1/3 is normally more accurate than Simpson 3/8 for the same h.
This comparison is based on the leading composite truncation-error constants; special integrands can of course produce smaller or even zero error in either rule.


DEGREE OF EXACTNESS
Both Simpson 1/3 and Simpson 3/8 integrate all polynomials of degree ≤3 exactly. Their distinction in generic accuracy for the same h comes from the leading fourth-derivative error constant, not a different polynomial degree of exactness.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Begin with equal-step interpolation because closed Newton–Cotes weights assume equally spaced nodes.
2. Integrate the interpolating polynomial rather than differentiating it.
3. State the panel-count restrictions for composite use.
4. Compare accuracy using like-for-like h and the leading error constants.
5. Distinguish convergence order from error constant: both are O(h⁴), but the constants differ.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Writing Simpson 1/3 weights as 1,3,3,1.
• Forgetting that 1/3 requires an even number of subintervals.
• Forgetting that 3/8 requires a multiple of 3 subintervals.
• Claiming Simpson 3/8 has higher polynomial exactness because it uses four nodes; both are exact through cubic degree.
• Claiming one rule is universally more accurate without specifying the same h/smoothness comparison.
• Comparing 1/180 and 1/80 backwards.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Newton–Cotes formulas are obtained by interpolating f at equally spaced nodes with the Lagrange polynomial and integrating it, giving ∫f dx≈hΣCᵢfᵢ. For n=2, Simpson 1/3 is h/3(f₀+4f₁+f₂), used with an even number of subintervals. For n=3, Simpson 3/8 is 3h/8(f₀+3f₁+3f₂+f₃), used with subinterval count divisible by 3. Both composite rules are O(h⁴), but their leading errors are −(b−a)h⁴f⁽⁴⁾/180 and −(b−a)h⁴f⁽⁴⁾/80 respectively. Hence, for the same h and smoothness, Simpson 1/3 normally has the smaller error.

questions.question: Define Romberg’s Method. Compute ∫₀¹ dx/(1+x²) using Simpson 1/3 rule and use Romberg method for better approximation.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Dr. Hem Raj Pandey’s course lecture notes §3.5.2 and Example 3.5.1 use the exact integral and explicitly ask for trapezoidal and Simpson 1/3 estimates followed by Romberg improvement. The example is therefore a direct course-solution match.
The teacher works with rounded tabulated f(x) values, so the printed intermediate numbers are approximate. v1.2 preserves the teacher’s rounded table in Audit while recomputing the same formulas from f(x)=1/(1+x²) at full working precision.


WHAT IS BEING ASKED?
First show a Simpson 1/3 estimate for the integral. Then explain and apply Romberg extrapolation to nested approximations so the leading discretization errors are cancelled systematically. A final exact-value check is available because ∫ dx/(1+x²)=arctan x.


PREREQUISITES
Composite trapezoidal rule; Simpson 1/3 rule; Richardson extrapolation; equally halved step sizes; error-order notation.


INTUITION
The trapezoidal rule has an error expansion beginning with h². If we calculate trapezoidal approximations with h, h/2, h/4, …, the leading h² error can be cancelled by a weighted combination. Repeating the cancellation builds the triangular Romberg table and raises the formal error order by two powers at each column.
Simpson 1/3 itself can be viewed as the first Richardson correction of two nested trapezoidal estimates.


ROMBERG FORMULA
Let R(k,1)=T(h_k), where h_k=(b−a)/2^(k−1). Then
R(k,j)=R(k,j−1)+[R(k,j−1)−R(k−1,j−1)]/[4^(j−1)−1],   j=2,…,k.
The denominator 4^(j−1)−1 is chosen to cancel the leading error term of the previous column.


STEP 1 — SIMPSON 1/3 WITH h=0.5
For f(x)=1/(1+x²):
f(0)=1,
f(0.5)=0.8,
f(1)=0.5.


With two subintervals of width h=0.5,
S = (h/3)[f(0)+4f(0.5)+f(1)]
  = (0.5/3)[1+4(0.8)+0.5]
  = 0.783333333333333.


The instructor’s rounded-table presentation prints this as approximately 0.7834.


STEP 2 — NESTED TRAPEZOIDAL APPROXIMATIONS
Using exact function evaluations:
T(h=1)      = 0.750000000000000
T(h=0.5)    = 0.775000000000000
T(h=0.25)   = 0.782794117647059
T(h=0.125)  = 0.784747123622772


STEP 3 — ROMBERG TABLE
Column R(k,1): trapezoidal values.
First extrapolation uses denominator 3.
Second extrapolation uses denominator 15.
Third extrapolation uses denominator 63.


R(1,1) = 0.750000000000000


R(2,1) = 0.775000000000000
R(2,2) = 0.783333333333333


R(3,1) = 0.782794117647059
R(3,2) = 0.785392156862745
R(3,3) = 0.785529411764706


R(4,1) = 0.784747123622772
R(4,2) = 0.785398125614677
R(4,3) = 0.785398523531472
R(4,4) = 0.785396445940468


WHY THESE COLUMNS WORK
R(k,2) combines two O(h²) trapezoidal estimates and cancels the h² term, producing an O(h⁴) estimate. In particular, R(2,2)=0.783333333333333 is exactly the Simpson h=0.5 value.
R(k,3) cancels the leading h⁴ term using the factor 16−1=15.
R(k,4) cancels the leading h⁶ term using the factor 64−1=63.
Stop when the requested table depth is reached or successive high-order entries have stabilized to the required tolerance.


FINAL RESULT AND CHECK
Using the four-level standard Romberg table,
R(4,4) = 0.785396445940468.


The exact value is
I = arctan(1)−arctan(0) = π/4 = 0.785398163397448.


Therefore
R(4,4)−π/4 = −0.000001717456980 ≈ −1.71746×10⁻⁶.


An important numerical observation is that R(4,2)=0.785398125614677 is even closer to π/4 for this finite table. Higher extrapolation order is not a guarantee of monotonic error reduction at every finite level; the proper check is the actual stabilization/error behavior, not “largest j must always be best.”


MATH QA
PASS — Simpson h=0.5 recomputes to 0.783333333333333.
PASS — nested trapezoids recomputed directly from f(x), not from rounded source-table values.
PASS — each Romberg coefficient uses 4^(j−1)−1 = 3, 15, 63.
PASS — R(2,2) equals the Simpson h=0.5 estimate, confirming the first extrapolation identity.
PASS — exact check π/4=0.785398163397448.
PASS — R(4,4) error is approximately −1.71746×10⁻⁶.


SOURCE DISCREPANCIES RETAINED IN AUDIT
The instructor’s trapezoidal part uses rounded f-values and reports approximately 0.775, 0.7827, 0.7847, with Romberg approximately 0.7854. These are consistent with a rounded teaching table.
In the Simpson h=0.25 line, the printed symbolic formula shows a 2y₃ term, while the numerical substitution uses 2×0.8, which is y₂. The arithmetic intent is the standard Simpson even-node term; v1.2 uses y₂.
In the Simpson h=0.125 numerical line, the printed odd-node coefficient appears as 8 even though the formula immediately above uses 4 and the reported result approximately 0.7853 is consistent with coefficient 4. v1.2 treats 8 as a source typesetting error.
The source subsection “Romberg method by Simpson’s 1/3 Rule” introduces the valid first Simpson Richardson factor 16/15, but its displayed higher extrapolation formulas repeat the same 1/15 denominator. A full Richardson ladder from an O(h⁴) sequence would use increasing cancellation factors (15, 63, 255, …). The example’s final Simpson-side 0.7852 is not used as the checked Study View result. The standard trapezoid-based Romberg table above is mathematically reproducible and matches the frozen verified answer.


RELATED COURSE CONTEXT
NMA-Q-0080: Newton–Cotes derivation and Simpson rules; already STUDENT_READY in Batch 01.
NMA-Q-0084: derivation of Simpson 1/3 error; selected in Batch 02.
HRP Example 3.5.1: exact worked source for this question.
The Euler–Maclaurin material in the same integration unit provides a contrasting endpoint-correction strategy.


COMMON MISTAKES
Calling any repeated Simpson calculation “Romberg” without specifying the Richardson recurrence.
Using 4 instead of 4^(j−1) in every Romberg column.
Mixing the trapezoidal step length with the number of subintervals.
Rounding f(x) too early and then interpreting the rounded table as exact arithmetic.
Assuming the highest extrapolation column must always have the smallest finite-level error.
Copying the teacher’s printed Simpson typos without checking which node/coefficient the arithmetic actually uses.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Romberg integration applies Richardson extrapolation to nested trapezoidal approximations:
R(k,1)=T(h_k),
R(k,j)=R(k,j−1)+[R(k,j−1)−R(k−1,j−1)]/[4^(j−1)−1].


For f(x)=1/(1+x²), Simpson 1/3 with h=0.5 gives
S=(0.5/3)[1+4(0.8)+0.5]=0.7833333333.


Using h=1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, the trapezoidal values are
0.7500000000, 0.7750000000, 0.7827941176, 0.7847471236.
The Romberg table gives
R(4,2)=0.7853981256,
R(4,3)=0.7853985235,
R(4,4)=0.7853964459.
Thus a four-level Romberg result is approximately 0.785396446.
Check: π/4=0.7853981634, so the R(4,4) error is about −1.72×10⁻⁶.

questions.question: Romberg method of integration.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Frozen status: SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. Exact occurrence: P2-PROV-2023-FALL-Q7C, printed 7(c), within an any-two short-note group. Dr. Hem Raj Pandey’s registered lecture notes contain §3.5 Romberg Integration, §3.5.1 Romberg by Trapezoidal Rule and §3.5.2 Romberg by Simpson 1/3, including a worked Romberg example. Because the exam asks directly for the Romberg method and the registered course notes directly present that theory, provenance is DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION.
INTUITION
The composite trapezoidal rule has an even-power error expansion beginning with O(h²) for a sufficiently smooth integrand. Compute trapezoidal estimates on nested meshes h, h/2, h/4, … and combine them so the leading error term cancels. Repeating this Richardson extrapolation builds the triangular Romberg table.
ROMBERG CONSTRUCTION
Let h_k=(b−a)/2^(k−1) and let R(k,1)=T(h_k), the composite trapezoidal estimate on that mesh.
For j=2,…,k, use
R(k,j)=R(k,j−1)+[R(k,j−1)−R(k−1,j−1)]/[4^(j−1)−1].
The first extrapolation denominator is 3, the next 15, then 63, and so on. Column 2 removes the leading h² term, column 3 removes the leading h⁴ term, etc.
ORDER AND SIMPSON CONNECTION
R(k,1) is trapezoidal and normally O(h²). R(k,2) is O(h⁴) and is algebraically Simpson-like for nested trapezoidal estimates. Successive columns formally raise the even-power order by two when the smooth even-power error model is valid.
ALGORITHM
1. Compute T(h) on the coarsest mesh.
2. Halve the step and reuse nested nodes to compute the next trapezoidal estimate.
3. Set the new first-column value R(k,1).
4. Fill the row left-to-right with Richardson corrections using 4^(j−1)−1.
5. Continue refinement until the required table depth or tolerance is reached.
LIMITATIONS
Romberg is most effective for smooth integrands whose trapezoidal error admits the assumed even-power expansion. Endpoint singularities, discontinuities or severe non-smoothness can spoil the expected extrapolation behavior. Higher table order is not a guarantee of monotonic finite-level error reduction; stabilization must still be checked.
COMMON MISTAKES
• Calling repeated trapezoidal calculations “Romberg” without Richardson extrapolation.
• Using denominator 3 in every extrapolation column.
• Using 4^j−1 with an inconsistent column indexing convention; define the recurrence before substituting.
• Assuming the highest column must always be numerically closest at a finite mesh.
• Applying the standard smooth-error argument across a singularity without qualification.
EXAM-READY ANSWER
Romberg integration combines nested composite-trapezoidal approximations with Richardson extrapolation. Put R(k,1)=T(h_k), h_k=(b−a)/2^(k−1), and form R(k,j)=R(k,j−1)+[R(k,j−1)−R(k−1,j−1)]/[4^(j−1)−1]. The denominators are 3,15,63,… . Each column cancels the leading even-power error of the previous column, so the formal orders progress O(h²), O(h⁴), O(h⁶), … for sufficiently smooth f. The first extrapolation is Simpson-like.

questions.question: Derive the error in Simpson 1/3 rule.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Dr. Hem Raj Pandey’s course lecture notes §3.2.2 derive the error of Simpson’s 1/3 rule directly by Taylor expansion over one two-subinterval strip and then sum the strip errors over [a,b]. The frozen record occurs twice (2021 Spring and Fall) and is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. This is an exact instructor-course derivation match, so the primary provenance tier is DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION.


ERROR CONVENTION
Use
E = exact integral − Simpson approximation.
With this convention the leading Simpson error is negative when f⁽⁴⁾ is positive. If the opposite convention is used, the sign reverses. The absolute error bound is independent of this sign convention.


PREREQUISITES
Taylor expansion through the fourth derivative; Simpson 1/3 weights 1–4–1; composite Simpson rule with an even number of subintervals; continuity of f⁽⁴⁾; mean-value form of a summed error.


INTUITION
Simpson 1/3 integrates every polynomial of degree at most three exactly. Therefore the first Taylor term that can survive in the error is the fourth-derivative term. One Simpson panel spans two subintervals of width h, so its leading error is proportional to h⁵. A fixed interval contains O(1/h) such panels, giving a composite error of order h⁴.


WORKED DERIVATION — ONE SIMPSON PANEL
Let x₀ be the left endpoint of one Simpson panel and let
y(x)=f(x),  y₀=f(x₀),  y₁=f(x₀+h),  y₂=f(x₀+2h).


Taylor-expand about x₀:
y(x)=y₀+(x−x₀)y₀′+(x−x₀)²y₀″/2!+(x−x₀)³y₀‴/3!+(x−x₀)⁴y₀⁽⁴⁾/4!+⋯.


At x=x₀+h:
y₁=y₀+h y₀′+h²y₀″/2!+h³y₀‴/3!+h⁴y₀⁽⁴⁾/4!+⋯.


At x=x₀+2h:
y₂=y₀+2h y₀′+2h²y₀″+(4/3)h³y₀‴+(2/3)h⁴y₀⁽⁴⁾+⋯.


The Simpson area over this panel is
A₁=(h/3)(y₀+4y₁+y₂).


Substituting the Taylor expansions and collecting terms gives
A₁
=2h y₀+2h²y₀′+(4/3)h³y₀″+(2/3)h⁴y₀‴+(5/18)h⁵y₀⁽⁴⁾+⋯.      (1)


Now integrate the Taylor expansion exactly from x₀ to x₀+2h:
I₁=∫[x₀,x₀+2h] y(x)dx
=2h y₀+2h²y₀′+(4/3)h³y₀″+(2/3)h⁴y₀‴+(4/15)h⁵y₀⁽⁴⁾+⋯.      (2)


Subtracting (1) from (2),
E₁=I₁−A₁
=[4/15−5/18]h⁵y₀⁽⁴⁾+⋯
=−(1/90)h⁵y₀⁽⁴⁾+⋯.


Thus the leading error of one Simpson panel is
E_panel ≈ −h⁵ f⁽⁴⁾/90.


WHY THE h⁵ TERM APPEARS
The coefficients of y₀, y₀′, y₀″ and y₀‴ are identical in the exact integral and the Simpson approximation. This is the Taylor-series expression of Simpson’s exactness for cubic polynomials. The first mismatch is
4/15−5/18=−1/90
in the fourth-derivative contribution.


COMPOSITE SIMPSON ERROR
Let [a,b] be divided into 2n equal subintervals of width h, so
b−a=2nh.


There are n Simpson panels. Summing the panel errors,
E=∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx−S
=−(h⁵/90)[f⁽⁴⁾(ξ₁)+f⁽⁴⁾(ξ₂)+⋯+f⁽⁴⁾(ξₙ)]
for suitable points ξᵢ in their panels.


If f∈C⁴[a,b], the mean-value theorem for sums gives some ξ∈(a,b) such that
E=−(n h⁵/90)f⁽⁴⁾(ξ).


Since n h=(b−a)/2,
E=−[(b−a)h⁴/180] f⁽⁴⁾(ξ).


Therefore
E = O(h⁴).


ABSOLUTE ERROR BOUND
If
|f⁽⁴⁾(x)|≤M  on [a,b],
then
|E|≤M(b−a)h⁴/180.


Because h=(b−a)/(2n),
|E|≤M(b−a)⁵/(2880 n⁴).


MATH QA
PASS — one-panel coefficient check: 4/15−5/18=−1/90.
PASS — dimension/order check: one-panel error is O(h⁵), and n≈(b−a)/(2h), so the composite error is O(h⁴).
PASS — polynomial exactness check: if f is any cubic, f⁽⁴⁾=0 and the derived error vanishes.
PASS — x⁴ test on [0,2h]: exact integral is 32h⁵/5 and Simpson gives 20h⁵/3, so exact−Simpson=−4h⁵/15. Since f⁽⁴⁾=24, the formula gives −h⁵(24)/90=−4h⁵/15 exactly.
PASS — bound conversion: substituting h=(b−a)/(2n) into M(b−a)h⁴/180 gives M(b−a)⁵/(2880n⁴).


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
Taylor expansion exposes which derivative first produces non-cancelling error.
Comparing one Simpson panel with the exact integral isolates the local error coefficient without mixing multiple panels.
Summing n panel errors converts local O(h⁵) behavior to composite O(h⁴).
The continuity assumption on f⁽⁴⁾ allows the summed derivative values to be represented by f⁽⁴⁾(ξ).
The maximum-derivative bound turns the signed error formula into a practical guaranteed magnitude bound.


RELATED COURSE CONTEXT
NMA-Q-0080: Newton–Cotes derivation and Simpson weights, STUDENT_READY in Batch 01.
NMA-Q-0082: Romberg integration, reconstructed and math-QA passed in Batch 02; its first Richardson correction connects directly to Simpson’s fourth-order behavior.
HRP §3.2.1 gives the analogous trapezoidal error derivation and shows second-order global error.
HRP §3.2.3 continues with the Simpson 3/8 error derivation.


COMMON MISTAKES
Writing −(b−a)h⁵f⁽⁴⁾/180 instead of h⁴ in the composite formula.
Forgetting that Simpson 1/3 requires an even number 2n of equal subintervals.
Confusing the panel count n with the subinterval count 2n.
Quoting the sign without defining whether error means exact−approximate or approximate−exact.
Using a fourth-derivative formula without stating sufficient smoothness.
Writing the bound without absolute-value bars.
Stopping at “O(h⁴)” when the question asks for a derivation.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Let E=∫ₐᵇf(x)dx−S, where S is composite Simpson 1/3 with 2n equal subintervals, h=(b−a)/(2n).
For one panel [x₀,x₀+2h], Taylor expansion about x₀ gives
A₁=(h/3)(y₀+4y₁+y₂)
=2hy₀+2h²y₀′+(4/3)h³y₀″+(2/3)h⁴y₀‴+(5/18)h⁵y₀⁽⁴⁾+⋯,
while
∫[x₀,x₀+2h]y(x)dx
=2hy₀+2h²y₀′+(4/3)h³y₀″+(2/3)h⁴y₀‴+(4/15)h⁵y₀⁽⁴⁾+⋯.
Hence
E₁=−h⁵y₀⁽⁴⁾/90+⋯.
Summing n panels and using f∈C⁴[a,b],
E=−(n h⁵/90)f⁽⁴⁾(ξ)
=−(b−a)h⁴ f⁽⁴⁾(ξ)/180,
ξ∈(a,b).
Thus Simpson 1/3 has composite error O(h⁴). If |f⁽⁴⁾|≤M,
|E|≤M(b−a)h⁴/180
=M(b−a)⁵/(2880n⁴).

questions.question: For distance s=[0,10,20,30,40,50,60] ft and velocity v=[47,58,64,65,61,52,38] ft/sec, estimate travel time over 60 ft using Simpson 1/3 rule and Simpson 3/8 rule; compare the results.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Frozen U04 status is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. The 2025 Fall exam supplies the complete distance/velocity table. HRP notes supply composite Newton–Cotes/Simpson method authority. The frozen independent audit gives Simpson 1/3=1.0635210872239484 s and Simpson 3/8=1.0643752105492144 s.


WHAT IS BEING INTEGRATED — WHY RECIPROCAL VELOCITY
Velocity v=ds/dt, so dt=ds/v(s). Hence total travel time is
t = integral_0^60 [1/v(s)] ds.
Therefore Simpson’s rules must be applied to f(s)=1/v(s), not to v itself. Units: (sec/ft)×ft=sec.


DATA TABLE
s(ft) | v(ft/s) | f=1/v (s/ft)
0 | 47 | 0.021276595745
10 | 58 | 0.017241379310
20 | 64 | 0.015625000000
30 | 65 | 0.015384615385
40 | 61 | 0.016393442623
50 | 52 | 0.019230769231
60 | 38 | 0.026315789474


The spacing is h=10 ft and there are n=6 equal subintervals. Six is even, so composite Simpson 1/3 is permitted; six is also divisible by 3, so composite Simpson 3/8 is permitted.


SIMPSON 1/3
For n=6,
t_(1/3)=(h/3)[f_0+f_6+4(f_1+f_3+f_5)+2(f_2+f_4)].
Substitution gives
t_(1/3)=(10/3)[0.021276595745+0.026315789474
+4(0.017241379310+0.015384615385+0.019230769231)
+2(0.015625000000+0.016393442623)]
=1.0635210872239484 s.


boxed: t_(1/3)≈1.063521087 s.


SIMPSON 3/8
For n=6, the interior indices divisible by 3 receive weight 2 and the remaining interior indices receive weight 3:
t_(3/8)=(3h/8)[f_0+f_6+3(f_1+f_2+f_4+f_5)+2f_3].
Thus
t_(3/8)=(30/8)[0.021276595745+0.026315789474
+3(0.017241379310+0.015625000000+0.016393442623+0.019230769231)
+2(0.015384615385)]
=1.0643752105492144 s.


boxed: t_(3/8)≈1.064375211 s.


COMPARISON
Absolute difference:
|t_(3/8)-t_(1/3)|=0.0008541233252659 s.
Relative to their mean this is about 0.0803%, so the two independent six-panel Newton–Cotes estimates agree very closely.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Convert v to 1/v because the independent variable in the table is distance and the desired quantity is time.
2. Confirm equal h before using composite Simpson weights.
3. Check n=6 satisfies both rule requirements before applying either formula.
4. Keep the 1/3 and 3/8 weight patterns separate; they are different quadrature formulas over the same data.
5. Compare the two values as an internal consistency check, not as proof that either is exact.


MATH QA
PASS — h=10 ft, n=6.
PASS — reciprocal-velocity units integrate to seconds.
PASS — Simpson 1/3 independently recomputed as 1.0635210872239484 s.
PASS — Simpson 3/8 independently recomputed as 1.0643752105492144 s.
PASS — difference independently recomputed as 0.0008541233252659 s.
PASS — all values match the frozen independent audit.


COMMON MISTAKES
Integrating v(s) instead of 1/v(s).
Using time spacing even though the data are spaced in distance.
Forgetting that Simpson 1/3 requires an even number of subintervals.
Forgetting that Simpson 3/8 requires n divisible by 3.
Giving weight 2 to the wrong 3/8 indices.
Dropping units or reporting feet instead of seconds.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Since v=ds/dt,
t=integral_0^60 ds/v(s).
With h=10 ft and f_i=1/v_i,
Simpson 1/3 gives
t=(10/3)[f_0+f_6+4(f_1+f_3+f_5)+2(f_2+f_4)]
≈1.063521087 s.
Simpson 3/8 gives
t=(30/8)[f_0+f_6+3(f_1+f_2+f_4+f_5)+2f_3]
≈1.064375211 s.
The estimates differ by only 0.000854123 s, so they agree closely.

questions.question: Discuss error on Simpson’s rule.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Frozen status: SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. Exact occurrence: P2-PROV-2025-SPRING-Q3A, printed 3(a), 7 marks. Dr. Hem Raj Pandey’s registered lecture notes §3.2.2 directly derive the error in Simpson 1/3 rule by Taylor expansion. The same registered derivation has already been source-verified in v1.2 record NMA-Q-0084. Because this occurrence asks directly for Simpson-rule error, provenance is DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION.
ERROR CONVENTION
Define E = exact integral − Simpson approximation. With this convention the leading composite error is negative when f⁽⁴⁾ is positive. If the opposite error convention is used, only the sign reverses; the absolute bound is unchanged.
ONE SIMPSON PANEL
For one panel [x₀,x₀+2h], Simpson 1/3 gives S₁=(h/3)[f(x₀)+4f(x₀+h)+f(x₀+2h)]. Taylor expansion about x₀ shows that the exact integral and Simpson approximation agree through cubic terms. The first mismatch is in the fourth-derivative contribution, giving
E_panel = −h⁵ f⁽⁴⁾(ξ)/90
for some ξ in the panel, under sufficient smoothness.
COMPOSITE ERROR
Let [a,b] be divided into 2n equal subintervals of width h, so b−a=2nh and there are n Simpson panels. Summing panel errors and using continuity of f⁽⁴⁾ gives
E = −(n h⁵/90) f⁽⁴⁾(ξ)
= −(b−a)h⁴ f⁽⁴⁾(ξ)/180,   ξ∈(a,b).
Therefore composite Simpson 1/3 is fourth-order globally: E=O(h⁴).
ABSOLUTE ERROR BOUND
If |f⁽⁴⁾(x)|≤M on [a,b], then |E|≤M(b−a)h⁴/180. Since h=(b−a)/(2n), this can also be written |E|≤M(b−a)⁵/(2880 n⁴).
INDEPENDENT QA IDEA
Simpson 1/3 integrates every cubic polynomial exactly, so f⁽⁴⁾=0 implies zero error. For f(x)=x⁴ on a single [0,2h] panel, exact−Simpson=−4h⁵/15, while −h⁵·24/90=−4h⁵/15, confirming the coefficient.
COMMON MISTAKES
• Writing h⁵ instead of h⁴ in the composite error.
• Forgetting Simpson 1/3 requires an even number of equal subintervals.
• Confusing n panels with 2n subintervals.
• Quoting a signed formula without stating the error convention.
• Using the fourth-derivative formula without sufficient smoothness.
EXAM-READY ANSWER
For composite Simpson 1/3 with 2n equal subintervals, h=(b−a)/(2n), define E=∫ₐᵇf(x)dx−S. Taylor expansion of one 2h panel gives E_panel=−h⁵f⁽⁴⁾(ξ)/90. Summing n panels yields E=−(b−a)h⁴f⁽⁴⁾(ξ)/180, so the method is O(h⁴). If |f⁽⁴⁾|≤M, then |E|≤M(b−a)h⁴/180=M(b−a)⁵/(2880n⁴).

questions.question: Discuss error on Trapezoidal rule.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Frozen status: SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. Exact occurrence: P2-PROV-2024-FALL-Q3A, printed 3(a), 7 marks. Dr. Hem Raj Pandey’s registered lecture notes §3.2.1 directly cover the error in the trapezoidal rule, immediately before the direct Simpson-error derivation in §3.2.2. Therefore this theory occurrence is classified DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION.
ERROR CONVENTION
Define E = exact integral − trapezoidal approximation. With this convention the leading error is negative when f″ is positive. Reversing the convention reverses the sign but not the magnitude bound.
ONE TRAPEZOIDAL PANEL
Over one subinterval [x_i,x_i+h], the trapezoidal approximation is T_i=(h/2)[f(x_i)+f(x_i+h)]. Taylor expansion of f(x_i+h) and exact integration of the Taylor series show agreement in constant and first-derivative terms. The leading mismatch is the second-derivative term:
E_panel = −h³ f″(ξ_i)/12
for some ξ_i in the panel, under sufficient smoothness.
COMPOSITE ERROR
Divide [a,b] into n equal subintervals of width h=(b−a)/n. Summing the n panel errors and applying the mean-value form gives
E = −(n h³/12) f″(ξ)
= −(b−a)h² f″(ξ)/12,   ξ∈(a,b).
Hence the composite trapezoidal rule is globally second-order: E=O(h²).
ABSOLUTE ERROR BOUND
If |f″(x)|≤M on [a,b], then |E|≤M(b−a)h²/12. With h=(b−a)/n, |E|≤M(b−a)³/(12n²).
INDEPENDENT QA IDEA
The trapezoidal rule is exact for linear functions, so f″=0 gives zero error. For f(x)=x² on one panel [0,h], exact−trapezoidal=h³/3−h³/2=−h³/6; since f″=2, −h³f″/12=−h³/6, confirming the local coefficient.
COMMON MISTAKES
• Writing composite error proportional to h³ instead of h².
• Using f⁽⁴⁾ instead of f″ for the trapezoidal leading error.
• Forgetting to define whether error is exact−approximation or approximation−exact.
• Using a maximum-derivative bound without absolute values.
• Claiming the rule is exact for quadratics; it is exact only through degree one.
EXAM-READY ANSWER
For composite trapezoidal quadrature with n equal subintervals, h=(b−a)/n, define E=∫ₐᵇf(x)dx−T. Taylor expansion on one panel gives E_panel=−h³f″(ξ_i)/12. Summing n panels yields E=−(b−a)h²f″(ξ)/12, so the composite rule is O(h²). If |f″|≤M, then |E|≤M(b−a)h²/12=M(b−a)³/(12n²).

questions.question: Solve by Gauss–Jordan method: 2x₁+4x₂−6x₃=−8; x₁+3x₂+x₃=10; 2x₁−4x₂−2x₃=−12.
questions.student_view:
1. Form the augmented matrix
[ 2   4  -6 |  -8 ]
[ 1   3   1 |  10 ]
[ 2  -4  -2 | -12 ]


Gauss–Jordan elimination uses elementary row operations until the coefficient block becomes the identity matrix.


2. Put a convenient unit pivot in row 1
Swap R₁ and R₂:
[ 1   3   1 | 10 ]
[ 2   4  -6 | -8 ]
[ 2  -4  -2 |-12 ]


Eliminate x₁ below the first pivot:
R₂ ← R₂−2R₁ gives [0,-2,-8|-28].
R₃ ← R₃−2R₁ gives [0,-10,-4|-32].


3. Make the second pivot unity
R₂ ← −(1/2)R₂:
[0,1,4|14].


Eliminate the second column from row 3:
R₃ ← R₃+10R₂ = [0,0,36|108].
Then R₃ ← R₃/36 = [0,0,1|3].
Therefore x₃=3.


4. Clear above the third pivot
R₂ ← R₂−4R₃ = [0,1,0|2], so x₂=2.
R₁ ← R₁−R₃ = [1,3,0|7].
R₁ ← R₁−3R₂ = [1,0,0|1], so x₁=1.


Reduced augmented matrix:
[1,0,0|1]
[0,1,0|2]
[0,0,1|3]


FINAL ANSWER
x₁=1, x₂=2, x₃=3.


INDEPENDENT CHECK
Substitute [1,2,3] into the printed equations:
2(1)+4(2)−6(3)=−8,
1+3(2)+3=10,
2(1)−4(2)−2(3)=−12.
All three residuals are exactly zero. The coefficient determinant is 72≠0, so the solution is unique.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Write [A|b], interchange R₁ and R₂, then use R₂←R₂−2R₁ and R₃←R₃−2R₁. Scale R₂ by −1/2, use R₃←R₃+10R₂ and R₃←R₃/36. Back-clearing the pivot columns gives [I|1,2,3]ᵀ. Hence x₁=1, x₂=2, x₃=3.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Performing elimination only below pivots and calling it Gauss–Jordan without clearing above them.
• Applying a row operation to coefficients but not to the augmented right-hand side.
• Failing to verify the final vector in the original equations.

questions.question:
Solve by Gauss–Seidel:
10x₁−2x₂−x₃−x₄=3
−2x₁+10x₂−x₃−x₄=15
−x₁−x₂+10x₃−2x₄=27
−x₁−x₂−2x₃+10x₄=−9.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
HRP §4.7.2 gives the general Gauss–Seidel formula and an instructor-worked 3×3 example showing the same successive-displacement rule: each newly computed component is used immediately in the same iteration. The exact four-equation exam system is not worked in the notes, so the primary provenance tier remains COURSE_METHOD_MATCHED.


PREREQUISITES
Rearranging linear equations for diagonal variables; stationary iterations; diagonal dominance; infinity-norm change/residual; direct linear-system verification.


WHY GAUSS–SEIDEL SHOULD CONVERGE HERE
Each diagonal coefficient is 10. In every row the sum of absolute off-diagonal coefficients is 4, so
|aᵢᵢ|=10>4=Σ_{j≠i}|aᵢⱼ|.
The matrix is strictly diagonally dominant. Therefore Gauss–Seidel convergence is guaranteed for this system.


ITERATION EQUATIONS
Solve each row for its diagonal variable:
x₁=(3+2x₂+x₃+x₄)/10,
x₂=(15+2x₁+x₃+x₄)/10,
x₃=(27+x₁+x₂+2x₄)/10,
x₄=(−9+x₁+x₂+2x₃)/10.


In iteration k+1, use the newest available values immediately:
x₁⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ uses x₂⁽ᵏ⁾,x₃⁽ᵏ⁾,x₄⁽ᵏ⁾;
x₂⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ uses x₁⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ and old x₃,x₄;
x₃⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ uses new x₁,x₂ and old x₄;
x₄⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ uses new x₁,x₂,x₃.
This newest-value reuse is the defining difference from Jacobi iteration.


START
Use x⁽⁰⁾=[0,0,0,0]ᵀ.


ITERATION 1
x₁⁽¹⁾=3/10=0.300000.
x₂⁽¹⁾=(15+2(0.3))/10=1.560000.
x₃⁽¹⁾=(27+0.3+1.56)/10=2.886000.
x₄⁽¹⁾=(−9+0.3+1.56+2(2.886))/10=−0.136800.


ITERATION 2
x₁⁽²⁾=(3+2(1.56)+2.886−0.1368)/10=0.886920.
x₂⁽²⁾=(15+2(0.88692)+2.886−0.1368)/10=1.952304.
x₃⁽²⁾=(27+0.88692+1.952304+2(−0.1368))/10=2.9565624.
x₄⁽²⁾=(−9+0.88692+1.952304+2(2.9565624))/10=−0.02476512.


ITERATION TABLE
k | x₁ | x₂ | x₃ | x₄ | max change
1 | 0.30000000 | 1.56000000 | 2.88600000 | −0.13680000 | 2.88600000
2 | 0.88692000 | 1.95230400 | 2.95656240 | −0.02476512 | 0.58692000
3 | 0.98364053 | 1.98990783 | 2.99240181 | −0.00416480 | 0.09672053
4 | 0.99680527 | 1.99818475 | 2.99866604 | −0.00076779 | 0.01316474
5 | 0.99942678 | 1.99967518 | 2.99975664 | −0.00013848 | 0.00262151
6 | 0.99989685 | 1.99994119 | 2.99995611 | −0.00002497 | 0.00047008
15 | 1.00000000 | 2.00000000 | 3.00000000 | −5.09×10⁻¹² | 9.56×10⁻¹¹


STOPPING AND CHECKS
A practical stopping rule is maxᵢ|xᵢ⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾−xᵢ⁽ᵏ⁾|<tolerance, followed by a residual check.
At k=15 the maximum iterate change is about 9.56×10⁻¹¹.
The residual A x−b has max absolute component about 1.73×10⁻¹⁰.
The direct solution is exactly
x=[1,2,3,0]ᵀ.
Substitution gives all four original equations exactly.


INDEPENDENT ITERATION-MATRIX CHECK
Writing A=D+L+U, the Gauss–Seidel iteration matrix is
B_GS=−(D+L)⁻¹U.
Its spectral radius is approximately

questions.question: Explain ill conditioned system. Describe the convergence theorem for Gauss–Seidel iteration method.
questions.student_view:
For Ax=b, conditioning asks how sensitive the exact solution x is to small perturbations in the data A or b. A system is ill-conditioned when small relative changes in the input can cause large relative changes in the solution.
For a chosen consistent matrix norm, the condition number is κ(A)=||A||·||A⁻¹||, provided A is nonsingular. A large κ(A) indicates high sensitivity; κ(A) near 1 indicates comparatively good conditioning.
A standard first-order perturbation interpretation, when A is fixed and b changes, is ||δx||/||x|| ≤ κ(A)·||δb||/||b||. More general perturbations in A require a corresponding denominator condition; the key exam point is that κ(A) amplifies data error.
Scaling can improve numerical representation and comparison of equation magnitudes, but it cannot remove genuine near-linear dependence in A.
CONDITIONING VS NUMERICAL STABILITY
Conditioning is a property of the mathematical problem. Stability is a property of the numerical algorithm. A stable algorithm can still return a sensitive answer for an ill-conditioned problem because the problem itself amplifies small perturbations.
GAUSS–SEIDEL CONVERGENCE THEOREM
Write A=D+L+U, where D is the diagonal part, L the strict lower part and U the strict upper part. Gauss–Seidel can be written as
x^(k+1)=T_GS x^(k)+c,
with T_GS=−(D+L)⁻¹U and c=(D+L)⁻¹b.
For this fixed stationary splitting, Gauss–Seidel converges for every initial vector if and only if the spectral radius satisfies ρ(T_GS)<1.
Strict row diagonal dominance is a widely used sufficient condition for convergence; it is not a necessary condition. A real symmetric positive-definite matrix is another standard sufficient setting for Gauss–Seidel convergence.
WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Define sensitivity first, because ill-conditioning is about the problem rather than the iteration algorithm.
2. Use κ(A) to quantify amplification of relative input errors.
3. Separate conditioning from stability so a poor result is not automatically blamed on the numerical method.
4. Express Gauss–Seidel as a stationary iteration so its exact convergence criterion can be stated using ρ(T_GS).
5. Label diagonal dominance and SPD as sufficient conditions, not as the necessary-and-sufficient theorem.
COMMON MISTAKES
• Saying diagonal dominance is necessary for every convergent Gauss–Seidel system.
• Confusing large residual with ill-conditioning; conditioning concerns sensitivity, while residual is a different diagnostic.
• Claiming scaling changes the exact solution or cures genuine near-singularity.
• Writing κ(A)=||A||/||A⁻¹|| instead of the product.
• Omitting the spectral-radius criterion ρ(T_GS)<1.
EXAM-READY ANSWER
An ill-conditioned system Ax=b is one in which small perturbations in A or b may cause large changes in x. For a nonsingular A, κ(A)=||A||·||A⁻¹|| measures sensitivity; for fixed A, ||δx||/||x|| is bounded approximately by κ(A)||δb||/||b||. Conditioning is a property of the problem, whereas stability is a property of the algorithm.
For Gauss–Seidel, A=D+L+U and x^(k+1)=−(D+L)⁻¹U x^(k)+(D+L)⁻¹b. Let T_GS=−(D+L)⁻¹U. The stationary iteration converges for every initial vector iff ρ(T_GS)<1. Strict diagonal dominance and symmetric positive definiteness are important sufficient conditions.
SEMANTIC MATH COLOR / PATTERN MAP
condition_number → κ(A); perturbation → δb, δx; splitting → D,L,U; iteration_matrix → T_GS; spectral_radius → ρ(T_GS); convergence_gate → ρ(T_GS)<1.
VISUAL MODEL
Panel A: well-conditioned versus nearly dependent equation geometry. Panel B: input perturbation amplified by κ(A). Panel C: D+L+U splitting and Gauss–Seidel update flow. Panel D: eigenvalues of T_GS inside/outside the unit circle. Interactive focus: selecting a sufficient condition explains why it supports, but does not define, convergence.

questions.question: Explain ill-conditioned system. Describe the convergence theorem for Gauss–Seidel iterative methods.
questions.student_view:
For Ax=b, conditioning measures how sensitive the exact solution x is to small changes in the input data.


For a nonsingular A and a consistent matrix norm,
κ(A)=||A||·||A⁻¹||.


A large κ(A) means that small relative perturbations in A or b may produce much larger relative changes in x. For fixed A with a perturbation δb,
||δx||/||x|| ≤ κ(A)·||δb||/||b||
in the standard first-order interpretation.


Thus an ill-conditioned system is a mathematically sensitive problem. It is not the same thing as an unstable numerical algorithm.


CONDITIONING VS STABILITY
Conditioning belongs to the problem Ax=b.
Stability belongs to the algorithm used to solve it.
Even a stable solver cannot remove genuine sensitivity caused by a nearly singular or nearly dependent coefficient matrix.


GAUSS–SEIDEL ITERATION
Split
A=D+L+U,
where D is diagonal, L is strictly lower triangular and U is strictly upper triangular.


Gauss–Seidel is
x^(k+1)=−(D+L)⁻¹U x^(k)+(D+L)⁻¹b.


Define
T_GS=−(D+L)⁻¹U.


CONVERGENCE THEOREM
For this fixed stationary iteration, Gauss–Seidel converges for every starting vector if and only if
ρ(T_GS)<1,
where ρ denotes spectral radius.


Useful sufficient conditions include:
• strict diagonal dominance;
• for real matrices, symmetric positive definiteness.


Pandey’s lecture notes explicitly present diagonal dominance as a sufficient convergence condition for the iterative methods. It must not be misstated as a necessary condition.


WHY THE THEOREM IS WRITTEN THIS WAY
If e^(k)=x^(k)−x* is the error, then
e^(k+1)=T_GS e^(k),
so
e^(k)=T_GS^k e^(0).
The error tends to zero for every initial error exactly when powers of T_GS tend to zero, which is equivalent to ρ(T_GS)<1.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Saying diagonal dominance is necessary for Gauss–Seidel convergence.
• Confusing a large residual with ill-conditioning.
• Writing κ(A)=||A||/||A⁻¹|| instead of the product.
• Claiming scaling can cure genuine near-singularity.
• Giving only the component update formula without the convergence criterion.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
An ill-conditioned system Ax=b is one in which small changes in A or b may cause large changes in x. For nonsingular A, κ(A)=||A||·||A⁻¹|| measures this sensitivity; for fixed A, relative solution perturbation is bounded in first order by κ(A) times the relative perturbation in b. Conditioning is a property of the problem, whereas numerical stability is a property of the algorithm.


For Gauss–Seidel, write A=D+L+U. Then
x^(k+1)=T_GS x^(k)+(D+L)⁻¹b,
T_GS=−(D+L)⁻¹U.
The method converges for every initial vector iff ρ(T_GS)<1. Strict diagonal dominance and symmetric positive definiteness are important sufficient conditions, not necessary conditions in general.


PREREQUISITES
Matrix norms; inverse matrix; stationary iterations; eigenvalues and spectral radius; diagonal dominance.


SEMANTIC MATH COLOR / PATTERN MAP
system → A,x,b; condition_number → κ(A); perturbations → δb,δx; splitting → D,L,U; iteration_matrix → T_GS; spectral_radius → ρ(T_GS); exact_gate → ρ(T_GS)<1.


VISUAL MODEL
Panel A: well-conditioned versus nearly dependent equation geometry. Panel B: input perturbation amplified according to κ(A). Panel C: D+L+U splitting and Gauss–Seidel latest-value update flow. Panel D: eigenvalues of T_GS relative to the unit circle, with diagonal dominance shown only as a sufficient-condition card.

questions.student_view:
1. Meaning of an ill-conditioned system
For a linear system Ax=b, conditioning asks how sensitive the exact mathematical solution x is to small perturbations in the data A or b. A system is ill-conditioned when a small relative change in the coefficients or right-hand side can produce a large relative change in the solution.


A standard matrix condition number is
κ(A)=||A||·||A⁻¹||,
for a nonsingular matrix A and a chosen compatible norm.


A small/moderate κ(A) indicates comparatively low sensitivity. A very large κ(A) indicates that the system is ill-conditioned. If A is singular, A⁻¹ does not exist and the corresponding condition number is effectively unbounded.


2. Perturbation interpretation
For a perturbation mainly in b, the familiar first-order sensitivity form is
||δx||/||x|| ≤ κ(A) · ||δb||/||b||,
subject to the usual assumptions for the bound.


This shows why a large condition number is dangerous: even if the data error is small, κ(A) can magnify its effect in the solution.


3. Conditioning is not the same as algorithmic stability
Conditioning belongs to the mathematical problem. Stability belongs to the numerical algorithm used to solve it. A stable algorithm cannot remove genuine ill-conditioning; it can only avoid adding unnecessary numerical error. Conversely, a well-conditioned problem can still be computed poorly by an unstable implementation.


4. Typical causes and symptoms
• nearly dependent equations/rows or columns;
• coefficients whose geometry makes A close to singular;
• large changes in the computed solution after tiny input perturbations;
• loss of reliable significant digits;
• large condition number.


Scaling can sometimes improve representation and numerical behavior, but scaling cannot remove genuine near-dependence in the underlying equations.


FINAL ANSWER
An ill-conditioned system is one whose solution is highly sensitive to small perturbations in its coefficients or right-hand side. For Ax=b, conditioning is commonly measured by κ(A)=||A||·||A⁻¹||. A large κ(A) means that small relative data errors may cause much larger relative solution errors. Ill-conditioning is a property of the mathematical problem, whereas numerical stability is a property of the algorithm.


INDEPENDENT THEORETICAL CHECK
The condition-number definition is dimensionless because ||A|| and ||A⁻¹|| have reciprocal scaling. If A approaches singularity, ||A⁻¹|| becomes large, so κ(A) grows, matching the sensitivity interpretation. This is consistent with the registered linear-systems treatment.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
For Ax=b, a system is ill-conditioned if a very small change in A or b causes a large change in x. Its sensitivity is measured by the condition number κ(A)=||A||·||A⁻¹||. For perturbations in b, the relative solution error is bounded in scale by κ(A) times the relative data error. Hence large κ(A) means loss of accuracy and high sensitivity. Ill-conditioning is a property of the equations; algorithmic stability is a separate issue.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Calling a slowly converging iterative method “ill-conditioned” without discussing sensitivity of Ax=b.
• Treating diagonal dominance as the definition of good conditioning.
• Assuming scaling can eliminate genuine near-singularity.
• Confusing residual size with conditioning; a small residual does not by itself guarantee a small solution error for an ill-conditioned system.

questions.question: Ill conditioned systems.
questions.student_view:
Consider
Ax=b.
The system is ill-conditioned if a very small change in A or b can cause a comparatively large change in the exact solution x.


For nonsingular A,
κ(A)=||A||·||A⁻¹||
is the condition number in a chosen consistent matrix norm.


Interpretation:
• κ(A) close to 1 → relatively well-conditioned.
• κ(A) large → sensitive/ill-conditioned.
• κ(A)→∞ as A approaches singularity.


For fixed A and a small perturbation δb,
||δx||/||x|| ≤ κ(A)·||δb||/||b||
in the standard first-order bound.


GEOMETRIC / ENGINEERING INTUITION
If two equations are nearly linearly dependent, their intersection is poorly determined. A tiny change in coefficients can move the intersection substantially. This is why nearly singular structural/numerical systems may produce solution components that are very sensitive to rounding or measurement error.


CONDITIONING IS NOT STABILITY
Conditioning is a property of the mathematical problem.
Stability is a property of the numerical algorithm.
A stable algorithm may faithfully reveal that an ill-conditioned problem is sensitive; it cannot make the underlying problem well-conditioned.


SCALING
Scaling rows/variables may improve numerical representation and reduce avoidable floating-point imbalance, but it does not remove genuine near-linear dependence.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Defining ill-conditioning only as “large rounding error” without mentioning sensitivity of the exact problem.
• Confusing a singular matrix with an ill-conditioned but nonsingular matrix.
• Writing the condition number as a ratio instead of ||A||·||A⁻¹||.
• Claiming scaling always cures ill-conditioning.

questions.question: Find the inverse of A=[[2,−2,4],[2,3,2],[−1,1,1]] using LU decomposition method.
questions.student_view:
1. Principle
To find A⁻¹ using LU decomposition, factor A=LU once and solve AX=I column by column. Each column of X=A⁻¹ is the solution of Ax=e_j. This avoids recomputing elimination independently for each right-hand side.


2. Doolittle factorization
For
A = [[2,-2,4],[2,3,2],[-1,1,1]],
a no-pivot Doolittle factorization is
L = [[1,0,0],[1,1,0],[-1/2,0,1]],
U = [[2,-2,4],[0,5,-2],[0,0,3]].
Direct multiplication verifies LU=A.


3. First inverse column: Ax=e₁
Solve Lz=e₁:
z=[1,-1,1/2]ᵀ.
Then solve Ux=z:
x₃=1/6,
x₂=-2/15,
x₁=1/30.
Thus column 1 is [1/30,-2/15,1/6]ᵀ.


4. Second inverse column: Ax=e₂
Solve Lz=e₂ gives z=[0,1,0]ᵀ.
Back substitution through U gives
x₃=0,
x₂=1/5,
x₁=1/5.
Thus column 2 is [1/5,1/5,0]ᵀ.


5. Third inverse column: Ax=e₃
Solve Lz=e₃ gives z=[0,0,1]ᵀ.
Back substitution gives
x₃=1/3,
x₂=2/15,
x₁=-8/15.
Thus column 3 is [-8/15,2/15,1/3]ᵀ.


FINAL ANSWER
A⁻¹ =
[[ 1/30,  1/5, -8/15],
 [-2/15,  1/5,  2/15],
 [ 1/6,   0,    1/3 ]].


Decimal form:
[[ 0.03333333, 0.2, -0.53333333],
 [-0.13333333, 0.2, 0.13333333],
 [ 0.16666667, 0, 0.33333333]].


INDEPENDENT CHECK
Exact multiplication A·A⁻¹=I₃. The maximum absolute identity residual is 0 in exact rational arithmetic.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Factor A=LU with L=[[1,0,0],[1,1,0],[-1/2,0,1]] and U=[[2,-2,4],[0,5,-2],[0,0,3]]. Solve Ly=e_j and Ux=y for j=1,2,3. The three solution columns give A⁻¹=[[1/30,1/5,-8/15],[-2/15,1/5,2/15],[1/6,0,1/3]]. Verify AA⁻¹=I.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Explicitly inverting L and U when triangular solves are simpler and more stable conceptually.
• Placing the three solved vectors as rows instead of columns.
• Omitting the identity check.

Elimination/factorization divides by a pivot. A zero pivot stops the calculation, while a very small pivot can strongly amplify round-off. Pivoting interchanges rows (and, for complete pivoting, potentially columns) so a safer pivot is used.


WHY SCALING?
Scaling places rows/variables on comparable magnitude levels. It does not change the exact mathematical solution; it improves numerical comparison of candidate pivots and reduces misleading effects caused only by unequal coefficient scales. A common scaled-pivot comparison uses |a_ik|/s_i with s_i=max_j|a_ij|.


ITERATIVE REARRANGEMENT
x₁=(−2+2x₂+x₃)/5
x₂=(6+x₁+3x₃)/8
x₃=(16+3x₁+x₂)/7


Use the frozen zero start x^(0)=[0,0,0]^T.


GAUSS–JACOBI: FOUR ITERATIONS
k | x₁ | x₂ | x₃
1 | −0.40000000 | 0.75000000 | 2.28571429
2 | 0.35714286 | 1.55714286 | 2.22142857
3 | 0.66714286 | 1.62767857 | 2.66122449
4 | 0.78331633 | 1.83135204 | 2.80415816


boxed: x_J^(4)=[0.78331633,1.83135204,2.80415816]^T.


GAUSS–SEIDEL: FOUR ITERATIONS
k | x₁ | x₂ | x₃ | max change
1 | −0.40000000 | 0.70000000 | 2.21428571 | 2.21428571
2 | 0.32285714 | 1.62071429 | 2.65561224 | 0.92071429
3 | 0.77940816 | 1.84328061 | 2.88307222 | 0.45655102

boxed: x_GS^(4)=[0.91392668,1.94539289,2.95531042]^T.


REFERENCE SOLUTION AND RESIDUALS
Exact solution: [1,2,3]^T.
Jacobi fourth-step residual:
A x_J^(4)−b≈[0.55028061,0.54497449,0.55219388]^T,
||r||∞≈0.55219388.
Gauss–Seidel fourth-step residual:
A x_GS^(4)−b≈[0.27646282,0.21671478,0]^T,
||r||∞≈0.27646282.

1. Explain pivoting/scaling separately from the iterative solve.
2. Rearrange around the dominant diagonal entries.
3. Use the same zero start for the frozen four-step comparison.
4. Preserve Jacobi versus Gauss–Seidel update timing.
5. Stop after exactly four sweeps and verify against the original system.

• Claiming scaling changes the exact solution.

x₁=(−2+2x₂+x₃)/5,
x₂=(6+x₁+3x₃)/8,
x₃=(16+3x₁+x₂)/7,
four Jacobi iterations give
boxed: [0.78331633,1.83135204,2.80415816],
and four Gauss–Seidel iterations give
boxed: [0.91392668,1.94539289,2.95531042].
The reference solution is [1,2,3]; fourth-step infinity residuals are about 0.55219 and 0.27646.

questions.question:
Solve by Jacobi iteration method:
10x₁−2x₂−x₃−x₄=3,
−2x₁+10x₂−x₃−x₄=15,
−x₁−x₂+10x₃−2x₄=27,
−x₁−x₂−2x₃+10x₄=−9.

SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. The complete 4×4 system is present. HRP supplies Jacobi/iterative linear-system method authority. No relaxation factor or missing starting values are required by the printed problem; the standard zero-vector start is used only as the transparent iteration initialization for the v1.2 reconstruction and is not presented as an exam-given datum.


WHY JACOBI CONVERGES HERE
Each diagonal coefficient has magnitude 10, while the sum of the off-diagonal magnitudes in every row is 4. Thus the system is strictly diagonally dominant row by row: 10>4. This gives a strong convergence basis for Jacobi iteration.


ITERATION EQUATIONS
Rearrange each equation for its diagonal variable:
x₁⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾=(3+2x₂⁽ᵏ⁾+x₃⁽ᵏ⁾+x₄⁽ᵏ⁾)/10,
x₂⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾=(15+2x₁⁽ᵏ⁾+x₃⁽ᵏ⁾+x₄⁽ᵏ⁾)/10,
x₃⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾=(27+x₁⁽ᵏ⁾+x₂⁽ᵏ⁾+2x₄⁽ᵏ⁾)/10,
x₄⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾=(−9+x₁⁽ᵏ⁾+x₂⁽ᵏ⁾+2x₃⁽ᵏ⁾)/10.


Important Jacobi rule: every right-hand side at iteration k+1 uses only values from iteration k.


ITERATION TRACE FROM x⁽⁰⁾=[0,0,0,0]ᵀ
k=1: [0.300000, 1.500000, 2.700000, −0.900000]
k=2: [0.780000, 1.740000, 2.700000, −0.180000]
k=3: [0.900000, 1.908000, 2.916000, −0.108000]
k=4: [0.962400, 1.960800, 2.959200, −0.036000]
k=5: [0.984480, 1.984800, 2.985120, −0.015840]
k=6: [0.993888, 1.993824, 2.993760, −0.006048]
Continuing gives convergence toward [1,2,3,0]. The frozen study trace at k=25 is approximately [1,2,3,−1.68885×10⁻¹⁰].


FINAL ANSWER
boxed: x₁≈1, x₂≈2, x₃≈3, x₄≈0.


INDEPENDENT CHECK
Substitute [1,2,3,0]:
10(1)−2(2)−3−0=3,
−2(1)+10(2)−3−0=15,
−1−2+10(3)−0=27,
−1−2−2(3)+0=−9.
Therefore Ax−b=[0,0,0,0] and max absolute residual=0. Frozen independent audit: PASS.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Rearrange around the diagonal terms before iterating.
2. Check diagonal dominance so the expected convergence is justified rather than assumed.
3. Keep old and new vectors separate; otherwise the method silently becomes Gauss–Seidel.
4. Track successive values until changes are small.
5. Use a residual check Ax−b to verify the limiting vector satisfies the original equations.


COMMON MISTAKES
Using newly computed x₁ in the same Jacobi sweep.
Copying a sign incorrectly while rearranging the negative off-diagonal terms.
Forgetting the −9 right-hand side in the fourth equation.
Stopping after a fixed small number of sweeps without checking convergence.
Reporting only the iteration table and omitting substitution/residual verification.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
The Jacobi rearrangement is
x₁=(3+2x₂+x₃+x₄)/10,
x₂=(15+2x₁+x₃+x₄)/10,
x₃=(27+x₁+x₂+2x₄)/10,
x₄=(−9+x₁+x₂+2x₃)/10.
Starting from the zero vector gives successive approximations
[0.3,1.5,2.7,−0.9],
[0.78,1.74,2.7,−0.18],
[0.9,1.908,2.916,−0.108], …
which converge to
boxed: [x₁,x₂,x₃,x₄]≈[1,2,3,0].
Direct substitution gives zero residual.

SOURCE ALIGNMENT


Course method authority: Dr. Hem Raj Pandey lecture notes §4.3.2 Thomas Algorithm, printed p.68 onward. The notes define the tridiagonal form aᵢxᵢ₋₁+bᵢxᵢ+cᵢxᵢ₊₁=dᵢ and the recurrences
Pᵢ = −cᵢ/(bᵢ+aᵢPᵢ₋₁),
Qᵢ = (dᵢ−aᵢQᵢ₋₁)/(bᵢ+aᵢPᵢ₋₁),
followed by xₙ=Qₙ and xᵢ=Pᵢxᵢ₊₁+Qᵢ.


WHY THIS METHOD?


The coefficient matrix is tridiagonal: only the main diagonal and the immediately adjacent diagonals are nonzero. Thomas Algorithm exploits that structure, avoiding general Gaussian elimination work.


GIVEN COEFFICIENTS


For aᵢxᵢ₋₁+bᵢxᵢ+cᵢxᵢ₊₁=dᵢ:


i=1: a₁=0,  b₁=−2, c₁=1, d₁=3
i=2: a₂=1,  b₂=−4, c₂=1, d₂=1
i=3: a₃=1,  b₃=−4, c₃=1, d₃=2
i=4: a₄=1,  b₄=−2, c₄=0, d₄=−2


FORWARD SWEEP


Initialize P₀=Q₀=0.


Row 1:
P₁ = −1/(−2) = 1/2
Q₁ = 3/(−2) = −3/2


Row 2:
denominator = b₂+a₂P₁ = −4+1/2 = −7/2
P₂ = −1/(−7/2) = 2/7
Q₂ = [1−1(−3/2)]/(−7/2)
   = (5/2)/(−7/2)
   = −5/7


Row 3:
denominator = b₃+a₃P₂ = −4+2/7 = −26/7
P₃ = −1/(−26/7) = 7/26
Q₃ = [2−1(−5/7)]/(−26/7)
   = (19/7)/(−26/7)
   = −19/26


Row 4:
denominator = b₄+a₄P₃ = −2+7/26 = −45/26
P₄ = 0
Q₄ = [−2−1(−19/26)]/(−45/26)
   = (−33/26)/(−45/26)
   = 11/15


WHY THE FORWARD SWEEP?


Each pair (Pᵢ,Qᵢ) rewrites xᵢ in the compact form xᵢ=Pᵢxᵢ₊₁+Qᵢ. This removes the lower-diagonal dependency one row at a time.


BACK SUBSTITUTION


x₄ = Q₄ = 11/15


x₃ = P₃x₄+Q₃
   = (7/26)(11/15)−19/26
   = −8/15


x₂ = P₂x₃+Q₂
   = (2/7)(−8/15)−5/7
   = −13/15


x₁ = P₁x₂+Q₁
   = (1/2)(−13/15)−3/2
   = −29/15


FINAL ANSWER


x₁ = −29/15 ≈ −1.933333
x₂ = −13/15 ≈ −0.866667
x₃ = −8/15  ≈ −0.533333
x₄ =  11/15 ≈  0.733333


CHECK — SUBSTITUTE BACK


Equation 1:
−2(−29/15)+(−13/15)=45/15=3 ✓


Equation 2:
−29/15−4(−13/15)−8/15=15/15=1 ✓


Equation 3:
−13/15−4(−8/15)+11/15=30/15=2 ✓


Equation 4:
−8/15−2(11/15)=−30/15=−2 ✓


Therefore Ax−b=[0,0,0,0] exactly.


COMMON MISTAKES


- losing the sign in Pᵢ=−cᵢ/(bᵢ+aᵢPᵢ₋₁);
- using c₄≠0 even though the final row has no x₅ term;
- starting back substitution before completing the P,Q sweep;
- rounding P and Q too early; exact fractions make the check cleaner.


EXAM-READY ANSWER


Using the Thomas recurrences
Pᵢ=−cᵢ/(bᵢ+aᵢPᵢ₋₁),
Qᵢ=(dᵢ−aᵢQᵢ₋₁)/(bᵢ+aᵢPᵢ₋₁),
with P₀=Q₀=0, we obtain


(P₁,Q₁)=(1/2,−3/2),
(P₂,Q₂)=(2/7,−5/7),
(P₃,Q₃)=(7/26,−19/26),
(P₄,Q₄)=(0,11/15).


Back substitution gives
x₄=11/15,
x₃=−8/15,
x₂=−13/15,
x₁=−29/15.


Hence
x=[−29/15,−13/15,−8/15,11/15]ᵀ,
and Ax−b=0.

PART A — SIGNIFICANCE OF PIVOTING
During Gaussian elimination or LU factorization, a pivot is used as a divisor. If the pivot is zero, elimination fails. If it is very small compared with other available entries, division can amplify round-off error.
The registered instructor notes therefore define pivoting as interchanging rows so a better nonzero pivot is used. In partial pivoting, one searches the current column below the pivot for the largest available magnitude and swaps rows. Complete pivoting searches more broadly across the remaining rows and columns but is computationally more involved.


PART B — SIGNIFICANCE OF SCALING
Scaling rescales equations or variables so coefficients with very different magnitudes are brought to comparable numerical levels. Its purpose is not to change the mathematical solution; it improves numerical comparison of candidate pivots and reduces misleading magnitude effects caused purely by units or coefficient scale.
A common scaled-pivot idea compares |aᵢk| with a row scale sᵢ=max_j|aᵢj| and chooses a large ratio |aᵢk|/sᵢ. This scaling discussion is a standard numerical-stability reconstruction and is not claimed as a verbatim formula from the registered lecture PDF.


WHY PIVOTING/SCALING MATTER HERE

The first pivot −5 is nonzero and the Doolittle elimination proceeds without row exchange. Thus no pivot swap is required for the exact arithmetic reconstruction below. The conceptual significance of pivoting/scaling remains important for general numerical robustness.

The registered source writes

where L is lower triangular and U is upper triangular. For Doolittle factorization, diagonal entries of L are 1.
For this system,

=−8−(−1/5)(2)
=−8+2/5
=−38/5.

=3−(−1/5)(1)
=16/5.

=[1−(−3/5)(2)]/(−38/5)

=−7−(−3/5)(1)−(−11/38)(16/5)

Multiplying L and U reproduces A exactly; therefore the factorization is algebraically consistent.


STEP 5 — FORWARD SUBSTITUTION Ly=b
Let y=[y₁,y₂,y₃]^T.
From row 1:
y₁=2.
Row 2:
−(1/5)y₁+y₂=−6,
so
y₂=−6+2/5=−28/5.
Row 3:
−(3/5)y₁−(11/38)y₂+y₃=−16,
which gives
y₃=−312/19.
Therefore
y=[2,−28/5,−312/19]^T.


STEP 6 — BACK SUBSTITUTION Ux=y
Third equation:
(−104/19)x₃=−312/19,
so
boxed: x₃=3.
Second equation:
(−38/5)x₂+(16/5)(3)=−28/5.
Multiply by 5:
−38x₂+48=−28,
so
boxed: x₂=2.
First equation:
−5x₁+2(2)+3=2,
so
−5x₁=−5,
boxed: x₁=1.
Hence
boxed: (x₁,x₂,x₃)=(1,2,3).


INDEPENDENT RESIDUAL CHECK
Equation 1: −5(1)+2(2)+3=2 ✓
Equation 2: 1−8(2)+3(3)=−6 ✓
Equation 3: 3(1)+2−7(3)=−16 ✓
The frozen independent audit reports max absolute residual 0; PASS.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Inspect pivots because zero or tiny pivots can make elimination fail or become unstable.
2. Separate numerical scaling from the mathematical system: scaling changes representation, not the exact solution.
3. Factor A once into L and U.
4. Solve Ly=b by forward substitution.
5. Solve Ux=y by backward substitution.
6. Verify LU=A and Ax=b independently.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Confusing pivoting with scaling.
• Claiming a row swap is mandatory here even though the first pivot is nonzero and the chosen Doolittle path is valid.
• Using l₂₁=−5 instead of −1/5.
• Forgetting that Doolittle sets the diagonal of L equal to 1.
• Solving Ux=b directly instead of first solving Ly=b.
• Rounding fractions too early and introducing avoidable residual error.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Pivoting replaces a zero/small pivot by a safer one, usually by row interchange; it reduces failure and round-off amplification. Scaling normalizes coefficient magnitudes so pivot comparisons are not distorted by unequal equation scales.
For
A=[[-5,2,1],[1,−8,3],[3,1,−7]],
Doolittle factorization gives
L=[[1,0,0],[-1/5,1,0],[-3/5,−11/38,1]],
U=[[-5,2,1],[0,−38/5,16/5],[0,0,−104/19]].
Solving Ly=b gives
y=[2,−28/5,−312/19]^T.
Back substitution then gives
boxed: (x₁,x₂,x₃)=(1,2,3).
Substitution into all three original equations gives zero residual.

questions.question:
Solve
5x₁−2x₃=7,
3x₁+5x₂+x₃=2,
−3x₂+4x₃=−4
using SOR with relaxation factor ω=1.10 and perform a minimum of four iterations.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
HRP §4.7.3 gives the successive-displacement SOR formula and Example 4.7.4 works a different 3×3 system with ω=1.25. The exact exam system is not worked by the instructor, so the primary provenance tier is COURSE_METHOD_MATCHED. The exam data are complete: ω=1.10 and minimum four iterations are explicit.


PREREQUISITES
Gauss–Seidel successive displacement; relaxation factor ω; rearranging equations for diagonal variables; iteration tables; residual and direct-solution checks; spectral radius as an independent convergence diagnostic.


SOR FORMULA
For a Gauss–Seidel-style successive sweep,
xᵢ⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾=(1−ω)xᵢ⁽ᵏ⁾+(ω/aᵢᵢ)[bᵢ−Σ_{j<i}aᵢⱼxⱼ⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾−Σ_{j>i}aᵢⱼxⱼ⁽ᵏ⁾].


The instructor notes classify ω=1 as the ordinary Gauss–Seidel update and ω>1 as over-relaxation. Here ω=1.10, so each Gauss–Seidel correction is deliberately pushed 10% beyond the unrelaxed value.


REARRANGED UPDATES
From the three equations,
Gauss–Seidel target for x₁:
g₁=(7+2x₃)/5.
Thus
x₁(new)=−0.1x₁(old)+1.1g₁.


For x₂:
g₂=(2−3x₁(new)−x₃(old))/5,
so
x₂(new)=−0.1x₂(old)+1.1g₂.


For x₃:
g₃=(−4+3x₂(new))/4,
so
x₃(new)=−0.1x₃(old)+1.1g₃.


START
Use the standard zero initial vector
x⁽⁰⁾=[0,0,0]ᵀ.


ITERATION 1
x₁⁽¹⁾=1.1(7/5)=1.540000.


x₂⁽¹⁾=1.1[2−3(1.54)]/5
=−0.576400.


x₃⁽¹⁾=1.1[−4+3(−0.5764)]/4
=−1.575530.


Therefore
x⁽¹⁾=[1.54,−0.5764,−1.57553]ᵀ.


ITERATION 2
Using the newest values successively,
x₁⁽²⁾=−0.1(1.54)+1.1[7+2(−1.57553)]/5
=0.6927668.


x₂⁽²⁾=−0.1(−0.5764)+1.1[2−3(0.6927668)−(−1.57553)]/5
=0.387030512.


x₃⁽²⁾=−0.1(−1.57553)+1.1[−4+3(0.387030512)]/4
=−0.6231468276.


ITERATION TABLE
k | x₁ | x₂ | x₃ | max change
1 | 1.54000000 | −0.57640000 | −1.57553000 | 1.57553000
2 | 0.69276680 | 0.387030512 | −0.623146828 | 0.963430512
3 | 1.196538716 | −0.251326302 | −1.245029516 | 0.638356814
4 | 0.872533141 | 0.163167250 | −0.840884067 | 0.414493552
5 | 1.082757696 | −0.105942310 | −1.103313999 | 0.269109560
6 | 0.946266071 | 0.068787704 | −0.932918744 | 0.174730014
56 | 0.999999999977 | 2.8813661×10⁻¹¹ | −0.999999999972 | 7.3190681×10⁻¹¹


The exam asks for at least four iterations, so rows 1–4 satisfy the minimum. They do not yet constitute a converged numerical solution: row 4 still has a maximum change of about 0.41449. Continuing the iteration demonstrates the actual limit.


STOPPING AND RESIDUAL CHECK
At iteration 56,
maxᵢ|xᵢ⁽⁵⁶⁾−xᵢ⁽⁵⁵⁾|≈7.32×10⁻¹¹.


The iterate is approximately
x⁽⁵⁶⁾=[0.999999999977, 2.8813661×10⁻¹¹, −0.999999999972]ᵀ.


Substituting into the original equations gives residual
A x−b≈[−1.6874×10⁻¹⁰, 1.0464×10⁻¹⁰, 2.5954×10⁻¹¹]ᵀ,
so the maximum absolute residual is about 1.69×10⁻¹⁰.


DIRECT SOLUTION CHECK
Solving the system directly gives
x=[1,0,−1]ᵀ.
Check:
5(1)−2(−1)=7,
3(1)+5(0)+(−1)=2,
−3(0)+4(−1)=−4.
Thus the SOR limit is correct.


INDEPENDENT CONVERGENCE CHECK
For A=D+L+U, the successive SOR iteration matrix is
B_SOR=(D+ωL)⁻¹[(1−ω)D−ωU].
For this matrix and ω=1.10,
ρ(B_SOR)≈0.64929461<1.
Therefore the chosen SOR splitting converges. This is an independent matrix-level check; it is not inferred merely from the first four rows.


FINAL ANSWER
After the required first four iterations,
x⁽⁴⁾≈[0.87253314, 0.16316725, −0.84088407]ᵀ.
Continuing SOR with ω=1.10 converges to
x=[1,0,−1]ᵀ.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
Writing the Gauss–Seidel target gᵢ separates the linear equation from the relaxation operation.
Applying (1−ω)x_old+ωgᵢ shows exactly what over-relaxation changes compared with Gauss–Seidel.
Using each newly relaxed value immediately preserves the successive-displacement SOR method specified by the instructor.
Showing at least four rows answers the exam instruction; continuing beyond four distinguishes “minimum required work” from “converged solution.”
Residual and direct-solution checks verify the limit against the original system.
The spectral-radius check verifies convergence of the actual ω=1.10 iteration operator.


MATH QA
PASS — instructor SOR formula alignment.
PASS — ω=1.10 over-relaxation correctly applied.
PASS — iterations 1–6 reproduce the frozen values.
PASS — iteration 4=[0.872533141,0.163167250,−0.840884067]ᵀ.
PASS — iteration 56 reproduces the frozen converged vector.
PASS — direct solution [1,0,−1]ᵀ.
PASS — final max residual ≈1.69×10⁻¹⁰.
PASS — ρ(B_SOR)≈0.64929461<1.


RELATED COURSE CONTEXT
HRP §4.7.3 provides the SOR recurrence and Example 4.7.4 with ω=1.25.
NMA-Q-0089 in this Batch 02 is the Gauss–Seidel counterpart; setting ω=1 in the SOR formula recovers the ordinary successive update.
Other SOR records in the master set show why an unspecified ω or a divergent splitting cannot be silently promoted to an SOR result.


COMMON MISTAKES
Computing a Gauss–Seidel value and forgetting the relaxation blend with the old component.
Using old x₁ when updating x₂ or old x₂ when updating x₃; SOR here uses successive displacement.
Treating four iterations as convergence merely because the question says minimum four iterations.
Using ω=0.10 instead of 1.10.
Applying the relaxation factor twice to the same correction.
Checking only iterate change and not the original residual.
Assuming every ω>1 automatically converges; convergence must be checked for the actual system/splitting.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
For successive SOR,
xᵢ⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾=(1−ω)xᵢ⁽ᵏ⁾+(ω/aᵢᵢ)[bᵢ−Σ_{j<i}aᵢⱼxⱼ⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾−Σ_{j>i}aᵢⱼxⱼ⁽ᵏ⁾],
with ω=1.10 and x⁽⁰⁾=0.
The updates are based on
x₁=(7+2x₃)/5,
x₂=(2−3x₁−x₃)/5,
x₃=(−4+3x₂)/4.
The first four SOR iterates are
x⁽¹⁾=[1.540000,−0.576400,−1.575530]ᵀ,
x⁽²⁾=[0.6927668,0.387030512,−0.623146828]ᵀ,
x⁽³⁾=[1.196538716,−0.251326302,−1.245029516]ᵀ,
x⁽⁴⁾=[0.872533141,0.163167250,−0.840884067]ᵀ.
Continuing the iteration gives
x→[1,0,−1]ᵀ.
The direct substitution residual is zero for [1,0,−1]ᵀ.

questions.question:
Solve by SOR:
x1+x2+2x3-x4=5;
3x1+2x2+x3+4x4=2;
x1-2x2+3x3+x4=1;
x1+3x2-2x3-3x4=5.


SOURCE-RECOVERY OUTCOME
The frozen occurrence supplies the system and method name SOR but no relaxation factor omega. The frozen source-lock also records that the printed ordering/splitting is not convergent. No authoritative duplicate or course annotation was recovered that supplies an intended omega or alternate equation ordering. Therefore no unique source-supported SOR sequence can be promoted.


WHAT SOR REQUIRES
For A=D+L+U, a standard SOR iteration can be written


(D+omega L)x^(k+1)=[(1-omega)D-omega U]x^(k)+omega b,


or componentwise


x_i^(k+1)=(1-omega)x_i^(k)+(omega/a_ii)[b_i-sum_(j<i)a_ij x_j^(k+1)-sum_(j>i)a_ij x_j^(k)].


Thus the numerical sequence depends on the relaxation factor omega and on the ordering/splitting.


PRINTED-ORDER CONVERGENCE DIAGNOSTIC
For the matrix


A=[[1,1,2,-1],[3,2,1,4],[1,-2,3,1],[1,3,-2,-3]],


ordinary Gauss-Seidel corresponds to omega=1. Its iteration matrix has spectral radius


rho(T_GS)≈3.3976556517>1.


Therefore the printed-order Gauss-Seidel core diverges rather than supplying a convergent baseline for SOR.


A numerical diagnostic scan over standard positive omega values 0<omega<2 did not find rho(T_SOR)<1 for the printed ordering; as omega approaches 0 the spectral radius approaches 1 from above. This diagnostic is mathematical QA only, not a source-authorized replacement ordering.


ALGEBRAIC REFERENCE SOLUTION — NOT AN SOR RESULT
The system itself has the exact solution


boxed: x=[1,1,1,-1]^T.


Substitution gives Ax-b=0 exactly.


This reference vector is useful for residual checks if a valid SOR policy is later recovered, but it must not be represented as though SOR produced it under the missing source settings.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Identify omega before iterating because different relaxation factors produce different SOR sequences.
2. Check convergence of the chosen splitting; method names alone do not guarantee convergence.
3. Keep the direct algebraic solution separate from the requested iterative method.
4. Do not invent row reordering, scaling or omega merely to make the iteration converge.
5. Promote an SOR numerical answer only after authoritative settings or a governed selection criterion are available.


MATH QA
PASS — exact direct solution is [1,1,1,-1]^T with zero residual.
PASS — frozen printed-order Gauss-Seidel spectral radius is approximately 3.3976556517>1.
PASS — omega is absent from the source.
PASS — no authoritative alternate ordering/splitting was recovered.
PASS — no SOR numerical value is promoted.


COMMON MISTAKES
Assuming omega=1 without saying so; that is Gauss-Seidel, not a uniquely specified SOR task.
Choosing an arbitrary omega such as 1.1 because another problem used it.
Reporting the direct solution as an SOR result.
Ignoring a divergent iteration matrix.
Reordering equations silently to force diagonal dominance.
Claiming 0<omega<2 guarantees convergence for every matrix; such guarantees require additional matrix conditions.
