questions.question: Adams–Moulton Method.
questions.student_view:
For y′=f(t,y), a multistep method uses several previously known derivative values. The Adams–Moulton corrector is implicit because f_{n+1}=f(t_{n+1},y_{n+1}) depends on the unknown future value. A predictor first estimates y_{n+1}; that predicted value supplies f_{n+1}, after which the implicit corrector improves the estimate.


FOUR-STEP PAIR FROM THE REGISTERED COURSE NOTES
Let f_n=f(t_n,y_n)=y′_n and use equally spaced points with step h.


Predictor (four-step Adams–Bashforth):
y_{n+1}^{(P)} = y_n + (h/24)[55f_n − 59f_{n−1} + 37f_{n−2} − 9f_{n−3}].


Evaluate
f_{n+1}^{(P)} = f(t_{n+1},y_{n+1}^{(P)}).


Corrector (four-step Adams–Moulton):
y_{n+1}^{(C)} = y_n + (h/24)[9f_{n+1}^{(P)} + 19f_n − 5f_{n−1} + f_{n−2}].


The corrector can be iterated again by recomputing f_{n+1} from the corrected y_{n+1} if a tighter implicit solve is required.


SOURCE DERIVATION IDEA
Pandey begins with y_{n+1}−y_n=∫_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}}f(t,y)dt and substitutes Newton’s backward interpolation expansion for f. Integrating the backward-difference polynomial gives the Adams coefficients. Neglecting the higher backward-difference remainder yields the practical predictor/corrector pair above.


STARTING VALUES — IMPORTANT
A four-step method cannot begin from y_0 alone. Values y_1,y_2,y_3 (or equivalent derivative history) are needed before the recurrence can be used. They are normally supplied by an accurate one-step method such as classical RK4 or by given tabulated starting values. This requirement is part of the frozen answer and must not be hidden.


ALGORITHM
1. Obtain y_0,y_1,y_2,y_3 at equally spaced t-values, usually with RK4 if they are not given.
2. Store f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3.
3. Use the Adams–Bashforth predictor to compute y_{n+1}^{(P)}.
4. Compute f_{n+1}^{(P)}.
5. Apply the Adams–Moulton corrector.
6. Optionally repeat the corrector until successive corrected values meet the tolerance.
7. Advance the history window and continue.


WHY THIS METHOD IS USEFUL
After the startup cost, each new step reuses old function evaluations, so multistep predictor–corrector schemes can be efficient. The trade-off is dependence on a history of previous points and reduced convenience when step sizes change frequently.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Calling the explicit predictor itself “Adams–Moulton”; it is the Adams–Bashforth predictor paired with the implicit Adams–Moulton corrector.
• Forgetting the h/24 factor.
• Using wrong coefficients or wrong time ordering.
• Attempting a four-step recurrence without three additional starting values.
• Computing f_{n+1} from y_n instead of the predicted/corrected future value.
• Treating the corrector as explicit without evaluating the future derivative.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
For y′=f(t,y) with equal step h, the four-step Adams predictor–corrector pair is
P: y_{n+1}=y_n+(h/24)(55f_n−59f_{n−1}+37f_{n−2}−9f_{n−3}),
C: y_{n+1}=y_n+(h/24)(9f_{n+1}+19f_n−5f_{n−1}+f_{n−2}).
The predictor gives an estimate of y_{n+1}; use it to evaluate f_{n+1}, then apply the implicit Adams–Moulton corrector. Because it is a four-step method, y_1,y_2,y_3 must be supplied or generated first, commonly with RK4.


SEMANTIC MATH COLOR / PATTERN MAP
step_size → h; history_values → y_n,y_{n−1},…; history_slopes → f_n,f_{n−1},…; predictor → y_{n+1}^{(P)}; future_slope → f_{n+1}; corrector → y_{n+1}^{(C)}.


VISUAL MODEL
Panel A: four known history points and one future point. Panel B: predictor arrow using 55,−59,37,−9 coefficients. Panel C: future slope evaluation. Panel D: corrector arrow using 9,19,−5,1 coefficients. Interactive focus: toggle one or repeated corrector passes and show their effect.


AUDIT NOTES

questions.question: What is the basic difference between the one-step and multistep methods? Derive the predictor as well as corrector formulas for Adams–Moulton Method.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Frozen status: SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. Exact occurrence: P2-PROV-2019-SPRING-Q5A, printed 5(a), 7 marks. The registered instructor notes NMA-SRC-LECTURE-HRP-001, PDF pp.102–109 / printed pp.97–104, directly derive the four-step Adams predictor–corrector pair from backward-difference interpolation and show RK4 generation of starting values. Because the requested theory/formulas are directly present in the registered course notes, final provenance is DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION. The explicit predictor is the four-step Adams–Bashforth member of the pair; the implicit corrector is the four-step Adams–Moulton formula.


ONE-STEP METHOD
A one-step method computes yₙ₊₁ using information at the current point (xₙ,yₙ), possibly through internal stage evaluations. Euler and Runge–Kutta methods are standard examples. They are self-starting once the initial condition is known.


MULTISTEP METHOD
A multistep method computes yₙ₊₁ using several previously computed solution/derivative values, for example fₙ,fₙ₋₁,fₙ₋₂,… . Adams methods are multistep methods. They require sufficient starting values, commonly generated by a one-step method such as RK4.


DERIVATION SETUP
For y′=f(x,y) with equally spaced x-values xₙ=x₀+nh,
yₙ₊₁−yₙ = ∫(xₙ to xₙ₊₁) f(x,y) dx.
Put x=xₙ+sh, so dx=h ds and s runs from 0 to 1:
yₙ₊₁=yₙ+h∫₀¹ f(xₙ+sh) ds.
Approximate f by an interpolation polynomial through stored derivative values and integrate the polynomial term-by-term.


ADAMS FOUR-STEP PREDICTOR
Using the backward-difference interpolation based on fₙ,fₙ₋₁,fₙ₋₂,fₙ₋₃ and integrating over one forward step gives the explicit predictor
boxed: yₙ₊₁^P = yₙ + h[55fₙ−59fₙ₋₁+37fₙ₋₂−9fₙ₋₃]/24.
Because the right side uses only known previous derivative values, this is a predictor. In standard terminology it is the four-step Adams–Bashforth formula used in the Adams predictor–corrector pair.


ADAMS–MOULTON CORRECTOR
After predicting yₙ₊₁^P, evaluate
fₙ₊₁^P=f(xₙ₊₁,yₙ₊₁^P).
Integrating the interpolation formula that includes the new endpoint derivative gives the implicit corrector
boxed: yₙ₊₁^C = yₙ + h[9fₙ₊₁^P+19fₙ−5fₙ₋₁+fₙ₋₂]/24.
The corrected value may be used to recompute fₙ₊₁ and, when required, the correction can be iterated.


WHY A PREDICTOR IS NEEDED
The Adams–Moulton formula contains fₙ₊₁, but fₙ₊₁ depends on the unknown yₙ₊₁. The explicit Adams–Bashforth formula supplies an initial predicted yₙ₊₁^P so the endpoint derivative can be estimated and inserted into the corrector.


STARTING VALUES
The four-step predictor needs y and f data at four consecutive points before the multistep recurrence can begin. The registered instructor notes demonstrate generating the required starters by RK4. No numerical starter values are needed in this theory question.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Start from the exact integral identity yₙ₊₁−yₙ=∫f dx.
2. Use equal-step interpolation of derivative values because Adams coefficients assume constant h.
3. Integrate the interpolating polynomial to obtain the fixed rational coefficients.
4. Predict first because the implicit corrector needs an endpoint derivative.
5. Use a self-starting method such as RK4 to generate initial multistep history.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Calling the predictor itself an Adams–Moulton formula; the standard explicit predictor is Adams–Bashforth.
• Omitting the factor h/24.
• Using coefficients 55,−59,37,−9 in the corrector.
• Evaluating fₙ₊₁ before a value of yₙ₊₁ has been predicted.
• Forgetting that multistep methods require stored starting history.
• Applying the stated fixed-coefficient formulas to unequal step sizes without re-derivation.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
One-step methods use the current point to advance one step and are self-starting; multistep methods reuse several previous derivative/solution values and therefore need starter values. For y′=f(x,y), integrate yₙ₊₁−yₙ over one step and approximate f by the backward-difference interpolant. The four-step Adams predictor–corrector pair is
Predictor: boxed yₙ₊₁^P=yₙ+h(55fₙ−59fₙ₋₁+37fₙ₋₂−9fₙ₋₃)/24.
Corrector: boxed yₙ₊₁^C=yₙ+h(9fₙ₊₁^P+19fₙ−5fₙ₋₁+fₙ₋₂)/24.
The required starting values are commonly generated by RK4.

questions.question: Derive the formula of Adams–Moulton Method. Use it to find y(0.8) for dy/dx=1+y², where y=0 when x=0.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT AND LIMITATION
The frozen U06 record is SOURCE_LOCK_PARTIAL. The 2019 internal-exam occurrence supplies the IVP and target y(0.8), but it does not print the step size h. The registered HRP course notes (predictor–corrector / Adams–Moulton section, PDF pp.102–109, printed pp.97–104) derive the four-step Adams predictor/corrector pair from Newton backward differences and demonstrate RK4 startup. Therefore the derivation is course-supported, while a unique numerical y(0.8) is not. The frozen audit retains h=0.2 only as a conditional study path.


PREREQUISITES
First-order IVP y'=f(x,y); equally spaced grid x_n=x_0+nh; function values f_n=f(x_n,y_n); Newton backward interpolation; numerical integration of an interpolating polynomial; multistep startup values.


WHY ADAMS METHODS ARE MULTISTEP
From the IVP,
y_(n+1)-y_n = integral_(x_n)^(x_(n+1)) f(x,y(x)) dx.
A one-step method approximates this integral using information local to the present step. Adams methods instead approximate f by an interpolation polynomial built from several stored f-values, so past derivative information is reused. That is why a four-step formula cannot begin from y_0 alone: enough equally spaced starter values must already exist.


FOUR-STEP ADAMS–BASHFORTH PREDICTOR — DERIVATION
Set s=(x-x_n)/h, so dx=h ds and the next step corresponds to s from 0 to 1. Using Newton's backward interpolation about x_n,
f(x) = f_n + s nabla f_n + s(s+1)/2! nabla²f_n + s(s+1)(s+2)/3! nabla³f_n + ... .
Integrating from s=0 to 1 gives


y_(n+1)^P = y_n + h[ f_n + (1/2)nabla f_n + (5/12)nabla²f_n + (3/8)nabla³f_n ].


Use
nabla f_n=f_n-f_(n-1),
nabla²f_n=f_n-2f_(n-1)+f_(n-2),
nabla³f_n=f_n-3f_(n-1)+3f_(n-2)-f_(n-3).
Collecting coefficients gives


y_(n+1)^P = y_n + (h/24)[55f_n - 59f_(n-1) + 37f_(n-2) - 9f_(n-3)].


This is the source-registered four-step Adams predictor.


FOUR-STEP ADAMS–MOULTON CORRECTOR — DERIVATION
For the implicit corrector, interpolate through the new derivative f_(n+1) and three recent values. Equivalently expand backward about x_(n+1), integrate backward-difference terms over the single interval, and simplify. This gives


y_(n+1)^C = y_n + (h/24)[9f_(n+1) + 19f_n - 5f_(n-1) + f_(n-2)].


Because f_(n+1)=f(x_(n+1),y_(n+1)) contains the unknown new y, the formula is implicit. Predictor–corrector use makes it practical: first compute y_(n+1)^P, evaluate
f_(n+1)^P=f(x_(n+1),y_(n+1)^P),
then perform the source-demonstrated correction


y_(n+1)^C = y_n + (h/24)[9f_(n+1)^P +19f_n -5f_(n-1)+f_(n-2)].


WHY THE PREDICTOR IS NEEDED
The corrector needs a derivative at the unknown future point. The explicit predictor supplies a provisional future y and therefore a provisional future slope. It is not an unrelated second method; it supplies the missing future information needed to evaluate the implicit Adams–Moulton correction.


SOURCE-LIMITED NUMERICAL PART
For y'=1+y², y(0)=0, the exact continuous IVP is y=tan x, but exact-solution knowledge does not determine the examiner's intended discrete step size. The four-step Adams formula requires four equally spaced y/f values before the x=0.8 prediction. Since h is not printed, there are multiple possible startup grids and therefore no unique canonical Adams numerical answer.


CONDITIONAL STUDY PATH — h=0.2 ONLY
The following path reproduces the frozen independent audit and MUST remain labelled conditional, not canonical.


Assume h=0.2 and use RK4 starters as demonstrated by the registered course procedure:
y_0=y(0)=0,
y_1=y(0.2)=0.20270740808053467,
y_2=y(0.4)=0.4227889928132791,
y_3=y(0.6)=0.6841334019907197.


With f_i=1+y_i², apply the four-step predictor at x_4=0.8:
y_4^P = y_3 + (0.2/24)[55f_3-59f_2+37f_1-9f_0]
       = 1.0234348818417511.


Then
f_4^P=1+(y_4^P)²,
and one four-step Adams–Moulton correction gives
y_4^C = y_3 + (0.2/24)[9f_4^P+19f_3-5f_2+f_1]
       = 1.0296904017413269.


Conditional result:
y(0.8) ≈ 1.029690402  IF h=0.2 with RK4 startup and one correction.


INDEPENDENT QA
Exact IVP reference: tan(0.8)=1.0296385570503641.
Conditional Adams error = 1.0296904017413269 - 1.0296385570503641 ≈ 5.18447e-5.
The predictor and corrector exactly match the frozen independent audit values.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Integrate y'=f over one step because Adams formulas approximate the step integral, not y directly.
2. Use backward interpolation because past f-values are already available at equally spaced points.
3. Expand backward differences to obtain the 55,-59,37,-9 predictor coefficients instead of merely memorizing them.
4. Include f_(n+1) in Adams–Moulton because the corrector gains accuracy by using future-end information.
5. Predict before correcting because f_(n+1) is initially unknown.
6. Refuse to promote y(0.8) numerically without h because the startup grid and all derivative history depend on it.


MATH QA
PASS — source-registered predictor coefficients: 55,-59,37,-9 over 24.
PASS — source-registered corrector coefficients: 9,19,-5,1 over 24.
PASS — four equally spaced starter values are identified as a method requirement.
PASS — conditional h=0.2 RK4 starters match frozen audit.
PASS — conditional predictor=1.0234348818417511.
PASS — conditional one-correction value=1.0296904017413269.
PASS — exact reference tan(0.8)=1.0296385570503641.
PASS — missing h remains a source limitation; no canonical numerical value promoted.


COMMON MISTAKES
Treating h=0.2 as printed data when it is not.
Starting a four-step method with only y(0).
Using non-equally-spaced starter values.
Using the corrector before obtaining a future slope estimate.
Mixing Milne and Adams coefficients.
Repeatedly correcting without stating that the registered course example demonstrates one correction.
Calling the conditional numerical value canonical.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
For equally spaced data, integrate Newton backward interpolation of f over one step. The four-step Adams predictor is


y_(n+1)^P=y_n+(h/24)[55f_n-59f_(n-1)+37f_(n-2)-9f_(n-3)].


Using the predicted future slope, the Adams–Moulton corrector is


y_(n+1)^C=y_n+(h/24)[9f_(n+1)^P+19f_n-5f_(n-1)+f_(n-2)].


Four equally spaced starters are required. In the printed problem y'=1+y², y(0)=0, y(0.8) cannot be uniquely computed because h is omitted. Conditional only, if h=0.2 and RK4 supplies the starters, one correction gives y(0.8)≈1.029690402.

questions.question: If y′=2e^x y and y(0)=2, find y(4) using Adams predictor–correction formula by calculating y(1), y(2), and y(3) using Euler’s modified formula.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_REVISED. The question fixes unit spacing h=1 through the requested starter points x=1,2,3. Registered HRP notes identify modified Euler with the second-order RK/Heun formula and derive the four-step Adams predictor plus Adams–Moulton corrector. The frozen audit also flags that h=1 is numerically unreliable for this rapidly growing IVP.


MODIFIED EULER / HEUN STARTERS
For f(x,y)=2e^x y and h=1, use
Predictor: y*=y_n+h f(x_n,y_n),
Corrector: y_(n+1)=y_n+(h/2)[f(x_n,y_n)+f(x_n+h,y*)].
Applying the course formula gives the source-locked starter sequence:
y0=2.000000000 at x=0,
y1≈20.30969097075427 at x=1,
y2≈1041.448696596255 at x=2,
y3≈338784.209999216 at x=3.
These enormous values are a warning that the coarse step is struggling with rapid exponential growth.


FOUR-STEP ADAMS PREDICTOR
Let f_i=f(x_i,y_i). With h=1,
y4^P = y3 + [55f3−59f2+37f1−9f0]/24.
Using the starter values,
boxed: y4^P≈31,489,155.240805995.


ONE ADAMS–MOULTON CORRECTION
The registered four-step corrector is
y4^C = y3 + [9f4^P+19f3−5f2+f1]/24,
where f4^P=f(4,y4^P).
One source-demonstrated correction gives
boxed: y(4)≈1.3005468484852846×10^9.


EXACT-SOLUTION QA
The ODE is separable:
dy/y=2e^x dx,
ln y=2e^x+C.
Using y(0)=2 gives
y(x)=2 exp[2(e^x−1)].
Thus
y(4)≈7.174499256119123×10^46.
The Adams value is therefore catastrophically inaccurate for the prescribed h=1. This does not make the arithmetic wrong; it demonstrates that the exam-prescribed coarse grid is unsuitable for this rapidly growing solution.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Generate three additional equally spaced starter values because a four-step Adams method needs four previous function values.
2. Use the registered modified-Euler/Heun starter method exactly as requested by the paper.
3. Evaluate f_i=2e^{x_i}y_i at each starter; Adams advances from stored derivative values.
4. Compute the explicit predictor before the implicit corrector because the corrector needs f at x4.
5. Apply only the source-demonstrated single correction unless another iteration policy is specified.
6. Compare with the exact IVP to diagnose the numerical reliability of h=1 rather than hiding the large error.


COMMON MISTAKES
Using RK4 starters when the question explicitly asks for modified Euler.
Using h=0.1 or another smaller step to make the answer look better.
Forgetting the factor e^x in f=2e^x y.
Feeding y4^P directly as the corrected value without evaluating f4^P.
Repeatedly correcting without a stated course policy.
Treating the huge discrepancy from the exact solution as an arithmetic failure instead of a step-size reliability issue.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Modified Euler/Heun with h=1 gives y1≈20.309691, y2≈1041.448697, y3≈338784.2100. The four-step Adams predictor
y4^P=y3+[55f3−59f2+37f1−9f0]/24
gives y4^P≈3.148915524×10^7. One Adams–Moulton correction
y4^C=y3+[9f4^P+19f3−5f2+f1]/24
gives
boxed: y(4)≈1.300546848×10^9.
However the exact IVP has y(4)≈7.174499×10^46, so h=1 is numerically unreliable for this rapidly growing problem.

questions.question:
The deflection of a cantilever beam is governed by
d⁴y/dx⁴ + 81y = 729x²,
with fixed-end conditions y(0)=y′(0)=0 and free-end conditions y″(1)=y‴(1)=0. Find the deflection at the pivotal mesh points for h=1/3.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The exam scans had an ambiguous free-end argument glyph, but Dr. Hem Raj Pandey’s course notes Problem 28 reproduce the exact differential equation, h=1/3 and the engineering boundary conditions explicitly as y(0)=y′(0)=0 and y″(1)=y‴(1)=0. This resolves the frozen review issue.
Problem 28 is an instructor-authored exact problem rather than a worked solution, so the primary provenance tier is COURSE_METHOD_MATCHED. The finite-difference reconstruction below is independently checked.


WHAT IS BEING ASKED?
Approximate y at x=1/3, 2/3 and 1 by replacing the fourth derivative with a centered five-point stencil. The derivative boundary conditions require ghost nodes outside the physical beam; those ghost values must be eliminated using the boundary conditions before solving for the three physical unknowns.


PREREQUISITES
Centered finite differences; fourth-derivative five-point stencil; first-, second- and third-derivative central formulas; ghost nodes; solution of a 3×3 linear system; cantilever fixed/free boundary interpretation.


INTUITION
The ODE is fourth order, so its centered stencil reaches two nodes to either side. Near x=0 and x=1, that stencil extends outside the beam. Instead of inventing those outside values, the four physical boundary conditions determine them. Once the ghost nodes are eliminated, only y₁, y₂ and y₃ remain.


MESH AND NOTATION
h=1/3,
x₀=0, x₁=1/3, x₂=2/3, x₃=1.
Let yᵢ≈y(xᵢ), with y₀=0.
Ghost nodes are y₋₁ to the left and y₄,y₅ to the right.


FOURTH-DERIVATIVE STENCIL
At node i,
y⁽⁴⁾(xᵢ) ≈ [yᵢ₋₂ −4yᵢ₋₁ +6yᵢ −4yᵢ₊₁ +yᵢ₊₂]/h⁴.


Because h=1/3, 1/h⁴=81. Substituting in
y⁽⁴⁾+81y=729x²
and dividing by 81 gives
yᵢ₋₂ −4yᵢ₋₁ +7yᵢ −4yᵢ₊₁ +yᵢ₊₂ = 9xᵢ².     (1)


BOUNDARY CONDITIONS → GHOST NODES
Fixed end x=0:
y₀=0.
Using y′(0)≈(y₁−y₋₁)/(2h)=0,
y₋₁=y₁.                                                     (2)


Free end x=1:
Using y″(1)≈(y₄−2y₃+y₂)/h²=0,
y₄=2y₃−y₂.                                                  (3)


Using the centered third derivative
y‴(1)≈[y₅−2y₄+2y₂−y₁]/(2h³)=0,
y₅=2y₄−2y₂+y₁.                                             (4)


WHY THESE GHOST RELATIONS MATTER
Equations (2)–(4) translate slope, zero bending moment and zero shear into algebraic relations that remove every outside-grid unknown. They are not extra physical deflection values; they are devices for enforcing the derivative boundary conditions while retaining centered stencils.


NODE EQUATION AT x₁=1/3
Equation (1) with i=1 gives
y₋₁−4y₀+7y₁−4y₂+y₃ = 9(1/3)² = 1.
Using y₀=0 and y₋₁=y₁:
8y₁−4y₂+y₃ = 1.                                            (5)


NODE EQUATION AT x₂=2/3
Equation (1) with i=2 gives
y₀−4y₁+7y₂−4y₃+y₄ = 9(2/3)² = 4.
Using y₀=0 and y₄=2y₃−y₂:
−4y₁+6y₂−2y₃ = 4.                                          (6)


NODE EQUATION AT x₃=1
Equation (1) with i=3 gives
y₁−4y₂+7y₃−4y₄+y₅ = 9.
Using (3) and (4):
2y₁−4y₂+3y₃ = 9.                                           (7)


SOLVE THE 3×3 SYSTEM
The system is
8y₁−4y₂+y₃=1,
−4y₁+6y₂−2y₃=4,
2y₁−4y₂+3y₃=9.


From (5),
y₃=1−8y₁+4y₂.


Substitute into (6):
12y₁−2y₂=6,
so
y₂=6y₁−3.                                                   (8)


Substitute y₃ from (5) into (7):
−11y₁+4y₂=3.                                                (9)


Using (8) in (9):
−11y₁+4(6y₁−3)=3,
13y₁=15,
so
y₁=15/13.


Then
y₂=6(15/13)−3=51/13,
and from (5),
y₃=97/13.


FINAL ANSWER
y(1/3)=15/13≈1.153846154,
y(2/3)=51/13≈3.923076923,
y(1)=97/13≈7.461538462.


MATH QA
PASS — substituting [15/13, 51/13, 97/13] into equations (5)–(7) gives exact residual [0,0,0].
PASS — h⁻⁴=81 is consistent with h=1/3.
PASS — fixed-end slope gives y₋₁=y₁.
PASS — free-end moment condition gives y₄=2y₃−y₂.
PASS — free-end shear condition gives y₅=2y₄−2y₂+y₁.
PASS — the source-resolved boundary conditions match cantilever mechanics: zero deflection/slope at the fixed end and zero moment/shear at the free end.


INDEPENDENT CONTINUOUS-BVP CHECK
Solving the continuous ODE with the same four boundary conditions gives approximately
y_exact(1/3)=1.093756748,
y_exact(2/3)=3.759337890,
y_exact(1)=7.060229430.
The h=1/3 finite-difference values therefore differ by about +0.06009, +0.16374 and +0.40131 respectively. This is consistent with a coarse mesh approximation and is a useful plausibility check; the exact continuous values do not replace the requested finite-difference answer.


WHY THE RESULT IS PLAUSIBLE
The loading term 729x² grows toward the free end, so the computed deflection increases monotonically from the fixed end to x=1. The ghost-node treatment enforces zero bending moment and shear without forcing zero deflection at the free end.


RELATED COURSE CONTEXT
HRP’s preceding finite-difference beam example demonstrates how fictitious/ghost points are eliminated by derivative boundary conditions.
NMA-Q-0136: Crank–Nicolson PDE record in Batch 01 uses the same general principle of turning differential relations into a linear algebra system.
Other Unit-6 BVP questions provide second-order boundary-value variants with simpler three-point stencils.


COMMON MISTAKES
Reading the ambiguous exam glyph as x=0 for all four boundary conditions; the instructor notes resolve the last two conditions at x=1.
Using 6yᵢ instead of 7yᵢ after adding the +81y term.
Using y₄=y₂, which is appropriate for a zero first derivative in a symmetric stencil, instead of the correct second-derivative condition y₄=2y₃−y₂.
Dropping the factor 2 in the centered third-derivative boundary relation.
Treating ghost nodes as additional independent unknowns instead of eliminating them.
Reporting only decimal values and hiding the exact fractions.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
With h=1/3,
y⁽⁴⁾ᵢ≈[yᵢ₋₂−4yᵢ₋₁+6yᵢ−4yᵢ₊₁+yᵢ₊₂]/h⁴.
Since 1/h⁴=81, the ODE becomes
yᵢ₋₂−4yᵢ₋₁+7yᵢ−4yᵢ₊₁+yᵢ₊₂=9xᵢ².


From the BCs:
y₋₁=y₁,
y₄=2y₃−y₂,
y₅=2y₄−2y₂+y₁.


At x=1/3, 2/3, 1:
8y₁−4y₂+y₃=1,
−4y₁+6y₂−2y₃=4,
2y₁−4y₂+3y₃=9.


Solving,
y₁=15/13, y₂=51/13, y₃=97/13.
Hence
y(1/3)≈1.153846,
y(2/3)≈3.923077,
y(1)≈7.461538.

questions.question:
A fixed beam of length 3 m is governed by
d⁴y/dx⁴+2y=x²/9+(2/3)x+4,
with y(0)=y′(0)=0 and y(3)=y′(3)=0. Find deflection at x=1 and x=2.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. The registered HRP notes reproduce this exact fixed–fixed beam worked example and solve it with h=1. The course example supplies the boundary treatment, fourth-derivative finite difference and resulting two-equation system, so this record qualifies as DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION.


MESH AND BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
With h=1:
x0=0, x1=1, x2=2, x3=3.
Let y_i=y(x_i). Given y0=0 and y3=0.
Centered slope conditions give
(y1−y_(−1))/(2h)=0 ⇒ y_(−1)=y1,
(y4−y2)/(2h)=0 ⇒ y4=y2.
The ghost values encode zero slope at the fixed ends.


FOURTH-DERIVATIVE STENCIL
For h=1,
y''''(x_i)≈y_(i−2)−4y_(i−1)+6y_i−4y_(i+1)+y_(i+2).


EQUATION AT x=1
The forcing is
1²/9+(2/3)(1)+4=43/9.
Thus
y_(−1)−4y0+6y1−4y2+y3+2y1=43/9.
Using y_(−1)=y1 and y0=y3=0:
9y1−4y2=43/9.


EQUATION AT x=2
The forcing is
2²/9+(2/3)(2)+4=52/9.
Thus
y0−4y1+6y2−4y3+y4+2y2=52/9.
Using y4=y2 and y0=y3=0:
−4y1+9y2=52/9.


DISCRETE SYSTEM
[9  −4][y1]=[43/9]
[−4  9][y2] [52/9]


Multiply by 9 if desired:
81y1−36y2=43,
−36y1+81y2=52.
Solving gives
boxed: y1=119/117≈1.017094017094017,
boxed: y2=128/117≈1.094017094017094.
Therefore y(1)=119/117 and y(2)=128/117.


INDEPENDENT CHECK
9(119/117)−4(128/117)=43/9 exactly.
−4(119/117)+9(128/117)=52/9 exactly.
The exact discrete residual is zero; the frozen floating audit reports max residual about 8.88×10^−16.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Choose h=1 because the 3 m span then has the two requested interior nodes x=1 and x=2, exactly as in the registered example.
2. Convert the slope boundary conditions to ghost-node equations before using the fourth-derivative stencil.
3. Use the centered fourth-derivative stencil because the governing beam equation is fourth order.
4. Evaluate the forcing separately at x=1 and x=2.
5. Substitute boundary/ghost values to reduce the problem to two unknowns.
6. Solve the 2×2 system and check its residual exactly.


COMMON MISTAKES
Using a second-derivative stencil for a fourth-order beam equation.
Ignoring the two slope boundary conditions.
Setting ghost values to zero instead of deriving them from y′=0.
Using 43/9 at both interior nodes.
Dropping the +2y term, which changes the diagonal coefficient from 9.
Calling x=1 and x=2 boundary points; they are the two interior mesh points.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
With h=1, the fourth-derivative stencil and zero-slope ghost relations y_(−1)=y1, y4=y2 give
9y1−4y2=43/9,
−4y1+9y2=52/9.
Solving,

questions.question:
State the different conditions/classes of solution of a partial differential equation. Using Crank–Nicolson method solve


∂u/∂t = ∂²u/∂x²,


u(x,0)=sin(πx), 0≤x≤1,
u(0,t)=u(1,t)=0.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT — FROZEN RECORD VS v1.2 RECOVERY
The frozen v1.1.0 record is SOURCE_LOCK_PARTIAL because its registered sources did not provide a Crank–Nicolson tableau and the exam wording itself does not prescribe Δx, Δt or a target time. That frozen status remains unchanged.


A deeper v1.2 Drive search recovered `pde_1.pdf`, Basic Numerical Methods §26.16.7, Example 26.68, whose problem is an exact match. Its solution explicitly chooses:
- h=Δx=1/4, k=Δt=1/8, r=k/h²=2, to compute t=1/8 in one step;
- h=1/4, k=1/16, r=1, to compute the same t=1/8 in two steps.


Therefore the mesh/time values are solution choices from the recovered reference, not values printed in the exam. Study View must say this explicitly.


IMPORTANT SOURCE-ERROR NOTE
The recovered example contains printed sign/arithmetic errors. Visual inspection of printed pp.26.66–26.67 confirms that the source builds asymmetric right-hand sides even though the initial condition sin(πx) and zero-end boundary conditions are symmetric about x=1/2. The printed asymmetric numerical values are therefore not copied into v1.2 Study View. The formula and chosen meshes are source-backed; the numerical systems below are independently corrected and checked.


PART A — PDE CLASSIFICATION / CONDITIONS
For a second-order linear PDE


A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + D u_x + E u_y + F u = G,


the source-backed discriminant classification is:
- elliptic if B²−4AC<0;
- parabolic if B²−4AC=0;
- hyperbolic if B²−4AC>0.


The heat equation u_t=u_xx is parabolic. A numerical heat-equation solution also requires an initial condition and boundary conditions. Here they are


u(x,0)=sin(πx),
u(0,t)=u(1,t)=0.


PART B — DERIVE THE CRANK–NICOLSON EQUATION
Let
x_i=i h,
t_j=j k,
u_i^j≈u(x_i,t_j),


and define
r=k/h²
because the diffusion coefficient is 1.


Crank–Nicolson evaluates the time derivative between levels j and j+1 and averages the spatial second derivative over both levels:


(u_i^(j+1)−u_i^j)/k
=1/2[(u_(i−1)^j−2u_i^j+u_(i+1)^j)/h²
     +(u_(i−1)^(j+1)−2u_i^(j+1)+u_(i+1)^(j+1))/h²].


Rearranging gives


−r u_(i−1)^(j+1)+(2+2r)u_i^(j+1)−r u_(i+1)^(j+1)
= r u_(i−1)^j+(2−2r)u_i^j+r u_(i+1)^j.


WHY IS IT IMPLICIT?
Unknown values at the new time level j+1 appear at neighboring spatial nodes, so each new row requires solving a tridiagonal linear system. This coupling is what gives Crank–Nicolson its strong stability behavior.


PART C — REFERENCE CHOICE 1: h=1/4, k=1/8, r=2
Interior nodes are
x₁=1/4, x₂=1/2, x₃=3/4.


Initial row:


U^0=[sin(π/4),sin(π/2),sin(3π/4)]^T
≈[0.7071067812,1,0.7071067812]^T.


Boundary values at x=0 and x=1 are zero for every time level.


For r=2, divide the general equation by 2:


−u_(i−1)^(j+1)+3u_i^(j+1)−u_(i+1)^(j+1)
=u_(i−1)^j−u_i^j+u_(i+1)^j.


At the first new row t=1/8:


3u₁−u₂ = 1−0.7071067812
          =0.2928932188,


−u₁+3u₂−u₃
=0.7071067812−1+0.7071067812
=0.4142135624,


−u₂+3u₃
=1−0.7071067812
=0.2928932188.


Solving gives


u(1/4,1/8)≈0.18469903,
u(1/2,1/8)≈0.26120387,
u(3/4,1/8)≈0.18469903.


The symmetry u₁=u₃ is preserved, as it must be.


PART D — REFERENCE CHOICE 2: h=1/4, k=1/16, r=1
For r=1,


−u_(i−1)^(j+1)+4u_i^(j+1)−u_(i+1)^(j+1)
=u_(i−1)^j+u_(i+1)^j.


First step, t=0→1/16:


4u₁−u₂=1,
−u₁+4u₂−u₃=2sin(π/4)=1.4142135624,
−u₂+4u₃=1.


Hence


U^1≈[0.38672954,0.54691816,0.38672954]^T.


Second step, t=1/16→1/8:


4u₁−u₂=0.54691816,
−u₁+4u₂−u₃=0.38672954+0.38672954=0.77345908,
−u₂+4u₃=0.54691816.


Therefore at t=1/8,


U^2≈[0.21150941,0.29911947,0.21150941]^T.


PART E — ANALYTICAL CHECK
For this continuous problem,


u(x,t)=e^(−π²t)sin(πx).


At t=1/8,


e^(−π²/8)≈0.2912129332,


so the exact interior row is approximately


[0.20591864,0.29121293,0.20591864]^T.


Comparison at t=1/8:
- one CN step with k=1/8: [0.18469903,0.26120387,0.18469903];
- two CN steps with k=1/16: [0.21150941,0.29911947,0.21150941];
- exact: [0.20591864,0.29121293,0.20591864].


The refined time step is closer to the exact solution, which is a useful independent QA check.


WHY THE RECOVERED BOOK NUMBERS WERE REJECTED
For symmetric initial data and symmetric zero boundaries, uniqueness of the discrete tridiagonal system implies a symmetric numerical row. Any source result with u(1/4,t)≠u(3/4,t) is immediately suspicious. Re-deriving the right-hand sides shows the printed reference changes required minus signs to plus signs; the resulting asymmetry is therefore a source arithmetic error, not a valid CN effect.


FINAL STUDENT-FACING ANSWER
The heat equation is parabolic. Under the recovered reference choice h=1/4, k=1/8 (r=2), Crank–Nicolson gives at t=1/8


u(1/4,1/8)≈0.184699,
u(1/2,1/8)≈0.261204,
u(3/4,1/8)≈0.184699.


If the smaller time step k=1/16 is used for two steps to the same t=1/8,


u(1/4,1/8)≈0.211509,
u(1/2,1/8)≈0.299119,
u(3/4,1/8)≈0.211509.


The exam itself does not uniquely prescribe h,k or target time, so these values must be labeled as the recovered reference’s explicit mesh choices, not as the only possible numerical table.


COMMON MISTAKES
- inventing Δx, Δt or a target time without labeling them as chosen assumptions;
- copying the recovered reference’s asymmetric printed numbers despite symmetric data;
- forgetting that Crank–Nicolson averages the spatial operator between two time levels;
- treating the implicit tridiagonal system as an explicit pointwise update;
- using r=k/h instead of r=k/h² for u_t=u_xx;
- dropping boundary contributions;
- failing to check symmetry;
- confusing PDE classification with boundary-condition type.

questions.question: Use Euler’s method to estimate y(0.4) when y′=x²+y², y(0)=0, h=0.2.
questions.student_view:
1. Euler formula
For y′=f(x,y), Euler’s method with step h is
y_(n+1)=y_n+h f(x_n,y_n).
Here f(x,y)=x²+y² and h=0.2.


2. Initial point
x₀=0, y₀=0.
f(x₀,y₀)=0²+0²=0.
Therefore
y₁=y₀+0.2(0)=0,
so at x₁=0.2, y(0.2)≈0.


3. Second step
At x₁=0.2, y₁=0:
f(0.2,0)=(0.2)²+0²=0.04.
Therefore
y₂=0+0.2(0.04)=0.008.
The new point is x₂=0.4.


FINAL ANSWER
y(0.4)≈0.008000 by Euler’s method.


INDEPENDENT CHECK
Direct independent application of the two stated Euler steps gives the sequence
(x,y)=(0,0) → (0.2,0) → (0.4,0.008).
This exactly reproduces the frozen numerical audit for the stated h=0.2.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Using y_(n+1)=y_n+h(x_n²+y_n²), h=0.2: y₁=0+0.2(0)=0 at x=0.2; y₂=0+0.2[(0.2)²+0²]=0.008 at x=0.4. Hence y(0.4)≈0.008.


WHY THE FIRST STEP DOES NOT CHANGE y
The differential equation’s slope at the initial point is f(0,0)=0. Euler follows the tangent slope over the first interval, so its first update is zero even though the slope becomes positive once x moves away from zero.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Using f(x_(n+1),y_n) instead of the explicit Euler slope f(x_n,y_n).
• Advancing x but forgetting to update the function evaluation point.
• Taking one step of size 0.4 even though h=0.2 is explicitly printed.

questions.question: Solve y′=x+y, y(0)=1 by Euler’s method. With step sizes 0.5 and 0.25 find y(1), compute errors, and compare with y=2e^x−x−1.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. HRP supplies forward Euler/RK1. The question prints both step sizes and the exact solution, so the numerical comparison is fully reproducible.


EULER FORMULA
For y'=f(x,y),
y_(n+1)=y_n+h f(x_n,y_n).
Here f=x+y.


CASE 1: h=0.5
x0=0, y0=1.
y1=1+0.5(0+1)=1.5 at x=0.5.
y2=1.5+0.5(0.5+1.5)=2.5 at x=1.
Thus
boxed: y_h=0.5(1)=2.5.


CASE 2: h=0.25
x0=0, y0=1.
y1=1+0.25(1)=1.25 at x=0.25.
y2=1.25+0.25(0.25+1.25)=1.625 at x=0.5.
y3=1.625+0.25(0.5+1.625)=2.15625 at x=0.75.
y4=2.15625+0.25(0.75+2.15625)=2.8828125 at x=1.
Thus
boxed: y_h=0.25(1)=2.8828125.


EXACT VALUE AND ERRORS
The supplied exact solution gives
y(1)=2e−2≈3.43656365691809.
Signed errors numerical−exact:
E_0.5=2.5−3.43656365691809≈−0.93656365691809.
E_0.25=2.8828125−3.43656365691809≈−0.55375115691809.
Absolute errors are about 0.936564 and 0.553751.
Halving h reduces the error, as expected for a first-order method. The coarse-step error ratio is about 1.69 rather than exactly 2; the theoretical factor approaches 2 only in the asymptotic small-h regime.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Use the same initial value and target x=1 for both grids so the error comparison is fair.
2. Recompute the full Euler path when h changes; intermediate nodes differ.
3. Use the left-end slope f(x_n,y_n) because this is forward Euler.
4. Compare both answers with the supplied exact solution using one consistent error convention.
5. Interpret refinement qualitatively as first order without forcing the coarse-grid ratio to equal exactly two.


COMMON MISTAKES
Using the improved/modified Euler formula instead of forward Euler.
Using the h=0.5 intermediate value inside the h=0.25 grid.
Evaluating f at x_(n+1) instead of x_n.
Comparing the two numerical answers to each other instead of to the exact solution.
Forgetting the sign convention when reporting error.
Claiming halving h must produce exactly half the error for these coarse grids.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Euler: y_(n+1)=y_n+h(x_n+y_n).
For h=0.5: y(0.5)=1.5 and boxed y(1)=2.5.
For h=0.25: y(0.25)=1.25, y(0.5)=1.625, y(0.75)=2.15625, boxed y(1)=2.8828125.
Exact y(1)=2e−2≈3.436563657. Hence errors are about −0.936563657 and −0.553751157 respectively. The smaller step reduces the error, consistent with Euler’s first-order accuracy.

questions.question:
Solve by Euler’s modified method
dy/dx=x+y,
y(0)=0,
and compute y(0.2) and y(0.4).
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
HRP Example 5.4.2 supplies the instructor’s Heun / second-order Runge–Kutta formula:
k₁=h f(x_n,y_n),
k₂=h f(x_n+h,y_n+k₁),
y_{n+1}=y_n+(k₁+k₂)/2.
The exact exam ODE is not the teacher’s worked example, so provenance remains COURSE_METHOD_MATCHED.


STEP-SIZE AUDIT
The exam wording does not explicitly print h. Because it asks for successive values at x=0.2 and x=0.4 starting from x=0, v1.2 interprets h=0.2. This is an explicit inference retained in both Study and Audit; it is not silently promoted to frozen source data.


PREREQUISITES
Initial-value ODEs; Euler predictor; slope f(x,y); trapezoidal averaging of two slopes; local/global error concepts.


METHOD INTUITION
Ordinary Euler uses only the slope at the beginning of a step. Modified Euler/Heun first predicts an endpoint with that slope, evaluates a second slope at the predicted endpoint, then advances using the average of the two slopes. This corrects much of the one-sided bias of simple Euler while keeping a two-stage calculation.


SETUP
f(x,y)=x+y,
h=0.2,
(x₀,y₀)=(0,0).


STEP 1: x=0 TO x=0.2
Initial slope stage:
k₁=h f(x₀,y₀)
=0.2(0+0)
=0.


Euler predictor:
y_predict=y₀+k₁=0.
Predicted endpoint is (0.2,0).


Endpoint slope stage:
k₂=h f(x₀+h,y₀+k₁)
=0.2(0.2+0)
=0.04.


Corrected Heun update:
y₁=y₀+(k₁+k₂)/2
=0+(0+0.04)/2
=0.020000.


Therefore
y(0.2)≈0.020000.


STEP 2: x=0.2 TO x=0.4
Now (x₁,y₁)=(0.2,0.02).


Initial slope stage:
k₁=0.2(0.2+0.02)
=0.044.


Euler predictor:
y_predict=0.02+0.044
=0.064.


Endpoint stage at x=0.4:
k₂=0.2(0.4+0.064)
=0.0928.


Corrected update:
y₂=0.02+(0.044+0.0928)/2
=0.02+0.0684
=0.088400.


Therefore
y(0.4)≈0.088400.


EXACT-SOLUTION CHECK
Solve
y'−y=x.
Using an integrating factor gives
y=e^x−x−1
for y(0)=0.
Hence
y_exact(0.2)=e^0.2−1.2≈0.02140275816,
y_exact(0.4)=e^0.4−1.4≈0.09182469764.


Errors of the h=0.2 Heun approximation are approximately
at x=0.2: 0.020000−0.02140275816=−0.00140275816,
at x=0.4: 0.088400−0.09182469764=−0.00342469764.
The numerical values are below the exact curve here, but they are close and improve substantially over a single-slope Euler interpretation at the same step size.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
Declaring h=0.2 makes the inferred step explicit and auditable.
The predictor supplies an estimate of the endpoint state so a second slope can be evaluated.
Averaging k₁ and k₂ is what distinguishes Heun/modified Euler from ordinary Euler.
Carrying y₁ into the second step ensures the requested y(0.4) is obtained successively rather than as an independent one-step jump.
The exact IVP solution provides an independent mathematical check but does not replace the requested numerical method.


MATH QA
PASS — conditional step h=0.2 matches target spacing.
PASS — step 1 k₁=0, k₂=0.04, y(0.2)=0.02.
PASS — step 2 k₁=0.044, predictor=0.064, k₂=0.0928, y(0.4)=0.0884.
PASS — frozen v1.1.0 values reproduced exactly.
PASS — exact solution y=e^x−x−1 satisfies y'=x+y and y(0)=0.
PASS — exact comparison values 0.02140275816 and 0.09182469764.


RELATED COURSE CONTEXT
HRP Example 5.4.2 is the direct instructor example of Heun’s second-order RK method.
NMA-Q-0167 in Batch 01 uses RK4 and provides a higher-order ODE comparison.
NMA-Q-0126 in this Batch 02 uses RK4 only as a startup mechanism for a multistep Adams method.


COMMON MISTAKES
Using h=0.2 without disclosing that it is inferred rather than printed.
Calling the predictor y_n+k₁ the final modified-Euler value.
Computing k₂ at (x_n+h,y_n) instead of the predicted state (x_n+h,y_n+k₁).
Forgetting the factor 1/2 in the average.
Starting the second step again from y(0)=0 instead of y(0.2)=0.02.
Mixing a variant modified-Euler iteration convention with the instructor’s Heun formula without disclosure.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Using the instructor Heun formula and h=0.2 inferred from the requested points,
k₁=h f(x_n,y_n),
k₂=h f(x_n+h,y_n+k₁),
y_{n+1}=y_n+(k₁+k₂)/2.
For f=x+y and (0,0):
k₁=0,
k₂=0.2(0.2)=0.04,
so
y(0.2)=0.02.
Next,
k₁=0.2(0.2+0.02)=0.044,
k₂=0.2(0.4+0.064)=0.0928,
so
y(0.4)=0.02+(0.044+0.0928)/2=0.0884.
Thus
y(0.2)≈0.0200,
y(0.4)≈0.0884.

questions.question: Solve the boundary value problem d²y/dx²=y with y(0)=0 and y(2)=3.627 by finite difference method.

This is a second-order boundary-value problem. The registered course material supports replacing y'' at an interior grid point x_i with the central-difference stencil
(y_{i+1}−2y_i+y_{i−1})/h².
For y''=y, the interior equation becomes
y_{i−1} − (2+h²)y_i + y_{i+1} = 0.
Boundary values y(0)=0 and y(2)=3.627 then enter the right-hand side of the resulting linear system.


Why the numerical answer is blocked
The occurrence does not specify h or the number of subintervals N. Those values determine the interior nodes and the dimension of the linear system. Choosing them would invent source data.


Exam-ready answer
Set x_i=ih on [0,2]. At every interior node use
y_{i−1} − (2+h²)y_i + y_{i+1}=0,
with y_0=0 and y_N=3.627. A unique numerical vector cannot be reported until h or N is supplied.

questions.question: A boundary value problem is y''+y+1=0 for 0≤x≤1, where y(0)=0 and y(1)=0. With h=0.5, use finite-difference method to determine y(0.5).
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. The exam fully specifies the interval, boundary values and h=0.5. HRP/Khadka supply the central finite-difference BVP method. There is only one interior node, x1=0.5.


DISCRETIZATION

y''(x1)≈(y2−2y1+y0)/h²=4(y2−2y1+y0).

INDEPENDENT CHECK

2. Use the centered second derivative because the governing ODE contains y''.
3. Insert the two Dirichlet boundary values before solving.

The frozen source-lock explicitly uses second-order one-sided derivative stencils at the Robin boundaries, derived from registered Taylor finite-difference formulas, and central second derivatives in the interior. Because another boundary derivative discretization could yield slightly different nodal values, this stencil choice remains explicit in Audit and Study View.


MESH
x_i=i h, i=0,...,4, with h=π/8≈0.392699081699.
Unknowns are y0,y1,y2,y3,y4 because the boundary conditions involve derivatives rather than prescribing endpoint values directly.


BOUNDARY EQUATIONS
At x=0, use second-order forward difference
y'(0)≈(-3y0+4y1-y2)/(2h).
From y0+y'(0)=2:
(2h−3)y0+4y1−y2=4h.
Numerically:
−2.2146018366 y0+4y1−y2=1.5707963268.


At x=π/2, use second-order backward difference

From y4+y'(π/2)=−1:

Numerically:
y2−4y3+3.7853981634 y4=−0.7853981634.

For i=1,2,3,
(y_(i−1)−2y_i+y_(i+1))/h²+y_i=0,
so
y_(i−1)+(h²−2)y_i+y_(i+1)=0.
Since h²≈0.15421256877, the central coefficient is h²−2≈−1.84578743123.


Thus the five-equation system is

y0+(h²−2)y1+y2=0,
y1+(h²−2)y2+y3=0,

2. Keep endpoint values as unknowns because Robin conditions mix y and y'.

questions.question: Discuss the Shooting method for boundary value problem with its algorithm.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. The registered Khadka Chapter 7 material explicitly describes the shooting algorithm and a worked example; HRP supplies the surrounding BVP/finite-difference context. The 2025 Internal printed question has a marks/choice-instruction conflict in its occurrence metadata, but the mathematical wording itself is clear and preserved.


CORE IDEA
Consider a second-order boundary-value problem
y''=F(x,y,y'),
y(a)=A,
y(b)=B.
Only y(a) is known at the left endpoint; the missing initial slope s=y'(a) is unknown. Shooting replaces the BVP by a family of initial-value problems and adjusts s until the computed terminal value at x=b matches B.


STEP 1 — CONVERT TO A FIRST-ORDER IVP SYSTEM
Set z=y'. Then
y'=z,
z'=F(x,y,z),
with initial data
y(a)=A,
z(a)=s.
For any trial slope s, an IVP solver such as RK4 can integrate this system from a to b.


STEP 2 — FIRST SHOT
Choose s1 and integrate to b. Let
Y1=y(b;s1),
R1=Y1−B.
R1 is the terminal mismatch. If |R1| is within the required tolerance, stop.


STEP 3 — SECOND SHOT
Choose another slope s2, integrate again, and compute
Y2=y(b;s2),
R2=Y2−B.
Two shots reveal how the terminal value changes with the guessed slope.


STEP 4 — UPDATE THE SLOPE
A standard interpolation/secant update is
s_new=s2−R2(s2−s1)/(R2−R1).
Equivalently,
s_new=s1+(B−Y1)(s2−s1)/(Y2−Y1).
This chooses the next initial slope by linearly interpolating the terminal mismatch to zero.


STEP 5 — REPEAT
Integrate again with s_new, compute R_new=y(b;s_new)−B, and repeat the slope update until the terminal mismatch is acceptably small.
For a linear BVP, dependence on the initial slope can be linear, so the interpolation of two accurate shots may determine the required slope in one update. For nonlinear BVPs, repeated shots are generally required.


ALGORITHM
Input: F, interval [a,b], boundary values A,B, two initial slope guesses s1,s2, IVP step size/method, tolerance tol.
1. Solve the IVP with s1; compute R1.
2. If |R1|≤tol, accept s1.
3. Solve with s2; compute R2.
4. If |R2|≤tol, accept s2.
5. Compute s3=s2−R2(s2−s1)/(R2−R1).
6. Shift the most recent slope/mismatch pair, integrate with s3, and recompute R3.
7. Continue until |R|≤tol.
8. Return the final IVP trajectory as the BVP solution approximation.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Convert to first order because standard IVP solvers advance first-order systems.
2. Treat y'(a) as an adjustable parameter because the far-end boundary condition replaces the missing initial slope.
3. Integrate all the way to b before judging a shot; the mismatch is defined at the terminal boundary.
4. Use two shots so the slope can be corrected by interpolation/secant logic instead of blind trial-and-error.
5. Stop on terminal mismatch, not merely on a small change in slope.
6. Keep the IVP integration accuracy sufficiently tight, because a poor IVP solve can corrupt the mismatch used to update s.


LIMITATIONS / FAILURE MODES
If R2≈R1, the secant denominator can be tiny and the update unstable.
Bad slope guesses can cause IVP blow-up or integration outside the useful solution branch.
Strongly nonlinear problems may have multiple BVP solutions or no solution.
A small terminal mismatch does not compensate for an inaccurate IVP integrator; integration error must also be controlled.


COMMON MISTAKES
Guessing y(a) even though the left boundary value is already prescribed.
Forgetting to introduce z=y'.
Updating the slope using interior-point error instead of y(b)−B.
Using only one slope guess with a secant formula.
Stopping because successive slopes are close while the terminal mismatch remains large.
Calling the method finite difference; shooting converts the BVP to IVP integration.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
For y''=F(x,y,y'), y(a)=A, y(b)=B, set z=y' and guess the missing slope s=z(a). Solve the IVP y'=z, z'=F(x,y,z), y(a)=A, z(a)=s to x=b. For two guesses s1,s2 obtain terminal values Y1,Y2 and residuals R1=Y1−B, R2=Y2−B. Update
s_new=s2−R2(s2−s1)/(R2−R1),
integrate again, and repeat until |y(b)−B| is within tolerance. The final IVP trajectory is the shooting approximation to the BVP.

questions.question: Milne’s Method.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. Registered HRP instructor notes derive Milne’s predictor and Simpson-type corrector for equally spaced points and describe the predictor–corrector procedure. This theory-only question can therefore be reconstructed as a DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION without introducing an exam-specific numerical scenario.


REQUIRED STARTING DATA
Milne is a multistep method. Before predicting y_(n+1), four equally spaced solution values are required:
(x_(n−3),y_(n−3)), (x_(n−2),y_(n−2)), (x_(n−1),y_(n−1)), (x_n,y_n),
with constant spacing h and f_i=f(x_i,y_i).
If the initial-value problem supplies only one starting value, a one-step method such as RK4 may be used to generate the additional starters when that startup policy is specified.


MILNE PREDICTOR
The registered predictor is
y_(n+1)^P = y_(n−3) + (4h/3)[2f_(n−2)−f_(n−1)+2f_n].
It uses already known derivative values to extrapolate a first estimate at x_(n+1).


PREDICTED SLOPE
Evaluate
f_(n+1)^P=f(x_(n+1),y_(n+1)^P).
This is necessary because the corrector uses derivative information at the new endpoint.


MILNE / SIMPSON CORRECTOR
The registered corrector is
y_(n+1)^C = y_(n−1) + (h/3)[f_(n−1)+4f_n+f_(n+1)^P].
The 1:4:1 pattern is Simpson-type weighting over the interval from x_(n−1) to x_(n+1).


CORRECTION POLICY / STOPPING
A standard course workflow is:
1. compute y_(n+1)^P;
2. compute f_(n+1)^P;
3. compute y_(n+1)^C;
4. if another correction is explicitly required, reevaluate f at the corrected y and repeat the corrector until the chosen difference/tolerance is met.
In this governed project, do not silently add repeated corrections when the source/example demonstrates only one correction or the exam does not state an iteration policy.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Require four equally spaced starters because the predictor coefficients come from a fixed-spacing multistep derivation.
2. Store f-values rather than recomputing the full history each step.
3. Predict first because the corrector needs an endpoint derivative that is not yet known.
4. Recompute the endpoint slope from the predicted/corrected state before applying another correction.
5. Keep the correction-count policy explicit so two people using the same formulas do not report different values merely because one iterated further.
6. Check convergence/change only after the method has produced a corrected value.


ALGORITHM
Given four equally spaced starter values and f_i:
A. Predictor: compute y_(n+1)^P.
B. Predicted slope: f_(n+1)^P=f(x_(n+1),y_(n+1)^P).
C. Corrector: compute y_(n+1)^C.
D. If required, set f_(n+1)=f(x_(n+1),y_(n+1)^C) and correct again.
E. Accept the corrected value according to the stated course/exam stopping rule.
F. Shift the four-value history forward and repeat for the next point.


COMMON MISTAKES
Trying to start Milne from only one initial value.
Using nonuniform h with the fixed Milne coefficients.
Writing the predictor coefficients in the wrong order.
Putting y_(n+1)^P directly into the corrector where f_(n+1)^P is required.
Forgetting that the corrector begins from y_(n−1), not y_n.
Repeating corrections indefinitely without a stated tolerance or course policy.
Confusing Milne predictor–corrector with Adams formulas merely because both are multistep methods.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Milne’s method requires four equally spaced starting values. With f_i=f(x_i,y_i),
Predictor:
y_(n+1)^P=y_(n−3)+(4h/3)[2f_(n−2)−f_(n−1)+2f_n].
Then calculate f_(n+1)^P=f(x_(n+1),y_(n+1)^P).
Corrector:
y_(n+1)^C=y_(n−1)+(h/3)[f_(n−1)+4f_n+f_(n+1)^P].
If the prescribed procedure requires another correction, reevaluate the endpoint slope with the corrected value and repeat until the chosen tolerance is satisfied. Four equally spaced starters are essential.

questions.question: Solve d²y/dx²+2dy/dx−3y=6x with y(0)=0, y′(0)=1 using fourth-order R–K method, h=0.2, for y(0.4).
questions.student_view:
1. Convert the second-order ODE to a first-order system


Let v=y′. Then


y′=v,


v′=6x−2v+3y.


Initial data:


x₀=0, y₀=0, v₀=1, h=0.2.


We apply classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta (RK4) to the vector state (y,v).


For each step, with F(x,y,v)=[v, 6x−2v+3y], define the four vector increments


K₁=hF(xₙ,yₙ,vₙ),
K₂=hF(xₙ+h/2, yₙ+K₁,y/2, vₙ+K₁,v/2),
K₃=hF(xₙ+h/2, yₙ+K₂,y/2, vₙ+K₂,v/2),
K₄=hF(xₙ+h, yₙ+K₃,y, vₙ+K₃,v),


and update


[yₙ₊₁,vₙ₊₁]=[yₙ,vₙ]+(K₁+2K₂+2K₃+K₄)/6.


2. First RK4 step: x=0 to x=0.2


At (x₀,y₀,v₀)=(0,0,1):


K₁=(0.200000, −0.400000).


Midpoint state for K₂:
(x,y,v)=(0.1, 0.1, 0.8), hence
K₂=(0.160000, −0.140000).


Midpoint state for K₃:
(x,y,v)=(0.1, 0.08, 0.93), hence
K₃=(0.186000, −0.204000).


Endpoint state for K₄:

questions.question: Solve y′=y²+x, y(0)=1 using Taylor’s series method and compute y(0.1) and y(0.2).

SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. The differential equation, initial condition and both target points are explicit. HRP supplies Taylor-series ODE method authority. The natural step is h=0.1 because the requested values are at 0.1 and 0.2 and the frozen audit uses two fourth-order Taylor steps; this step choice is stated as a reconstruction implementation consistent with the requested target sequence rather than invented exam wording.


TAYLOR METHOD
For a fourth-order step,
y(x+h)≈y+h y′+h²y″/2!+h³y‴/3!+h⁴y⁗/4!.


SUCCESSIVE DERIVATIVES
Given
y′=y²+x.
Differentiate:
y″=2yy′+1.
Differentiate again:
y‴=2(y′)²+2y y″.
And
y⁗=6y′y″+2y y‴.


STEP 1: FROM x=0 TO x=0.1
At x₀=0, y₀=1:
y′₀=1²+0=1.
y″₀=2(1)(1)+1=3.
y‴₀=2(1)²+2(1)(3)=8.
y⁗₀=6(1)(3)+2(1)(8)=34.


With h=0.1,
y(0.1)≈1+0.1(1)+(0.1²/2)(3)+(0.1³/6)(8)+(0.1⁴/24)(34).
The contributions are
1,
+0.1,
+0.015,
+0.0013333333,
+0.0001416667.
Therefore
boxed: y(0.1)≈1.116475000.


STEP 2: FROM x=0.1 TO x=0.2
Use x₁=0.1 and y₁=1.116475.
Then
y′₁=y₁²+0.1≈1.346516425625.
y″₁=2y₁y′₁+1≈4.006703852599.
y‴₁=2(y′₁)²+2y₁y″₁≈12.572982336618.
y⁗₁=6y′₁y″₁+2y₁y‴₁≈60.445396209390.


Hence
y(0.2)≈y₁+0.1y′₁+(0.1²/2)y″₁+(0.1³/6)y‴₁+(0.1⁴/24)y⁗₁
≈1.273507514699.
Therefore
boxed: y(0.2)≈1.273507515.


INDEPENDENT CHECK
Frozen independent recomputation gives exactly the same stored fourth-order Taylor values:
y(0.1)=1.116475,
y(0.2)=1.2735075146991388.
PASS.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Differentiate the ODE repeatedly because Taylor stepping needs y′,y″,y‴ and y⁗ at each step.
2. Recompute all derivatives at x=0.1 before the second step; reusing the x=0 derivatives would be wrong.
3. Keep factorial denominators explicit so each Taylor coefficient is correct.
4. Use sufficient intermediate precision because derivative values depend nonlinearly on y.
5. Label the fourth-order truncation and h=0.1 reconstruction choice transparently.

Treating y′=y²+x as a constant derivative across the step.
Differentiating y² as 2y instead of 2yy′ with respect to x.
Forgetting the +1 in y″=2yy′+1.
Using the derivatives at x=0 again to compute y(0.2).
Dropping factorials in the Taylor terms.
Rounding y(0.1) too aggressively before step 2.

y″=2yy′+1,
y‴=2(y′)²+2yy″,
y⁗=6y′y″+2yy‴.

y(0.1)=1+0.1+0.015+0.00133333+0.000141667

y′≈1.34651643,
y″≈4.00670385,
y‴≈12.57298234,
y⁗≈60.44539621,
so
boxed: y(0.2)≈1.273507515.

questions.question: Write the algorithms for fourth- and adaptive fifth-order RK methods to solve a first-order ordinary differential equation.
questions.student_view:
1. Problem setting
For a first-order IVP
y′=f(x,y),  y(xₙ)=yₙ,
choose a step h and advance from xₙ to xₙ₊₁=xₙ+h.


2. Source-locked classical RK4 algorithm
Compute
k₁ = h f(xₙ,yₙ),
k₂ = h f(xₙ+h/2, yₙ+k₁/2),
k₃ = h f(xₙ+h/2, yₙ+k₂/2),
k₄ = h f(xₙ+h, yₙ+k₃).
Then update
yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + (k₁+2k₂+2k₃+k₄)/6.
Repeat for each step.


Equivalent implementation sequence:
1. Read xₙ,yₙ,h and f.
2. Evaluate k₁.
3. Evaluate midpoint stage k₂ using k₁/2.
4. Evaluate midpoint stage k₃ using k₂/2.
5. Evaluate endpoint stage k₄ using k₃.
6. Form the weighted average (1,2,2,1)/6.
7. Set x←x+h, y←y+(k₁+2k₂+2k₃+k₄)/6.
8. Continue until the requested x is reached.


3. What “adaptive fifth-order RK” would require
A genuine adaptive RK algorithm normally needs a specific embedded pair with:
• a named Butcher tableau/stage coefficients;
• two different-order solution estimates from shared stages;
• an error estimate formed from their difference;
• an acceptance criterion based on a tolerance;
• a step-size update rule and safety factors/bounds.


The registered corpus available to this project does not identify which embedded fifth-order pair the exam setter intended and does not provide its tableau. Therefore a coefficient-level algorithm cannot be source-locked without importing outside material, which is prohibited for this governed reconstruction.


4. Safe source-limited adaptive outline
Only the generic logic can be stated without pretending specific coefficients are known:
• choose a source-specified embedded RK pair and its coefficients;
• compute all stages exactly from that pair;
• form the two embedded solution estimates;
• estimate local error from their difference;
• compare that error with the stated tolerance;
• accept or reject the step according to the specified method;
• update h using the pair’s stated controller;
• repeat.


This outline is not a substitute for the missing registered tableau and must not be presented as the requested complete fifth-order algorithm.


FINAL ANSWER
The classical RK4 algorithm is source-locked:
k₁=hf(xₙ,yₙ), k₂=hf(xₙ+h/2,yₙ+k₁/2), k₃=hf(xₙ+h/2,yₙ+k₂/2), k₄=hf(xₙ+h,yₙ+k₃), and yₙ₊₁=yₙ+(k₁+2k₂+2k₃+k₄)/6. For the adaptive fifth-order portion, the registered MTH504 corpus does not identify an embedded pair or provide its coefficients/tableau, so a complete coefficient-level algorithm cannot be supplied without invention. That portion remains SOURCE_LIMITED pending an authoritative registered source.


INDEPENDENT THEORETICAL CHECK
RK4 stage check: all four stages and the 1:2:2:1 weighted update are internally consistent with the registered classical RK4 algorithm.
Evidence gate: no canonical numerical result is promoted and no adaptive coefficients are introduced.
Dependency check: an adaptive embedded method necessarily depends on a specified pair/tableau and a tolerance/controller; these are exactly the missing evidence items.
No outside-method substitution was used to fill the source gap.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
For y′=f(x,y), classical RK4 uses the four stages k₁=hf(xₙ,yₙ), k₂=hf(xₙ+h/2,yₙ+k₁/2), k₃=hf(xₙ+h/2,yₙ+k₂/2), k₄=hf(xₙ+h,yₙ+k₃) and yₙ₊₁=yₙ+(k₁+2k₂+2k₃+k₄)/6. The registered course sources do not specify which adaptive fifth-order embedded RK pair/tableau is intended, so its coefficients and exact accept/reject controller cannot be reconstructed safely. State this limitation rather than inventing a tableau.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Forgetting the factor h inside the k-stages when using this convention.
• Using k₁ rather than k₂ in the third-stage y argument.
• Omitting the RK4 weights 1,2,2,1.
• Calling a fixed-step RK4 calculation “adaptive”.
• Inventing a popular embedded pair and presenting it as course-source authority.
• Omitting the tolerance/error-control dependency from an adaptive algorithm.

questions.question:
Define Taylor’s series method. Use it to determine y(0.1) for
y″−xy′−y=0,
y(0)=1,
y′(0)=0.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. The equation, both initial conditions and target y(0.1) are explicit. The registered HRP course material contains the corresponding worked Taylor example; therefore this record is classified DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION rather than merely method-matched.


DEFINITION
Taylor’s series method obtains a numerical solution by expanding y about a known point x₀:
y(x₀+h)=y₀+h y′₀+h²y″₀/2!+h³y‴₀/3!+h⁴y⁗₀/4!+⋯,
where the required successive derivatives are obtained from the differential equation and evaluated at the known state.


GOVERNING EQUATION
From
y″−xy′−y=0,
we have
y″=xy′+y.


At x=0, y=1, y′=0:
y″(0)=0(0)+1=1.


Differentiate y″=xy′+y:
y‴=y′+xy″+y′=2y′+xy″.
Thus
y‴(0)=0.


Differentiate again:
y⁗=2y″+(y″+xy‴)=3y″+xy‴.
Hence
y⁗(0)=3(1)+0=3.


TAYLOR SUBSTITUTION FOR h=0.1
Using y(0)=1, y′(0)=0, y″(0)=1, y‴(0)=0, y⁗(0)=3:
y(0.1)≈1
+0.1(0)
+(0.1²/2)(1)
+(0.1³/6)(0)
+(0.1⁴/24)(3).


Therefore
y(0.1)≈1+0.005+0.0000125
=1.0050125.


FINAL ANSWER
boxed: y(0.1)≈1.0050125.


INDEPENDENT CHECK
The frozen independent recomputation and registered worked example both give y(0.1)=1.0050125; PASS.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Rearrange the differential equation to express y″ directly.
2. Differentiate successively because Taylor coefficients require higher derivatives.
3. Evaluate every derivative at the same expansion point x=0.
4. Retain the factorial denominators from Taylor’s theorem.
5. Use the registered fourth-derivative truncation exactly as the course worked example does.


COMMON MISTAKES
Using y″=xy′−y instead of xy′+y.
Differentiating xy′ without the product rule.
Writing y‴=y′+xy″ instead of 2y′+xy″ after also differentiating +y.
Forgetting that y‴(0)=0.
Dropping 4! in the fourth-order term.
Adding terms beyond the registered worked derivation and then presenting a different value as the course answer.

y(x+h)=y+h y′+h²y″/2!+h³y‴/3!+h⁴y⁗/4!+⋯.
Here y″=xy′+y. At x=0:

 y(0.1)≈1+(0.1²/2)(1)+(0.1⁴/24)(3)

RK4 FORMULA
For y'=f(x,y):
k1=h f(x_n,y_n),
k2=h f(x_n+h/2,y_n+k1/2),
k3=h f(x_n+h/2,y_n+k2/2),
k4=h f(x_n+h,y_n+k3),
y_(n+1)=y_n+(k1+2k2+2k3+k4)/6.
Here f(x,y)=x+y and h=0.5.


FIRST STEP IN FULL: x=0 TO 0.5
At (0,1):
k1=0.5(0+1)=0.5.
k2=0.5(0.25+1+0.25)=0.75.
k3=0.5(0.25+1+0.375)=0.8125.
k4=0.5(0.5+1+0.8125)=1.15625.
Weighted sum=k1+2k2+2k3+k4=4.78125.
Increment=4.78125/6=0.796875.
Therefore y(0.5)=1.796875.


SUCCESSIVE RK4 VALUES
x | y_RK4
0.0 | 1.000000000000000
0.5 | 1.796875000000000
1.0 | 3.434692382812500
1.5 | 6.458750724792481

3.5 | 61.651149491533700
4.0 | 104.046035489950090


RESULT
boxed: y(4)≈104.04603548995009.


EXACT-SOLUTION CHECK
Solve y'−y=x. The exact IVP solution is
y=2e^x−x−1.
Thus y(4)=2e^4−5≈104.19630006628847.
Final RK4 error (numerical−exact)≈−0.15026457633838.
The absolute error is about 0.150265, small relative to the final magnitude but visible over eight coarse h=0.5 steps.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Keep the course-registered classical RK4 variant fixed; other fourth-order formulas may organize stages differently.
2. Evaluate two midpoint slopes because RK4 samples the local field inside the step, not only at endpoints.
3. Use the weighted 1:2:2:1 combination to obtain fourth-order local accuracy.
4. Carry the corrected y value into the next step without premature rounding.
5. Repeat exactly eight steps because (4−0)/0.5=8.
6. Compare with the exact IVP only as an independent QA check, not as a replacement for the RK4 work.


COMMON MISTAKES
Using h=1 instead of the printed h=0.5.
Forgetting that k1,...,k4 already contain h.
Evaluating k2 or k3 at x_n rather than x_n+h/2.
Using y_n+k2 instead of y_n+k2/2 in k3.
Dropping the 1:2:2:1 weighting.
Rounding each step too aggressively during an eight-step computation.
Reporting the exact value 104.1963 as the RK4 result.

For f=x+y and h=0.5, classical RK4 uses
k1=hf(x_n,y_n), k2=hf(x_n+h/2,y_n+k1/2), k3=hf(x_n+h/2,y_n+k2/2), k4=hf(x_n+h,y_n+k3),
y_(n+1)=y_n+(k1+2k2+2k3+k4)/6.
The first step gives y(0.5)=1.796875. Continuing to x=4 gives
boxed: y(4)≈104.04603549.

questions.question: Torsion on a 9 cm×9 cm square bar is governed by ∇²u=−4 with Dirichlet boundary u(x,y)=0 and printed h=1. The paper also says assume a 3 cm×3 cm grid and asks for “steady state temperature” at interior points by Gauss–Seidel until the minimum difference is correct to two decimal places.
questions.student_view:
What the source supports
The registered PDE material supports the standard five-point finite-difference stencil and Gauss–Seidel-style node updates for elliptic problems. For ∇²u=−4, a uniform square mesh with spacing h gives
(u_E+u_W+u_N+u_S−4u_P)/h² = −4,
so a node update would have the form
u_P = (u_E+u_W+u_N+u_S+4h²)/4,
with boundary values u=0.


Why the printed numerical task is conflicted
The occurrence simultaneously prints h=1 and also says to assume a 3 cm×3 cm grid. These do not define the same mesh on a 9 cm×9 cm square. The wording also changes physical language from torsion to “steady state temperature.” The registered sources explain the numerical stencil but do not adjudicate which printed mesh/physical interpretation was intended.


Exam-ready answer
State the five-point Poisson stencil and the zero Dirichlet boundary condition, but do not carry out a single canonical Gauss–Seidel table until the source conflict is resolved. The exam must first clarify whether the intended mesh uses h=1 cm or a 3 cm spacing/grid interpretation, and whether the torsion wording or the steady-temperature wording is the intended physical context.


INDEPENDENT MATHEMATICAL / LOGICAL QA
• The PDE ∇²u=−4 is elliptic and is compatible with the registered five-point stencil.
• If h=1 cm is interpreted literally on 0≤x,y≤9, the grid has 10 nodes per direction including boundaries and 8 interior nodes per direction.
• If “3 cm×3 cm grid” is interpreted as 3 cm spacing, the same square has 4 nodes per direction including boundaries and 2 interior nodes per direction.
• These interpretations produce different algebraic system sizes and different node values, confirming that the mesh conflict is consequential.
• No Gauss–Seidel iteration trajectory, tolerance sequence, or canonical interior value was generated.

questions.question: Laplacian equation.
questions.student_view:
1. What is the Laplace equation?


In two dimensions the Laplace equation is


u_xx + u_yy = 0.


It is a second-order linear partial differential equation. In the general second-order form


A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + … = G,


the classification uses B²−4AC. For Laplace’s equation A=1, B=0, C=1, so


B²−4AC = 0−4 = −4 < 0.


Therefore the Laplace equation is elliptic.


2. Finite-difference form on a square mesh


At an interior node P=(i,j) with equal grid spacing h in x and y, central differences give


u_xx ≈ [u_(i+1,j)−2u_(i,j)+u_(i−1,j)]/h²,


u_yy ≈ [u_(i,j+1)−2u_(i,j)+u_(i,j−1)]/h².


Substituting into u_xx+u_yy=0 gives


u_(i+1,j)+u_(i−1,j)+u_(i,j+1)+u_(i,j−1)−4u_(i,j)=0.


Hence the standard five-point formula is


u_(i,j) = [u_(i+1,j)+u_(i−1,j)+u_(i,j+1)+u_(i,j−1)]/4.


So the value at an interior mesh point is approximated by the average of its four nearest horizontal and vertical neighbours.


3. Iterative solution idea


When boundary values are known, the five-point equations for all interior nodes form a system of simultaneous algebraic equations.


Jacobi iteration uses neighbour values from the previous iteration when updating each interior node.


Gauss–Seidel iteration uses newly updated values immediately as they become available during the sweep.


Without boundary values there is no unique numerical grid solution to calculate, so this occurrence supports the equation, classification and finite-difference procedure only.


FINAL ANSWER


The Laplace equation is u_xx+u_yy=0. It is elliptic because B²−4AC=−4<0. On an equal square mesh, central differences give the five-point relation


u_(i,j)=[u_(i+1,j)+u_(i−1,j)+u_(i,j+1)+u_(i,j−1)]/4.


With prescribed boundary values, the interior equations may be solved directly or iteratively, commonly by Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel methods.


INDEPENDENT THEORETICAL CHECK


Classification check: for A=C=1 and B=0, the discriminant is −4, confirming elliptic type.


Stencil check: adding the independent second-order central-difference formulas for u_xx and u_yy and setting their sum to zero produces exactly the four-neighbour average formula above.


Consistency check: if all four neighbouring values equal a constant c, the stencil gives u_(i,j)=c, so constant harmonic fields are reproduced exactly.


EXAM-READY ANSWER


Laplace’s equation in two dimensions is u_xx+u_yy=0. It is elliptic. Using central differences on a square grid,


[u_(i+1,j)−2u_(i,j)+u_(i−1,j)]/h² + [u_(i,j+1)−2u_(i,j)+u_(i,j−1)]/h² = 0,


therefore


u_(i,j)=[u_(i+1,j)+u_(i−1,j)+u_(i,j+1)+u_(i,j−1)]/4.


Boundary values are required to obtain a numerical solution; the resulting interior equations can be iterated by Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel.


COMMON MISTAKES


• Calling Laplace’s equation parabolic or hyperbolic.
• Forgetting the factor 4 in the central-node coefficient.
• Using the five-point average without first imposing boundary values.
• Inventing numerical boundary conditions when none are printed.
• Confusing the Laplace equation u_xx+u_yy=0 with the Poisson equation u_xx+u_yy=f(x,y).

questions.question: Solution of partial differential equation.
questions.student_view:
A numerical PDE solution is not one universal formula. First identify the PDE class and the required initial/boundary data; then choose a mesh and replace derivatives by finite differences appropriate to that class.


1. CLASSIFY THE PDE
For the course convention
A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + D u_x + E u_y + F u = G,
use the discriminant B²−4AC:
• elliptic if B²−4AC<0;
• parabolic if B²−4AC=0;
• hyperbolic if B²−4AC>0.


Pandey examples:
• Laplace equation u_xx+u_yy=0 → elliptic.
• Heat-conduction type → parabolic.
• Wave type → hyperbolic.


2. BUILD A GRID
Let
x_i=i h, y_j=j k
for a steady two-dimensional problem, or
x_i=i h, t_n=n Δt
for a time-dependent problem. Boundary values and/or initial values must be supplied by the physical problem. No numerical solution is unique without the required data.


ELLIPTIC EXAMPLE — LAPLACE EQUATION
Using central second differences,
(u_{i+1,j}−2u_{i,j}+u_{i−1,j})/h²
+
(u_{i,j+1}−2u_{i,j}+u_{i,j−1})/k²=0.


For a square mesh h=k,
 u_{i,j}=¼(u_{i+1,j}+u_{i−1,j}+u_{i,j+1}+u_{i,j−1}).
This is Pandey’s standard five-point formula.


Point Jacobi uses only values from iteration n:
u_{i,j}^{(n+1)}=¼[u_{i−1,j}^{(n)}+u_{i+1,j}^{(n)}+u_{i,j−1}^{(n)}+u_{i,j+1}^{(n)}].


Gauss–Seidel uses the latest available updated values while scanning the mesh:
u_{i,j}^{(n+1)}=¼[u_{i−1,j}^{(n+1)}+u_{i+1,j}^{(n)}+u_{i,j−1}^{(n+1)}+u_{i,j+1}^{(n)}].


PARABOLIC EXAMPLE — HEAT EQUATION
For u_t=αu_xx, a standard explicit finite-difference form is
u_i^{n+1}=r u_{i−1}^n+(1−2r)u_i^n+r u_{i+1}^n,
where r=αΔt/h².
This requires an initial temperature distribution plus boundary conditions. For the standard FTCS scheme, r≤1/2 is the familiar one-dimensional stability condition. This detailed time-marching formula is registered-reference support, not attributed verbatim to the inspected Pandey §5.7 pages.


HYPERBOLIC EXAMPLE — WAVE EQUATION
For u_tt=c²u_xx, central differences lead to a two-time-level update such as
u_i^{n+1}=2u_i^n−u_i^{n−1}+s²(u_{i+1}^n−2u_i^n+u_{i−1}^n),
where s=cΔt/h.
A hyperbolic problem needs suitable initial displacement/velocity data and boundary conditions. The exact first-step treatment depends on those initial data and is not invented here.


WHY PDE CLASSIFICATION MATTERS
• Elliptic problems are usually boundary-value problems solved over the whole spatial domain.
• Parabolic problems propagate/diffuse an initial state forward in time.
• Hyperbolic problems propagate waves and require adequate initial conditions, often including velocity information.
Using the wrong stencil/data structure can make an otherwise correct finite-difference formula meaningless.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Starting numerical iterations before identifying the PDE type.
• Omitting boundary/initial conditions.
• Using the square-mesh five-point average when h≠k without adjustment.
• Mixing Jacobi old values with Gauss–Seidel latest values unintentionally.
• Treating FTCS stability restrictions as universal rules for every PDE scheme.
• Inventing missing numerical boundary values for a theory-only question.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
To solve a PDE numerically, first classify the second-order equation A u_xx+B u_xy+C u_yy+…=G using B²−4AC, then construct a mesh and replace derivatives by finite differences consistent with the PDE type and supplied initial/boundary conditions. For the elliptic Laplace equation and square mesh, Pandey’s five-point formula is
u_{i,j}=¼(u_{i+1,j}+u_{i−1,j}+u_{i,j+1}+u_{i,j−1}),
which may be solved iteratively by point Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel. Parabolic heat equations are commonly advanced in time with finite-difference schemes such as FTCS, while hyperbolic wave equations use space-and-time central differences with the required initial displacement/velocity and boundary data.


PREREQUISITES
Partial derivatives; PDE classification; finite differences; mesh notation; boundary and initial conditions; stationary iteration.


SEMANTIC MATH COLOR / PATTERN MAP
coefficients → A,B,C; discriminator → B²−4AC; mesh → h,k,Δt; elliptic_node → u_{i,j}; Jacobi_old → superscript n; GS_latest → n+1 neighbors; heat_ratio → r; wave_ratio → s.


VISUAL MODEL
Panel A: classification decision tree from B²−4AC. Panel B: 2D five-point stencil with center and four neighbors. Panel C: Jacobi versus Gauss–Seidel update-order animation. Panel D: heat and wave space-time grids showing required initial/boundary data.


AUDIT NOTES
Direct course authority: Pandey §5.7 for classification, mesh, five-point Laplace, point Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel. Detailed heat/wave time-marching formulas are explicitly registered-reference-supported supplements. No numerical boundary/initial values are introduced. Frozen mth504-v1.1.0 untouched.


QA STATUS

No-invented-data policy: PASS. Exam-ready answer: PASS. Semantic-math metadata: PASS. Visual model: SPECIFIED. Rendered formula/focus QA: PENDING. Mobile QA: PENDING. Final STUDENT_READY: PENDING_RENDER_QA.

questions.question: Describe partial differential equation of second order with its different forms.
questions.student_view:
Using the coefficient convention in the registered notes, a second-order linear PDE in two independent variables x and y is
A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + D u_x + E u_y + F u = G,
where A,B,C,D,E,F,G may be functions of x and y.


The classification depends on the second-order (principal) part. Define
Δ = B² − 4AC.


CLASSIFICATION
1. Elliptic: Δ<0.
   Registered example: Laplace equation u_xx+u_yy=0.
   Typical character: boundary-value behavior; information is coupled across the spatial domain.


2. Parabolic: Δ=0.
   Registered example: heat-conduction equation.
   Typical character: diffusion/evolution behavior; an initial distribution and spatial boundary data are commonly required.


3. Hyperbolic: Δ>0.
   Registered example: wave equation.
   Typical character: propagation along characteristic directions; initial data play a central role.


WHY ONLY A,B,C ENTER THE DISCRIMINANT
The PDE type is controlled locally by the quadratic second-derivative form. Lower-order terms D u_x+E u_y+F u and the forcing G affect the solution but do not change the elliptic/parabolic/hyperbolic classification of the principal part at that point.


COEFFICIENT-CONVENTION WARNING
This course writes the mixed term as B u_xy and therefore uses B²−4AC. Some books write 2B u_xy and then use B²−AC. Do not mix those two conventions in an exam answer.


NUMERICAL-METHOD CONNECTION
Pandey’s §5.7 immediately introduces the finite-difference method for PDEs and then the standard five-point formula for the Laplace equation. This connects PDE classification to method choice: elliptic problems are commonly discretized as spatial boundary-value systems, while time-dependent parabolic/hyperbolic problems require time-level treatment plus suitable initial/boundary data.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Using B²−AC while still writing the cross term as B u_xy.
• Including D,E,F,G in the discriminant.
• Classifying from the equation name rather than its principal coefficients.
• Forgetting that A,B,C may vary, so PDE type can in principle vary with location.
• Calling every second-order PDE elliptic because it contains second derivatives.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
A general second-order linear PDE can be written
A u_xx+B u_xy+C u_yy+D u_x+E u_y+Fu=G.
With this coefficient convention define Δ=B²−4AC. If Δ<0 the PDE is elliptic, if Δ=0 it is parabolic, and if Δ>0 it is hyperbolic. The registered course examples are Laplace, heat-conduction and wave equations respectively. The classification is determined by the second-order principal part; lower-order terms do not alter the discriminant classification.


SEMANTIC MATH COLOR / PATTERN MAP
principal_coefficients → A,B,C; mixed_term → B u_xy; discriminant → Δ=B²−4AC; elliptic → Δ<0; parabolic → Δ=0; hyperbolic → Δ>0.


VISUAL MODEL
Panel A: general PDE with principal terms highlighted. Panel B: a number line for Δ with elliptic/parabolic/hyperbolic regions. Panel C: representative Laplace/heat/wave icons. Panel D: method link from classification to boundary/initial data and finite differences.

SOURCE ALIGNMENT

GRID

A=U(1/3,1/3),
B=U(1/3,2/3),
C=U(2/3,1/3),

Since h²=1/9,
4U_P−(U_E+U_W+U_N+U_S)=9xy,
with known boundary neighbor values moved to the right-hand side.

−B−C+4D=204.

−A+4B−D=102
