questions.question: Classify partial differential equations of second order. Describe in detail the parabolic partial differential equation.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Frozen status: SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. Exact occurrence: P2-PROV-2022-SPRING-ASSESSMENT-Q9. Dr. Hem Raj Pandey’s registered §5.7 directly supplies the general second-order PDE, the B²−4AC classification and the heat equation as the parabolic example. The registered Khadka PDE chapter is the detailed-reference authority for parabolic heat finite differences. Because the exact extended parabolic treatment is not established as a verbatim Pandey section in the registered lecture-note pages, v1.2 classifies the full answer COURSE_METHOD_MATCHED rather than over-promoting it.


CLASSIFICATION
With the course convention
A u_xx+B u_xy+C u_yy+D u_x+E u_y+Fu=G,
define Δ=B²−4AC.
• Δ<0: elliptic.
• Δ=0: parabolic.
• Δ>0: hyperbolic.
The registered examples are Laplace, heat conduction and wave equations respectively.


PARABOLIC PDE — PHYSICAL IDEA
A standard parabolic model is one-dimensional heat diffusion,
u_t = α u_xx,   α>0,
where u(x,t) is temperature (or another diffusing quantity) and α is diffusivity. The future state depends on the current spatial distribution, so a well-posed problem normally requires an initial condition u(x,0)=g(x) and boundary conditions at the spatial ends, for example u(0,t)=p(t), u(L,t)=q(t).


FINITE-DIFFERENCE DISCRETIZATION
Let x_i=i h and t_n=n k. A standard forward-time, central-space approximation is
(u_i^{n+1}−u_i^n)/k = α(u_{i+1}^n−2u_i^n+u_{i−1}^n)/h².
Define r=αk/h². Then
u_i^{n+1}=r u_{i−1}^n+(1−2r)u_i^n+r u_{i+1}^n.
This is an explicit time-marching scheme: values at the new time level are obtained from the known previous level.


STABILITY NOTE
For this standard explicit heat scheme, the familiar one-dimensional stability restriction is r≤1/2. This statement is a numerical-analysis supplement consistent with the registered PDE-reference treatment; it is not attributed as a verbatim line from Pandey §5.7. If an implicit method is used instead, a linear system must be solved at each time level but the severe explicit time-step restriction is avoided.


WHY INITIAL AND BOUNDARY DATA ARE BOTH NEEDED
The PDE evolves in time, so the initial profile starts the process. Spatial second derivatives also couple neighboring points, so boundary values are needed to close the finite-difference equations at the edges. Without these data, a unique time evolution is not defined.


PARABOLIC CHARACTER
For the second-order classification, parabolic means Δ=0. In canonical form there is one repeated characteristic direction. In diffusion problems this produces smoothing: sharp spatial variations tend to spread and decay with time rather than propagate as undamped waves.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Using the wrong discriminant convention for the written mixed-derivative coefficient.
• Calling every time-dependent PDE parabolic.
• Giving only u_t=αu_xx without initial/boundary data.
• Mixing the space step h and time step k in r=αk/h².
• Claiming the explicit heat scheme is unconditionally stable.
• Presenting the finite-difference detail as verbatim Pandey text when only the classification/heat example is directly established there.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
For A u_xx+B u_xy+C u_yy+…=G, define Δ=B²−4AC. The equation is elliptic for Δ<0, parabolic for Δ=0 and hyperbolic for Δ>0. A standard parabolic equation is the heat equation u_t=αu_xx. With x_i=ih, t_n=nk, forward-time central-space discretization gives
u_i^{n+1}=r u_{i−1}^n+(1−2r)u_i^n+r u_{i+1}^n,
r=αk/h².
The problem requires an initial temperature distribution plus spatial boundary conditions. For the standard explicit one-dimensional scheme, r≤1/2 is the usual stability condition.

questions.question: Numerical solutions of partial differential equations.
questions.student_view:
A numerical PDE solution is not one universal formula. The PDE class determines the kind of data and numerical marching/solution structure that is appropriate. Therefore classify first, identify required boundary/initial data, construct a mesh, replace derivatives by finite differences, then solve and verify.


1. CLASSIFICATION
Using the course convention
A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + D u_x + E u_y + F u = G,
classify using Δ=B²−4AC:
• elliptic if Δ<0;
• parabolic if Δ=0;
• hyperbolic if Δ>0.
Typical forms are Laplace-type (elliptic), heat/diffusion-type (parabolic) and wave-type (hyperbolic).


2. FINITE-DIFFERENCE GRID
For a steady 2D problem let x_i=ih and y_j=jk. For time-dependent problems use x_i=ih and t_n=nΔt. Values prescribed on boundaries or at initial time come from the physical/source problem; they must not be invented.


3. ELLIPTIC PDE — LAPLACE FIVE-POINT FORMULA
For u_xx+u_yy=0, central differences give
(u_{i+1,j}−2u_{i,j}+u_{i−1,j})/h² +(u_{i,j+1}−2u_{i,j}+u_{i,j−1})/k²=0.
For a square mesh h=k this reduces to Pandey’s five-point relation
u_{i,j}=¼(u_{i+1,j}+u_{i−1,j}+u_{i,j+1}+u_{i,j−1}).
This converts the PDE at interior nodes into algebraic equations.


Point Jacobi uses only previous-iteration values:
u_{i,j}^{(m+1)}=¼[u_{i−1,j}^{(m)}+u_{i+1,j}^{(m)}+u_{i,j−1}^{(m)}+u_{i,j+1}^{(m)}].
Gauss–Seidel uses newly available values during the sweep, for example
u_{i,j}^{(m+1)}=¼[u_{i−1,j}^{(m+1)}+u_{i+1,j}^{(m)}+u_{i,j−1}^{(m+1)}+u_{i,j+1}^{(m)}].
Iterate until a stated change/residual tolerance is satisfied.


4. PARABOLIC PDE — HEAT EQUATION SUPPLEMENT
For u_t=αu_xx, a standard explicit FTCS discretization is
u_i^{n+1}=r u_{i−1}^n +(1−2r)u_i^n +r u_{i+1}^n,
where r=αΔt/h².
It advances a supplied initial temperature profile through time while enforcing boundary values. For the standard 1D FTCS heat scheme, r≤1/2 is the familiar stability condition. This detailed formula is registered-reference support and is not attributed verbatim to the inspected Pandey pages.


5. HYPERBOLIC PDE — WAVE EQUATION SUPPLEMENT
For u_tt=c²u_xx, central space/time differences give an update such as
u_i^{n+1}=2u_i^n−u_i^{n−1}+s²(u_{i+1}^n−2u_i^n+u_{i−1}^n),
where s=cΔt/h.
A wave problem requires suitable initial displacement/velocity and boundary data. The first time step depends on those supplied data; none are manufactured here.


GENERAL NUMERICAL PROCEDURE
1. Classify the PDE.
2. Identify domain, boundary conditions and any initial conditions.
3. Choose h, k and/or Δt from the problem or a governed refinement plan.
4. Replace derivatives by justified finite differences.
5. Assemble algebraic equations or time-marching updates.
6. Solve/iterate.
7. Check residual, convergence, stability where relevant, and mesh/time-step refinement.


INDEPENDENT THEORY QA
The five-point formula follows directly from central second differences and reduces correctly to the quarter-average only for h=k. Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel use old versus latest values consistently. The detailed heat/wave formulas are clearly separated as registered-reference supplements, preserving the provenance boundary. No numerical boundary or initial data are introduced.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Solving before classifying the PDE.
• Using the square-mesh quarter-average when h≠k.
• Mixing Jacobi old values with Gauss–Seidel latest values unintentionally.
• Omitting required boundary/initial conditions.
• Treating r≤1/2 as a universal condition for every parabolic scheme.
• Inventing a mesh, boundary value or first-time-step datum not present in the source problem.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
For numerical solution of a PDE, first classify A u_xx+B u_xy+C u_yy+…=G using B²−4AC, identify the required boundary/initial data, form a grid and replace derivatives by finite differences. For the elliptic Laplace equation, central differences give, on a square mesh,
u_{i,j}=¼(u_{i+1,j}+u_{i−1,j}+u_{i,j+1}+u_{i,j−1}),
which may be solved iteratively by point Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel. Parabolic heat equations are commonly advanced in time with schemes such as FTCS, while hyperbolic wave equations use space-time finite differences with the required initial displacement/velocity and boundary data. Every numerical result must be checked for convergence/residual and, where relevant, stability/refinement.

Panel D: heat and wave space-time grids with clearly marked required initial/boundary data and a provenance badge separating direct-course content from registered-reference supplements.

questions.question: Numerical solution of partial differential equations.
questions.student_view:
The method depends on PDE type and available data. A disciplined solution sequence is:
1. classify the PDE;
2. identify the physical domain and required boundary/initial conditions;
3. construct a spatial/time grid;
4. replace derivatives by suitable finite differences;
5. form algebraic equations or a time-marching recurrence;
6. solve or iterate;
7. check residual/convergence and stability/refinement when relevant.


PDE CLASSIFICATION
For the course form
A u_xx+B u_xy+C u_yy+D u_x+E u_y+F u=G,
use Δ=B²−4AC:
Δ<0 elliptic, Δ=0 parabolic, Δ>0 hyperbolic.


ELLIPTIC CASE — LAPLACE EQUATION
For u_xx+u_yy=0, use central second differences:
(u_{i+1,j}−2u_{i,j}+u_{i−1,j})/h² +(u_{i,j+1}−2u_{i,j}+u_{i,j−1})/k²=0.
For h=k,
u_{i,j}=¼(u_{i+1,j}+u_{i−1,j}+u_{i,j+1}+u_{i,j−1}).
This is the direct course five-point formula.


Jacobi update:
u_{i,j}^{(m+1)}=¼[u_{i−1,j}^{(m)}+u_{i+1,j}^{(m)}+u_{i,j−1}^{(m)}+u_{i,j+1}^{(m)}].
Gauss–Seidel uses the latest available updated neighbors during the same sweep, for example
u_{i,j}^{(m+1)}=¼[u_{i−1,j}^{(m+1)}+u_{i+1,j}^{(m)}+u_{i,j−1}^{(m+1)}+u_{i,j+1}^{(m)}].
Continue until a specified change or residual criterion is met.


PARABOLIC CASE — REGISTERED-REFERENCE SUPPLEMENT
For the one-dimensional heat equation u_t=αu_xx, a standard explicit FTCS form is
u_i^{n+1}=r u_{i−1}^{n}+(1−2r)u_i^n+r u_{i+1}^{n},
r=αΔt/h².
It requires a supplied initial profile and boundary conditions. For this standard one-dimensional FTCS scheme, r≤1/2 is the familiar stability restriction. This detailed recurrence is registered-reference support, not claimed as verbatim Pandey material.


HYPERBOLIC CASE — REGISTERED-REFERENCE SUPPLEMENT
For u_tt=c²u_xx, a central-difference recurrence is
u_i^{n+1}=2u_i^n−u_i^{n−1}+s²(u_{i+1}^n−2u_i^n+u_{i−1}^n),
s=cΔt/h.
Appropriate initial displacement/velocity and boundary values are necessary. The first-time-level construction depends on the supplied initial data and is not invented in this theory question.


WHY CLASSIFICATION AND DATA MATTER
Elliptic problems are typically boundary-value problems solved over the whole spatial region. Parabolic problems evolve an initial state by diffusion-like time marching. Hyperbolic problems propagate wave-like information and require adequate initial data, commonly including velocity. Using a correct stencil with the wrong class or missing data does not produce a valid physical solution.


INDEPENDENT THEORY QA
The square-grid five-point equation follows from the two central second differences. Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel are distinguished by previous-only versus latest-available values. The heat and wave recurrences are kept inside the registered-reference boundary and no missing mesh or boundary/initial values are supplied.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Failing to classify the PDE before selecting a scheme.
• Applying the quarter-average five-point expression when h≠k.
• Confusing Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel update order.
• Omitting boundary/initial conditions.
• Presenting the FTCS r≤1/2 restriction as universal for all PDE methods.
• Inventing source data to turn a theory question into a numerical example.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Numerical PDE solution begins by classifying A u_xx+B u_xy+C u_yy+…=G with B²−4AC, defining the required boundary/initial data, forming a grid and replacing derivatives by finite differences. For the elliptic Laplace equation, central differences on a square mesh give
u_{i,j}=¼(u_{i+1,j}+u_{i−1,j}+u_{i,j+1}+u_{i,j−1}),
and the resulting interior-node equations can be solved iteratively by Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel. Parabolic heat equations can be advanced by time-marching finite differences such as FTCS, while hyperbolic wave equations use space-time central differences with required initial displacement/velocity and boundary data. Convergence, residual, stability and refinement must be checked as appropriate.

questions.question:
A body of weight 10 kg falls from rest toward the earth with velocity v. Air resistance dependent on velocity is approximately 2v. Find the velocity after t=2 s using the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method with step size h=1 s.


SOURCE / REVIEW BOUNDARY
The exam wording repeatedly prints “weight 10 kg.” Kilogram is a mass unit, so the frozen v1.1.0 record already carries review flag PRINTED_WEIGHT_10_KG_INTERPRETED_AS_MASS. v1.2 preserves that flag rather than silently rewriting the source.


Course method authority: Dr. Hem Raj Pandey lecture notes, RK4 section (registered source locator PDF pp.95–101 / printed pp.90–96), which gives the classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta stages
k₁=h f(tₙ,vₙ),
k₂=h f(tₙ+h/2,vₙ+k₁/2),
k₃=h f(tₙ+h/2,vₙ+k₂/2),
k₄=h f(tₙ+h,vₙ+k₃),
and
vₙ₊₁=vₙ+(k₁+2k₂+2k₃+k₄)/6.


The instructor notes provide the RK4 method and worked ODE examples, but no exact worked falling-body problem with these same givens was recovered. Therefore the primary provenance remains COURSE_METHOD_MATCHED.


PHYSICAL MODEL
Take downward as positive. Interpreting the printed 10 kg as mass m=10 kg and resistance magnitude 2v acting upward,


m dv/dt = mg − 2v.


Thus


10 dv/dt = 10(9.81) − 2v,


dv/dt = 9.81 − 0.2v.


Initial condition:
v(0)=0.


WHY THIS ODE?
Gravity increases downward velocity while drag opposes motion and increases with v. The drag term therefore enters with a minus sign.


Let
f(t,v)=9.81−0.2v.


STEP 1 — ADVANCE FROM t=0 TO t=1
h=1, t₀=0, v₀=0.


k₁=1·f(0,0)
=9.81.


k₂=1·f(0.5,0+k₁/2)
=9.81−0.2(4.905)
=8.829.


k₃=1·f(0.5,0+k₂/2)
=9.81−0.2(4.4145)
=8.9271.


k₄=1·f(1,0+k₃)
=9.81−0.2(8.9271)
=8.02458.


Therefore


v₁
=0+[9.81+2(8.829)+2(8.9271)+8.02458]/6
=8.89113 m/s.


WHY FOUR STAGES?
RK4 samples the slope at the beginning, two midpoint estimates, and the endpoint. Their weighted average gives a fourth-order accurate one-step update without requiring higher derivatives of v.


STEP 2 — ADVANCE FROM t=1 TO t=2
Now t₁=1, v₁=8.89113.


k₁=1·f(1,8.89113)
=9.81−0.2(8.89113)
=8.031774.


k₂=1·f(1.5,8.89113+k₁/2)
=9.81−0.2(12.907017)
=7.2285966.


k₃=1·f(1.5,8.89113+k₂/2)
=9.81−0.2(12.5054283)
=7.30891434.


k₄=1·f(2,8.89113+k₃)
=9.81−0.2(16.20004434)
=6.569991132.


Hence


v₂
=8.89113+[8.031774+2(7.2285966)+2(7.30891434)+6.569991132]/6
=16.170594502 m/s.


FINAL ANSWER
The RK4 estimate after 2 s is


v(2) ≈ 16.1706 m/s downward.


Intermediate value:
v(1) ≈ 8.89113 m/s downward.


INDEPENDENT MATHEMATICAL CHECK — NOT THE COURSE-SOURCE SOLUTION
For the interpreted model dv/dt+0.2v=9.81, v(0)=0, the exact analytical solution is


v(t)=49.05(1−e^(−0.2t)).


Therefore
v_exact(1)=8.89125656 m/s,
v_exact(2)=16.17080174 m/s.


Errors:
|v_RK4(1)−v_exact(1)|≈0.00012656 m/s,
|v_RK4(2)−v_exact(2)|≈0.00020724 m/s.


This independently confirms the RK4 arithmetic and scale of the answer. It is an enrichment-layer math check, not a claim that the teacher source supplied the closed-form solution.


PLAUSIBILITY CHECK
The terminal velocity of the interpreted model satisfies 9.81−0.2v=0, giving
v_terminal=49.05 m/s.
The computed v(2)=16.17 m/s is positive, below terminal velocity, and increasing from rest, which is physically plausible.


COMMON MISTAKES
- treating “10 kg weight” as a force of 10 N without acknowledging the source-unit inconsistency;
- using +2v for drag when downward is positive;
- forgetting to divide the force equation by m=10;
- omitting the factor h inside k₁,…,k₄;
- using k₂ instead of k₃ in the endpoint stage;
- taking one h=2 step when the question specifies h=1;
- reporting only v(1) even though two RK4 steps are required to reach t=2;
- rounding stage values too aggressively.
questions.student_view:
EXAM-READY ANSWER
With downward positive and interpreting the printed 10 kg as mass,


10 dv/dt=10(9.81)−2v,
so
v′=9.81−0.2v,
with v(0)=0.


Using classical RK4 with h=1:


Step 0→1:
k₁=9.81,
k₂=8.829,
k₃=8.9271,
k₄=8.02458,


v(1)=8.89113 m/s.


Step 1→2:
k₁=8.031774,
k₂=7.2285966,
k₃=7.30891434,
k₄=6.569991132,


v(2)=16.170594502 m/s.


Therefore
v(2)≈16.1706 m/s downward.

questions.question:
Show that


d/dx [x^(-n) J_n(x)] = -x^(-n) J_(n+1)(x),


where J_n(x) is a Bessel function.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen Unit-7 source-locked record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. Two 2025 university-exam occurrences preserve the same identity. The registered Dr Hem Raj Pandey Chapter 6 source and the registered teacher special-function extract give this exact Bessel relation. The source first differentiates x^(-n)J_n(x) term-by-term and also rewrites the result as the recurrence x J_n'(x)=n J_n(x)-x J_(n+1)(x). Therefore the primary provenance tier is DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION.


WHAT IS BEING ASKED?
Prove that multiplying J_n(x) by x^(-n) converts its derivative into the next-order Bessel function J_(n+1)(x), with the factor -x^(-n).


PREREQUISITES
Product rule; power rule; Bessel functions of the first kind; the registered recurrence xJ_n'=nJ_n-xJ_(n+1); term-by-term differentiation of the convergent Bessel series.


INTUITION
The factor x^(-n) is not arbitrary. The derivative of x^(-n) contributes -n x^(-n-1)J_n, while the Bessel derivative contributes x^(-n)J_n'. The nJ_n/x terms cancel exactly when the registered Bessel recurrence is substituted, leaving only -x^(-n)J_(n+1).


DERIVATION 1 — SHORT COURSE-RECURRENCE PROOF
From the registered Bessel recurrence,


x J_n'(x) = n J_n(x) - x J_(n+1)(x).


Divide by x:


J_n'(x) - (n/x)J_n(x) = -J_(n+1)(x).      (1)


Now differentiate the product x^(-n)J_n(x):


d/dx[x^(-n)J_n(x)]
= -n x^(-n-1)J_n(x) + x^(-n)J_n'(x)
= x^(-n)[J_n'(x) - (n/x)J_n(x)].


Using (1),


d/dx[x^(-n)J_n(x)]
= -x^(-n)J_(n+1)(x).


Hence


boxed: d/dx[x^(-n)J_n(x)] = -x^(-n)J_(n+1)(x).


WHY EACH STEP IS NECESSARY
1. Use the recurrence because it already contains the exact combination J_n'-(n/x)J_n that appears after differentiating x^(-n)J_n.
2. Factor out x^(-n) so the cancellation pattern is visible instead of hidden across two terms.
3. Stop once the bracket is replaced by -J_(n+1); no further recurrence manipulation is needed.


DERIVATION 2 — DIRECT SERIES VIEW
For integer n, the Bessel function of the first kind has the registered power-series form


J_n(x) = sum_(r=0)^infinity [(-1)^r / (r! Gamma(n+r+1))] (x/2)^(n+2r).


Multiplying by x^(-n),


x^(-n)J_n(x)
= sum_(r=0)^infinity [(-1)^r / (r! Gamma(n+r+1) 2^(n+2r))] x^(2r).


Differentiate term by term:


d/dx[x^(-n)J_n(x)]
= sum_(r=1)^infinity [(-1)^r 2r / (r! Gamma(n+r+1) 2^(n+2r))] x^(2r-1).


Use r/r! = 1/(r-1)! and shift the index k=r-1. Then the series becomes exactly


-x^(-n) J_(n+1)(x),


which proves the same identity directly from the Bessel series.


MATH QA
PASS — applying the product rule gives the combination x^(-n)[J_n'-(n/x)J_n].
PASS — the registered recurrence gives J_n'-(n/x)J_n=-J_(n+1).
PASS — the direct series proof has the same shifted-index coefficients as -x^(-n)J_(n+1).
PASS — n=0 gives J_0'(x)=-J_1(x), the standard low-order special case.
PASS — dimensional/power structure is consistent: both sides carry the same x-power family after the series index shift.


COMMON MISTAKES
Dropping the derivative of x^(-n).
Using +n x^(-n-1) instead of -n x^(-n-1).
Writing J_n'-(n/x)J_n=+J_(n+1) and losing the minus sign.
Using the other recurrence J_n'+(n/x)J_n=J_(n-1) without matching it to the factor x^(-n).
Shifting the series index without also changing r! to (r-1)!.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Using


xJ_n'=nJ_n-xJ_(n+1),


we have


J_n'-(n/x)J_n=-J_(n+1).


Therefore


d/dx[x^(-n)J_n]
=-n x^(-n-1)J_n+x^(-n)J_n'
=x^(-n)[J_n'-(n/x)J_n]
=-x^(-n)J_(n+1).


Hence proved.

questions.question: Find the relation of Bessel’s function when k=n. Using it prove that J_n(−x)=(−1)^n J_n(x).
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. HRP Chapter 6 derives the k=n branch of the Bessel-series solution and directly supports the requested parity relation. The derivation below follows that registered course series and keeps the integer-order condition explicit.


BESSEL k=n SERIES
For integer order n, the first-kind Bessel function is represented by
J_n(x)=Σ_(r=0)^∞ [(-1)^r/(Γ(r+1)Γ(n+r+1))](x/2)^(n+2r).
For integer n≥0 this is equivalently
J_n(x)=Σ_(r=0)^∞ [(-1)^r/(r!(n+r)!)](x/2)^(n+2r).
This is the k=n relation/branch used for the parity proof.


PARITY DERIVATION
Replace x by −x:
J_n(−x)=Σ_(r=0)^∞ [(-1)^r/(Γ(r+1)Γ(n+r+1))](-x/2)^(n+2r).
Because n and r are integers,
(-x/2)^(n+2r)=(-1)^(n+2r)(x/2)^(n+2r).
But (-1)^(2r)=1, so
(-1)^(n+2r)=(-1)^n.
The factor (-1)^n is independent of r and can be taken outside the sum:
J_n(−x)=(-1)^n Σ_(r=0)^∞ [(-1)^r/(Γ(r+1)Γ(n+r+1))](x/2)^(n+2r).
Therefore
boxed: J_n(−x)=(-1)^n J_n(x), for integer n.


INTERPRETATION
If n is even, (-1)^n=1, hence J_n(−x)=J_n(x): J_n is even.
If n is odd, (-1)^n=−1, hence J_n(−x)=−J_n(x): J_n is odd.
The integer-order condition matters because the simple real factor (-1)^n used here comes from the integer exponent n+2r in the registered series.


LOW-ORDER CHECKS
n=0: J_0 contains powers x^0,x^2,x^4,... and is even.
n=1: J_1 contains powers x^1,x^3,x^5,... and is odd.
n=2: J_2 contains powers x^2,x^4,x^6,... and is even.
These agree with J_n(−x)=(-1)^nJ_n(x).


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Start from the registered k=n series because the power structure n+2r makes parity visible term by term.
2. Replace x by −x without changing the gamma/factorial coefficients.
3. Separate (-1)^(n+2r) into (-1)^n(-1)^(2r).
4. Use integer r to set (-1)^(2r)=1.
5. Factor the remaining (-1)^n outside the entire series.
6. State the integer-order assumption explicitly before concluding even/odd behavior.


COMMON MISTAKES
Dropping the factor (-1)^r already present in the Bessel series.
Writing (-1)^(n+2r)=(-1)^(n+r).
Assuming (-1)^n is a simple ±1 parity factor for arbitrary non-integer order.
Trying to prove the relation from J_n(x) notation alone without using the series/recurrence source.
Calling every Bessel function even; odd integer orders are odd functions.
Confusing the series index r with the Bessel order n.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
For integer n,
J_n(x)=Σ_(r=0)^∞ (-1)^r/[Γ(r+1)Γ(n+r+1)] · (x/2)^(n+2r).
Therefore
J_n(−x)=Σ (-1)^r/[Γ(r+1)Γ(n+r+1)] · (-1)^(n+2r)(x/2)^(n+2r).
Since (-1)^(2r)=1,
J_n(−x)=(-1)^n J_n(x).
Hence J_n is even for even n and odd for odd n.

questions.question:
Find Bessel’s function. Using the definition show that
 d[xⁿJₙ(x)]/dx = xⁿJₙ₋₁(x),
and
 d[x⁻ⁿJₙ(x)]/dx = −x⁻ⁿJₙ₊₁(x).
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. The exact exam occurrence is P2-PROV-2019-INTERNAL-FALL-Q6B, printed 6(b), 8 marks. The registered HRP Special Functions chapter and the registered teacher Chapter 6 extract, PDF pp.9–12 / printed pp.119–122, equations (6.18)–(6.24), directly provide the integer-order Bessel first-kind series and the requested derivative identities. No outside identity is needed.


PREREQUISITES
1. For integer n≥0, use the registered Bessel first-kind power series.
2. Differentiate a convergent power series term by term.
3. Use r!=r(r−1)! and (n+r)!=(n+r)(n+r−1)! when cancelling derivative factors.
4. Re-index a series only after making the new lower limit explicit.


DEFINITION / REGISTERED SERIES
For integer n,
Jₙ(x)=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ (x/2)ⁿ⁺²ʳ / [r!(n+r)!].
Equivalently,
Jₙ(x)=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ xⁿ⁺²ʳ / [2ⁿ⁺²ʳ r!(n+r)!].
This is the k=n Bessel function of the first kind used by the registered course source.


WHY THIS METHOD
Both requested identities contain x raised to ±n multiplying Jₙ. Multiplying the registered series by that power first makes differentiation algebraically transparent: the derivative factor cancels exactly against one factorial, leaving the series for the neighboring order.


IDENTITY 1
Show that d[xⁿJₙ(x)]/dx=xⁿJₙ₋₁(x).


Start from
xⁿJₙ(x)=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ x²ⁿ⁺²ʳ / [2ⁿ⁺²ʳ r!(n+r)!].
Differentiate term by term:
d/dx[xⁿJₙ(x)]
=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ(2n+2r)x²ⁿ⁺²ʳ⁻¹ / [2ⁿ⁺²ʳ r!(n+r)!].
Since 2n+2r=2(n+r),
=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ x²ⁿ⁺²ʳ⁻¹ / [2ⁿ⁺²ʳ⁻¹ r!(n+r−1)!].
Now the registered series for order n−1 is
Jₙ₋₁(x)=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ xⁿ⁻¹⁺²ʳ / [2ⁿ⁻¹⁺²ʳ r!(n+r−1)!].
Multiplying by xⁿ gives
xⁿJₙ₋₁(x)=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ x²ⁿ⁺²ʳ⁻¹ / [2ⁿ⁺²ʳ⁻¹ r!(n+r−1)!].
Therefore
boxed: d[xⁿJₙ(x)]/dx=xⁿJₙ₋₁(x).


IDENTITY 2
Show that d[x⁻ⁿJₙ(x)]/dx=−x⁻ⁿJₙ₊₁(x).


Multiply the registered series by x⁻ⁿ:
x⁻ⁿJₙ(x)=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ x²ʳ / [2ⁿ⁺²ʳ r!(n+r)!].
Differentiate. The r=0 term is constant and vanishes:
d/dx[x⁻ⁿJₙ(x)]
=Σ[r=1→∞] (-1)ʳ(2r)x²ʳ⁻¹ / [2ⁿ⁺²ʳ r!(n+r)!]
=Σ[r=1→∞] (-1)ʳ x²ʳ⁻¹ / [2ⁿ⁺²ʳ⁻¹ (r−1)!(n+r)!].
Let s=r−1. Then r=s+1 and
=−Σ[s=0→∞] (-1)ˢ x²ˢ⁺¹ / [2ⁿ⁺²ˢ⁺¹ s!(n+s+1)!].
But
Jₙ₊₁(x)=Σ[s=0→∞] (-1)ˢ xⁿ⁺¹⁺²ˢ / [2ⁿ⁺¹⁺²ˢ s!(n+s+1)!],
so
x⁻ⁿJₙ₊₁(x)=Σ[s=0→∞] (-1)ˢ x²ˢ⁺¹ / [2ⁿ⁺²ˢ⁺¹ s!(n+s+1)!].
Hence
boxed: d[x⁻ⁿJₙ(x)]/dx=−x⁻ⁿJₙ₊₁(x).


INDEPENDENT CHECK
The frozen independent audit is a symbolic-identity sanity check and passes for integer orders n=0,1,2,3,4,5. The algebra above reproduces the registered neighboring-order identities exactly.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Use the registered k=n series so the proof remains source-grounded.
2. Multiply by xⁿ or x⁻ⁿ before differentiating; this exposes the cancellation pattern.
3. For the first identity, cancel n+r against (n+r)!.
4. For the second identity, note explicitly that the r=0 derivative is zero before re-indexing.
5. Match the resulting coefficients and powers to the complete neighboring-order series, not only its first few terms.


COMMON MISTAKES
Dropping the factor 2 when differentiating x²ⁿ⁺²ʳ.
Cancelling (n+r)! incorrectly.
Keeping an r=0 term in the differentiated second identity.
Re-indexing r→r−1 without changing the sign and exponents consistently.
Writing Jₙ₊₁ where Jₙ₋₁ belongs, or vice versa.
Proving only a few series terms rather than the general coefficient identity.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
For integer n,
Jₙ(x)=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳxⁿ⁺²ʳ/[2ⁿ⁺²ʳr!(n+r)!].
Thus
xⁿJₙ(x)=Σ (-1)ʳx²ⁿ⁺²ʳ/[2ⁿ⁺²ʳr!(n+r)!].
Differentiation gives
Σ (-1)ʳx²ⁿ⁺²ʳ⁻¹/[2ⁿ⁺²ʳ⁻¹r!(n+r−1)!]=xⁿJₙ₋₁(x).
Therefore d[xⁿJₙ]/dx=xⁿJₙ₋₁.
Also
x⁻ⁿJₙ(x)=Σ (-1)ʳx²ʳ/[2ⁿ⁺²ʳr!(n+r)!].
After differentiating, dropping the zero r=0 derivative and putting s=r−1,
 d[x⁻ⁿJₙ]/dx
=−Σ[s=0→∞](-1)ˢx²ˢ⁺¹/[2ⁿ⁺²ˢ⁺¹s!(n+s+1)!]
=−x⁻ⁿJₙ₊₁(x).
Hence both required identities are proved.

questions.question: Describe Bessel’s function and Legendre’s formula.
questions.student_view:
1. Bessel’s function — source-supported material
Bessel’s differential equation of order n is
x²y″ + xy′ + (x²−n²)y = 0.


For the k=n first-kind solution, the registered series is
Jₙ(x)=Σᵣ₌₀^∞ [(-1)ʳ /(Γ(r+1)Γ(n+r+1))] (x/2)^(n+2r).
For integer n≥0 this is the Bessel function of the first kind of order n used in the registered course chapter.


Useful interpretation: Bessel functions arise as special-function solutions of this second-order ODE; neighboring orders are connected by recurrence/derivative identities in the same chapter.


2. Legendre material actually named in the source
The registered chapter gives Legendre’s equation
(1−x²)y″ − 2xy′ + n(n+1)y = 0,
whose polynomial solutions for non-negative integer n are Legendre polynomials Pₙ(x).


The same source separately gives Rodrigues formula
Pₙ(x) = [1/(2ⁿ n!)] dⁿ/dxⁿ [(x²−1)ⁿ].


3. Why “Legendre’s formula” remains ambiguous
The source headings distinguish “Legendre’s Equation and Legendre’s Function” from “Rodrigue’s Formula.” Because the exam itself says only “Legendre’s formula,” it is not safe to rename Rodrigues formula as “Legendre’s formula,” nor safe to assume the setter meant only the differential equation. Both directly supported items should be studied, with the label ambiguity explicitly disclosed.


4. Small source-supported examples from Rodrigues formula
P₀(x)=1,
P₁(x)=x,
P₂(x)=(3x²−1)/2.
These illustrate the polynomial family governed by Legendre’s equation; they do not resolve which item the examiner intended by the ambiguous phrase.


FINAL ANSWER
Bessel’s function: the registered notes use Bessel’s equation x²y″+xy′+(x²−n²)y=0 and the first-kind series Jₙ(x)=Σᵣ₌₀^∞[(-1)ʳ/(Γ(r+1)Γ(n+r+1))](x/2)^(n+2r). For the Legendre portion, the registered source supports Legendre’s equation (1−x²)y″−2xy′+n(n+1)y=0 and separately Rodrigues formula Pₙ(x)=[1/(2ⁿn!)]dⁿ[(x²−1)ⁿ]/dxⁿ. The source does not itself name a separate “Legendre’s formula,” so no single one of these should be silently asserted as the intended answer without instructor/source clarification.


INDEPENDENT THEORETICAL CHECK
Bessel equation/series check: the displayed equation and k=n series match the registered Special Functions source-lock record.
Legendre equation check: the displayed ODE has the standard registered polynomial-solution form.
Rodrigues sanity check: n=0,1,2 gives P₀=1, P₁=x, P₂=(3x²−1)/2.
Source-label audit: mathematical computation cannot determine what the exam setter meant by the phrase “Legendre’s formula”; the ambiguity is therefore preserved rather than guessed away.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Bessel’s equation is x²y″+xy′+(x²−n²)y=0, with first-kind solution Jₙ represented in the registered notes by its k=n series. For Legendre material, write the source-supported Legendre equation (1−x²)y″−2xy′+n(n+1)y=0 and, separately, Rodrigues formula Pₙ(x)=[1/(2ⁿn!)]dⁿ[(x²−1)ⁿ]/dxⁿ. Add that the registered chapter does not name a distinct “Legendre’s formula,” so the assessment label is ambiguous and these supported items must not be silently conflated.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Renaming Rodrigues formula “Legendre’s formula” without source evidence.
• Giving only Rodrigues formula and hiding the label ambiguity.
• Confusing Bessel’s equation with Legendre’s equation.
• Omitting the order n in Bessel’s equation or the n(n+1) term in Legendre’s equation.
• Treating a source-label ambiguity as a mathematical contradiction.

questions.question:
Find the relation of Bessel’s function when k=n. Using it prove
Jₙ(−x)=(−1)ⁿJₙ(x).
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. The exact occurrence is P2-PROV-2023-FALL-Q5B, printed 5(b), 8 marks. The registered HRP Special Functions chapter and teacher Chapter 6 extract, PDF pp.10–13 / printed pp.120–123, equation (6.23), directly provide the k=n series used for this proof. The frozen master explicitly treats this as the source-supported parity argument.


PREREQUISITES
1. n is an integer order.
2. Use the registered k=n Bessel first-kind power series.
3. For any integer r, 2r is even, so (−1)²ʳ=1.
4. A common factor independent of the summation index can be taken outside the series.


REGISTERED k=n RELATION
For integer n,
Jₙ(x)=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ/(r!(n+r)!) · (x/2)ⁿ⁺²ʳ.
Equivalently,
Jₙ(x)=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ xⁿ⁺²ʳ/[2ⁿ⁺²ʳ r!(n+r)!].


WHY THIS METHOD
The requested result concerns replacing x by −x. In the registered series every power of x is n+2r. Because 2r is always even, every term acquires exactly the same sign factor (−1)ⁿ. The proof therefore follows immediately from the source series without needing recurrence relations or an outside identity.


DERIVATION
Replace x by −x in the registered series:
Jₙ(−x)
=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ/(r!(n+r)!) · ((−x)/2)ⁿ⁺²ʳ.
Now
((−x)/2)ⁿ⁺²ʳ
=(−1)ⁿ⁺²ʳ(x/2)ⁿ⁺²ʳ.
Since
(−1)ⁿ⁺²ʳ=(−1)ⁿ(−1)²ʳ=(−1)ⁿ,
we obtain
Jₙ(−x)
=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ(−1)ⁿ/(r!(n+r)!) · (x/2)ⁿ⁺²ʳ.
The factor (−1)ⁿ does not depend on r, hence
Jₙ(−x)
=(−1)ⁿ Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ/(r!(n+r)!) · (x/2)ⁿ⁺²ʳ
=(−1)ⁿJₙ(x).
Therefore
boxed: Jₙ(−x)=(−1)ⁿJₙ(x).


INTERPRETATION
If n is even, (−1)ⁿ=+1, so Jₙ(−x)=Jₙ(x): Jₙ is even.
If n is odd, (−1)ⁿ=−1, so Jₙ(−x)=−Jₙ(x): Jₙ is odd.
This even/odd statement is a consequence of the proved integer-order relation, not an extra assumed property.


INDEPENDENT CHECK
The frozen independent audit tests the parity relation symbolically for integer orders n=0,1,2,3,4,5,6 and passes every case. The series proof is exact for integer n.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. Start from the registered k=n series because that is the course-source relation requested by the question.
2. Substitute −x into the complete series, not only a truncated approximation.
3. Separate the sign as (−1)ⁿ⁺²ʳ=(−1)ⁿ(−1)²ʳ.
4. Use integer-order parity to reduce (−1)²ʳ to 1.
5. Factor the remaining (−1)ⁿ outside the sum and recognize the original Jₙ(x) series.


COMMON MISTAKES
Writing (−1)ⁿ⁺²ʳ=(−1)ⁿ⁺(−1)²ʳ instead of multiplying sign factors.
Forgetting that 2r is always even.
Leaving a sign depending on r after simplification.
Assuming the result for non-integer n without qualification.
Using the neighboring-order recurrence identities when the direct series proof is simpler and source-matched.
Showing only J₀ or J₁ instead of the general integer-order proof.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
For integer n, the k=n Bessel relation is
Jₙ(x)=Σ[r=0→∞] (-1)ʳ/(r!(n+r)!)(x/2)ⁿ⁺²ʳ.
Hence
Jₙ(−x)=Σ (-1)ʳ/(r!(n+r)!)((−x)/2)ⁿ⁺²ʳ
=Σ (-1)ʳ(−1)ⁿ⁺²ʳ/(r!(n+r)!)(x/2)ⁿ⁺²ʳ.
Because 2r is even,
(−1)ⁿ⁺²ʳ=(−1)ⁿ.
Therefore
Jₙ(−x)=(−1)ⁿΣ (-1)ʳ/(r!(n+r)!)(x/2)ⁿ⁺²ʳ
=boxed: (−1)ⁿJₙ(x).
Thus Jₙ is even for even n and odd for odd n.

questions.question:
For positive integer n, use/prove the generating relation


Σ_(n=0)^∞ z^n P_n(x) = (1−2xz+z²)^−1/2,


where P_n(x) is a polynomial of order n.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Dr. Hem Raj Pandey’s course notes, Chapter 6 §6.1.4 “Generating Function”, Theorem 6.1.2 (printed p.118), directly state and prove this relation by binomially expanding (1−2xz+z²)^−1/2 and grouping coefficients as
P₀(x)+zP₁(x)+z²P₂(x)+z³P₃(x)+… .


The registered teacher Chapter-6 extract points to the same theorem. The frozen source-lock revision explicitly replaced an older consequence-focused answer with this actual theorem/proof. Therefore the primary tier is DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION.


INTUITION
A generating function stores an entire sequence of polynomials inside one power series. If


G(x,z)=(1−2xz+z²)^−1/2,


then the coefficient multiplying z^n is, by definition here, P_n(x). Expanding G in powers of z therefore generates P₀,P₁,P₂,… all at once.


WHY USE A BINOMIAL EXPANSION?
The right-hand side has exponent −1/2. Writing


u=−2xz+z²


turns it into (1+u)^−1/2, for which the generalized binomial series is standard:


(1+u)^−1/2
=1−(1/2)u+(3/8)u²−(5/16)u³+(35/128)u⁴−… .


STEP 1 — SUBSTITUTE u=−2xz+z²


G(x,z)
=1−1/2(−2xz+z²)
 +3/8(−2xz+z²)²
 −5/16(−2xz+z²)³
 +35/128(−2xz+z²)⁴+… .


We now collect equal powers of z.


STEP 2 — COEFFICIENT OF z⁰
Only the leading 1 contributes:


P₀(x)=1.


STEP 3 — COEFFICIENT OF z¹
From −1/2(−2xz+z²), the z term is xz. Hence


P₁(x)=x.


STEP 4 — COEFFICIENT OF z²
Contributions are


−z²/2


and, from
(−2xz+z²)²=4x²z²−4xz³+z⁴,


the z² contribution is
(3/8)(4x²z²)=(3/2)x²z².


Therefore


P₂(x)=(3x²−1)/2.


STEP 5 — COEFFICIENT OF z³
From the u² term:


(3/8)(−4xz³)=−(3/2)xz³.


From the u³ term, the lowest z³ contribution is


(−2xz)³=−8x³z³,


so


−(5/16)(−8x³z³)=(5/2)x³z³.


Thus


P₃(x)=(5x³−3x)/2.


STEP 6 — NEXT TERM AS A PATTERN CHECK
Collecting z⁴ gives


P₄(x)=(35x⁴−30x²+3)/8.


Hence the expansion begins


(1−2xz+z²)^−1/2
=1
+xz
+[(3x²−1)/2]z²
+[(5x³−3x)/2]z³
+[(35x⁴−30x²+3)/8]z⁴
+… .


Recognizing the bracketed coefficients as the Legendre polynomials,


= P₀(x)+zP₁(x)+z²P₂(x)+z³P₃(x)+z⁴P₄(x)+…


= Σ_(n=0)^∞ z^n P_n(x).


Therefore


Σ_(n=0)^∞ z^n P_n(x)=(1−2xz+z²)^−1/2.


This proves the generating relation.


WHY IS P_n A POLYNOMIAL OF ORDER n?
At coefficient z^n, the highest possible power of x arises by repeatedly selecting the −2xz part from the binomial expansion; this produces an x^n term. Lower terms occur in descending powers with the same parity as n. Thus the coefficient of z^n is a polynomial of degree n.


PATTERN TO REMEMBER
P₀=1
P₁=x
P₂=(3x²−1)/2
P₃=(5x³−3x)/2
P₄=(35x⁴−30x²+3)/8


The power of z labels which Legendre polynomial is being generated.


MATH QA
PASS — generalized binomial coefficients for exponent −1/2 give 1, −1/2, 3/8, −5/16, 35/128,… .
PASS — coefficient z gives P₁=x.
PASS — coefficient z² gives P₂=(3x²−1)/2.
PASS — coefficient z³ gives P₃=(5x³−3x)/2.
PASS — coefficient z⁴ gives P₄=(35x⁴−30x²+3)/8.
PASS — these match the standard first Legendre polynomials and the registered course theorem.


COMMON MISTAKES
- treating z as the polynomial variable instead of the generating-series parameter;
- expanding in x instead of collecting powers of z;
- losing alternating generalized-binomial coefficients;
- stopping after merely stating the generating relation when the question expects a proof/use of it;
- writing P₂ or P₃ coefficients incorrectly;
- forgetting that the coefficient of z^n is the complete polynomial P_n(x), not only its leading term.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Let


G(x,z)=(1−2xz+z²)^−1/2.


Using


(1+u)^−1/2=1−u/2+3u²/8−5u³/16+…


with u=−2xz+z²,


G(x,z)
=1+xz+(3x²−1)z²/2+(5x³−3x)z³/2+… .


But


P₀=1,
P₁=x,
P₂=(3x²−1)/2,
P₃=(5x³−3x)/2,
… .


Therefore


G(x,z)=P₀+zP₁+z²P₂+z³P₃+…
=Σ_(n=0)^∞ z^nP_n(x).


Hence


Σ_(n=0)^∞ z^nP_n(x)=(1−2xz+z²)^−1/2.

questions.question: Show Pₙ(x) = [1/(2ⁿ n!)] dⁿ/dxⁿ [(x²−1)ⁿ] for all positive integers n.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Dr. Hem Raj Pandey’s course lecture notes §6.1.2, Theorem 6.1.1, state the Rodrigues formula and give the proof. The same source derives the Legendre differential equation from v=(x²−1)ⁿ, then fixes the normalization constant by Pₙ(1)=1. This is an exact instructor-course theorem/proof match, so the primary provenance tier is DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION.
The frozen record occurs three times and is already SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. v1.2 expands the proof pedagogically without modifying the frozen question or provenance.


WHAT IS BEING ASKED?
Derive the explicit derivative representation of the Legendre polynomial Pₙ(x), not merely state it. The proof must explain why dⁿ[(x²−1)ⁿ]/dxⁿ is a Legendre-equation solution and why the prefactor is exactly 1/(2ⁿn!).


PREREQUISITES
Leibniz rule for the nth derivative of a product; Legendre differential equation; normalization Pₙ(1)=1; differentiation order notation.


INTUITION
The polynomial (x²−1)ⁿ contains the endpoint factors (x−1)ⁿ(x+1)ⁿ. Differentiating it n times lowers its degree from 2n to n, which is exactly the degree required for Pₙ. The key is to prove that this nth derivative satisfies Legendre’s equation. The endpoint x=1 then fixes the otherwise arbitrary multiplicative constant.


WORKED DERIVATION
Let
v(x) = (x²−1)ⁿ.


Differentiate once:
v′ = 2nx(x²−1)ⁿ⁻¹.


Multiply by (x²−1):
(x²−1)v′ = 2nxv.                                      (1)


Now differentiate equation (1) exactly n+1 times.


For the left side, use Leibniz’ rule with u=x²−1. Since u′=2x, u″=2 and all higher derivatives of u vanish,
Dⁿ⁺¹[(x²−1)v′]
= (x²−1)v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾ + 2(n+1)xv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ + n(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾.


For the right side,
Dⁿ⁺¹[2nxv]
= 2n[xv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ + (n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾].


Equating both sides and collecting terms gives
(x²−1)v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾ + 2xv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ − n(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾ = 0.          (2)


Define
y = v⁽ⁿ⁾.


Then y′=v⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ and y″=v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾, so equation (2) becomes
(x²−1)y″ + 2xy′ − n(n+1)y = 0.


Multiplying by −1,
(1−x²)y″ − 2xy′ + n(n+1)y = 0,
which is Legendre’s differential equation.


Therefore v⁽ⁿ⁾ is a Legendre-equation solution. Hence
Pₙ(x) = C v⁽ⁿ⁾(x)
for some constant C.


Now determine C from the standard normalization Pₙ(1)=1. Write
v=(x−1)ⁿ(x+1)ⁿ.


Apply Leibniz’ rule to the nth derivative and set x=1. Every term still containing a positive power of (x−1) vanishes. The only surviving term differentiates (x−1)ⁿ exactly n times:
v⁽ⁿ⁾(1) = n!·(1+1)ⁿ = 2ⁿn!.


Thus
1 = Pₙ(1) = C·2ⁿn!,
so
C = 1/(2ⁿn!).


Therefore
Pₙ(x) = [1/(2ⁿn!)] dⁿ/dxⁿ [(x²−1)ⁿ].


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
Starting from v=(x²−1)ⁿ is useful because n derivatives produce a degree-n polynomial and the factors x±1 make endpoint normalization simple.
Differentiating (x²−1)v′=2nxv n+1 times is the bridge from the constructed polynomial v to Legendre’s differential equation.
Setting y=v⁽ⁿ⁾ converts the higher-derivative identity into the familiar second-order Legendre equation.
Using Pₙ(1)=1 is necessary because a homogeneous differential equation determines a solution only up to a multiplicative constant.
At x=1, Leibniz’ rule collapses to one surviving term, making the constant 1/(2ⁿn!) exact.


MATH QA
Leibniz coefficient check: C(n+1,2)·2 = n(n+1), so the left-side v⁽ⁿ⁾ coefficient before subtraction is correct.
Right-side product check: Dⁿ⁺¹[xv]=xv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾+(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾.
Collected equation check: the v⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ coefficient is 2(n+1)x−2nx=2x, and the v⁽ⁿ⁾ coefficient is n(n+1)−2n(n+1)=−n(n+1).
Endpoint check: Dⁿ[(x−1)ⁿ(x+1)ⁿ] at x=1 equals 2ⁿn!.
Low-order checks:
n=0 gives P₀=1.
n=1 gives P₁=x.
n=2 gives P₂=(3x²−1)/2.
n=3 gives P₃=(5x³−3x)/2.
All agree with the standard Legendre polynomials.


RELATED COURSE CONTEXT
NMA-Q-0173: generating relation for Legendre polynomials; already STUDENT_READY in Batch 01.
NMA-Q-0175: Legendre function/equation and the odd-n property Pₙ(0)=0; selected in Batch 02.
NMA-Q-0178: direct derivation of the Legendre differential equation from the same Rodrigues-proof identity; selected in Batch 02.
Instructor Example 6.1.1 proves Pₙ(0)=0 for odd n using the Legendre-polynomial power pattern.


COMMON MISTAKES
Stopping after stating Rodrigues’ formula instead of proving it.
Differentiating equation (1) n times instead of n+1 times.
Forgetting the binomial coefficients in Leibniz’ rule.
Losing the minus sign when converting (x²−1)y″+2xy′−n(n+1)y=0 to the standard Legendre form.
Claiming v⁽ⁿ⁾ equals Pₙ directly without fixing the multiplicative constant.
At x=1, keeping Leibniz terms that still contain (x−1); those terms vanish.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Let v=(x²−1)ⁿ. Then (x²−1)v′=2nxv. Differentiating n+1 times and applying Leibniz’ rule gives
(x²−1)v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾+2xv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾−n(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾=0.
Putting y=v⁽ⁿ⁾,
(1−x²)y″−2xy′+n(n+1)y=0,
so y is a Legendre-equation solution and Pₙ=Cv⁽ⁿ⁾. Since v=(x−1)ⁿ(x+1)ⁿ,
v⁽ⁿ⁾(1)=2ⁿn!.
Using Pₙ(1)=1 gives C=1/(2ⁿn!). Hence
Pₙ(x)=[1/(2ⁿn!)] dⁿ/dxⁿ[(x²−1)ⁿ].

questions.question: Define Legendre’s function. Derive the equation/series form of Legendre’s function. Using it show that Pₙ(0)=0 for all odd positive integers n.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
Dr. Hem Raj Pandey’s Chapter 6 §6.1 defines Legendre’s equation and calls its solutions Legendre functions. The chapter derives the first- and second-kind series by substituting a descending-power series into the equation. Example 6.1.1 then proves the exact requested odd-order property by writing n=2m+1 and substituting x=0.
Because the instructor source contains the exact definition/series derivation and exact worked parity example, the primary provenance tier is DIRECT_COURSE_SOLUTION.


DEFINITION
Legendre’s differential equation is
(1−x²)y″−2xy′+n(n+1)y=0.                                  (1)
A solution of equation (1) is called a Legendre function. For nonnegative integer n, the normalized polynomial solution of the first kind is denoted Pₙ(x).


SERIES CONSTRUCTION
Following the instructor source, assume a descending-power series
y = Σ aᵣ x^(k−r)
  = a₀xᵏ + a₁x^(k−1) + a₂x^(k−2)+⋯.


Then
y′ = Σ aᵣ(k−r)x^(k−r−1),
y″ = Σ aᵣ(k−r)(k−r−1)x^(k−r−2).


Substitute these in (1). Comparing the highest-power coefficient gives
a₀[n(n+1)−k(k+1)]=0.
Since a₀≠0,
k=n  or  k=−(n+1).


These two indices generate the first- and second-kind Legendre solutions.


FIRST-KIND POLYNOMIAL
Choose k=n. The coefficient comparison gives a₁=0, and all odd-indexed coefficients a₁,a₃,a₅,… vanish. The even-index recurrence produces
a₂ = −[n(n−1)/(2(2n−1))]a₀,
a₄ = +[n(n−1)(n−2)(n−3)/(2·4(2n−1)(2n−3))]a₀,
and so on.


With the source normalization
a₀ = 1·3·5···(2n−1)/n!,
the first-kind polynomial can be written
Pₙ(x)=Aₙ[
xⁿ
− n(n−1)/(2(2n−1)) x^(n−2)
+ n(n−1)(n−2)(n−3)/(2·4(2n−1)(2n−3)) x^(n−4)
− ⋯],
where
Aₙ=1·3·5···(2n−1)/n!.


WHY THE POWER PATTERN MATTERS
Every power in Pₙ differs from n by an even integer:
n, n−2, n−4, … .
Therefore Pₙ has the same parity as n. If n is even, only even powers appear; if n is odd, only odd powers appear.


PROOF THAT Pₙ(0)=0 FOR ODD n
Let
n=2m+1.
Then the first-kind series has powers
x^(2m+1), x^(2m−1), x^(2m−3), …, x.
Every term contains a positive odd power of x.


Hence, on setting x=0,
P₂ₘ₊₁(0)=0.
Therefore
Pₙ(0)=0 for every odd positive integer n.


LOW-ORDER CHECKS
P₁(x)=x, so P₁(0)=0.
P₃(x)=(5x³−3x)/2, so P₃(0)=0.
P₅(x)=(63x⁵−70x³+15x)/8, so P₅(0)=0.
The pattern agrees with the general proof.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
The series assumption converts the differential equation into algebraic coefficient conditions.
The highest-power comparison determines the two characteristic indices n and −(n+1).
Choosing k=n selects the polynomial first-kind solution Pₙ.
The vanishing odd-indexed coefficient chain forces the exponents to move in steps of two.
Once the power pattern is known, the odd-n value at x=0 follows immediately without evaluating any complicated coefficients.


MATH QA
PASS — substituting the series into Legendre’s equation yields k(k+1)=n(n+1), hence k=n or −(n+1).
PASS — the first-kind recurrence couples coefficients two indices apart, producing only powers n,n−2,n−4,… .
PASS — odd n therefore gives an odd polynomial: Pₙ(−x)=−Pₙ(x).
PASS — an odd polynomial necessarily satisfies Pₙ(0)=0.
PASS — checks for n=1,3,5 agree.


SOURCE REVIEW NOTE
Instructor Example 6.1.1 correctly obtains P₂ₘ₊₁(0)=0 after substituting x=0. Its last printed line says “If n is odd, Pₙ(x)=0,” dropping the argument zero. The preceding line, the proof, and the exam wording all show that the intended conclusion is Pₙ(0)=0. v1.2 corrects only the displayed conclusion in Study View and preserves the printed typo in Audit.


RELATED COURSE CONTEXT
NMA-Q-0174: Rodrigues formula, reconstructed in this Batch 02 and math-QA passed.
NMA-Q-0173: Legendre generating function, STUDENT_READY in Batch 01.
NMA-Q-0178: derivation of Legendre’s differential equation from Rodrigues’ identity, selected in Batch 02.
HRP Example 6.1.2 expands an ordinary cubic polynomial in the P₀,P₁,P₂,P₃ basis and reinforces the explicit low-order polynomial forms.


COMMON MISTAKES
Stating Legendre’s equation but not defining its solutions as Legendre functions.
Confusing the first-kind polynomial Pₙ with the second-kind solution Qₙ.
Trying to prove Pₙ(0)=0 from orthogonality; the source proof uses the power/parity structure directly.
Assuming every coefficient is nonzero; the recurrence splits into parity chains and the first-kind polynomial uses only powers n,n−2,… .
Copying the source’s final Pₙ(x)=0 typo, which would incorrectly claim the entire odd-order polynomial is identically zero.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Legendre’s equation is
(1−x²)y″−2xy′+n(n+1)y=0,
and its solutions are Legendre functions.


Assume
y=Σaᵣx^(k−r).
Substitution gives the highest-power condition
k(k+1)=n(n+1),
so k=n or k=−(n+1). For the first kind take k=n. The coefficient recurrence gives a₁=a₃=⋯=0 and
Pₙ(x)=Aₙ[xⁿ−c₂x^(n−2)+c₄x^(n−4)−⋯].
Thus Pₙ contains only powers n,n−2,n−4,… .


If n=2m+1 is odd, all these powers are positive odd powers:
P₂ₘ₊₁(x)=A[x^(2m+1)+B x^(2m−1)+⋯+Cx].
Therefore, at x=0,
P₂ₘ₊₁(0)=0.
Hence Pₙ(0)=0 for every odd n.

questions.question: Define Legendre’s Polynomial and prove P_n(0)=0 for n odd.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED_WITH_REVIEW_NOTE. HRP Chapter 6 and the registered special-function chapter extract define Legendre polynomials, state Rodrigues’ formula, list the low-order polynomials, and in Example 6.1.1 prove the odd-order zero-at-origin property. The frozen review flag PHASE4_UNSUPPORTED_ORTHOGONALITY_APPLICATION_EXTRAS_REMOVED remains active: this v1.2 record does not reintroduce unsupported orthogonality/application exposition.


DEFINITION
The Legendre polynomial of degree n is the first-kind polynomial solution P_n(x) of
(1-x^2)P_n''(x)-2xP_n'(x)+n(n+1)P_n(x)=0,
normalized in the course source by P_n(1)=1.
Rodrigues’ representation is
P_n(x)=[1/(2^n n!)] d^n[(x^2-1)^n]/dx^n.


WHY THE ODD-ORDER PROPERTY FOLLOWS
The polynomial (x^2-1)^n is an even function of x for every integer n. Differentiating an even function an odd number of times gives an odd function; differentiating it an even number of times gives an even function. Rodrigues’ formula takes exactly n derivatives. Therefore
P_n(-x)=(-1)^n P_n(x).
So for odd n,
P_n(-x)=-P_n(x),
meaning P_n is odd.


Set x=0:
P_n(0)=-P_n(0).
Hence
2P_n(0)=0,
and therefore
boxed: P_n(0)=0 for odd n.


EQUIVALENT SERIES/PARITY VIEW
The registered first-kind Legendre series contains powers n,n-2,n-4,... only. If n=2m+1 is odd, all retained powers are odd:
x^(2m+1), x^(2m-1), ..., x.
Every term therefore vanishes at x=0. This is the same parity conclusion expressed through the source’s series structure.


LOW-ORDER CHECKS
P_1(x)=x, so P_1(0)=0.
P_3(x)=(1/2)(5x^3-3x), so P_3(0)=0.
P_5(x)=(1/8)(63x^5-70x^3+15x), so P_5(0)=0.
The frozen independent audit tested odd orders 1,3,5,7 and passed.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
1. State the Legendre differential equation so the object being defined is mathematically identified.
2. Use Rodrigues’ formula because it exposes the parity of P_n directly.
3. Observe that (x^2-1)^n is even before differentiating; parity is the key invariant.
4. Use exactly n derivatives, so derivative parity becomes (-1)^n.
5. Set x=0 only after proving odd parity; the zero value is a consequence, not an assumption.


COMMON MISTAKES
Claiming P_n(0)=0 for every n.
Forgetting that even-order Legendre polynomials generally have nonzero values at x=0.
Using orthogonality as the proof when the registered course example proves the result from series/parity.
Writing Rodrigues’ prefactor incorrectly.
Reintroducing unsupported application/orthogonality material removed by the frozen review.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Legendre polynomial P_n(x) is the normalized polynomial solution of
(1-x^2)P_n''-2xP_n'+n(n+1)P_n=0,
with Rodrigues’ formula
P_n(x)=1/(2^n n!) d^n[(x^2-1)^n]/dx^n.
Since (x^2-1)^n is even, after n derivatives
P_n(-x)=(-1)^nP_n(x).
For odd n, P_n is odd, so at x=0,
P_n(0)=-P_n(0),
hence P_n(0)=0.

questions.question: What are recurrence formulae? Prove the two printed Legendre relations, the first beginning n(n+1)Pₙ₊₁(x)=(2n+1)xPₙ(x)−nPₙ₋₁(x), and the second beginning nPₙ(x)=xP′ₙ(x)−P′ₙ₋₁(x).
questions.student_view:
What a recurrence formula is
A recurrence formula relates members of a sequence or family at neighboring orders so that higher-order functions can be obtained from lower-order ones.


Registered Legendre recurrence
The registered chapter derives the standard three-term recurrence
(n+1)Pₙ₊₁(x)=(2n+1)xPₙ(x)−nPₙ₋₁(x).
A compact derivation begins with the generating function
G(x,t)=Σₙ₌₀^∞Pₙ(x)tⁿ=(1−2xt+t²)^−1/2.
Differentiating with respect to t gives
(1−2xt+t²)G_t=(x−t)G.
Comparing coefficients of tⁿ yields
(n+1)Pₙ₊₁−2nxPₙ+(n−1)Pₙ₋₁=xPₙ−Pₙ₋₁,
which rearranges to the standard recurrence above.


Why the printed first relation cannot be proved as written
The exam inserts an additional leading factor n on the left, printing n(n+1)Pₙ₊₁. That is not equivalent to the registered recurrence for general n. The source conflict must be shown explicitly rather than silently correcting the exam.


Second printed identity
The second printed identity
nPₙ(x)=xP′ₙ(x)−P′ₙ₋₁(x)
is algebraically consistent with Legendre polynomials and passed the independent symbolic audit. It may be presented as valid reference mathematics, while the overall exam question remains conflicted because the first required relation is false as printed.


Exam-ready answer
Define recurrence formulae, write and derive the registered standard recurrence, then state clearly that the exam's first relation contains an extra leading n and cannot be honestly proved for general n. Preserve the second identity separately as valid. A corrected full exam answer requires instructor/corrected-source confirmation of the first relation.


INDEPENDENT MATHEMATICAL / SYMBOLIC QA
Use P₁=x, P₂=(3x²−1)/2, P₃=(5x³−3x)/2.
• For n=2, the standard recurrence gives 3P₃=5xP₂−2P₁, which simplifies identically on both sides.
• The printed first relation instead gives 6P₃=5xP₂−2P₁. Since the right side equals 3P₃, the printed residual is 3P₃=(15x³−9x)/2, not identically zero.
• The failure is therefore structural, not a rounding issue. The registered source-lock audit checked orders n=1..5: standard recurrence PASS for all, printed extra-n form FAIL in general.
• For n=2, the second identity gives 2P₂=xP₂′−P₁′=3x²−1=2P₂, confirming consistency.

questions.question:
Derive
(1−x²)d²y/dx²−2x dy/dx+n(n+1)y=0.
questions.student_view:
SOURCE ALIGNMENT
HRP §6.1.2, Rodrigues-formula proof equations (6.11)–(6.13), explicitly generates the requested Legendre differential equation. The frozen record was revised because an earlier Phase-4 answer did not actually answer the derivation request; the registered instructor proof restores the correct derivation. This is an exact direct-course proof match.


PREREQUISITES
Product differentiation; Leibniz theorem for repeated derivatives; derivative-order notation; substitution of a higher derivative as a new dependent variable.


INTUITION
Start from the polynomial v=(x²−1)ⁿ. Its special factor structure produces a simple first-order identity involving v and v′. Repeated differentiation of that identity creates exactly the coefficient pattern needed for Legendre’s second-order equation. The substitution y=v⁽ⁿ⁾ then collapses the high-order derivative relation back to a second-order ODE.


STEP 1 — BUILD THE SOURCE IDENTITY
Let
v=(x²−1)ⁿ.                                            (6.11)
Then
v′=2nx(x²−1)ⁿ⁻¹.
Multiplying by (x²−1),
(x²−1)v′=2nxv.                                         (6.12)


WHY THIS IDENTITY IS USEFUL
The left side is a product of the quadratic x²−1 and v′. Since the third and higher derivatives of x²−1 vanish, Leibniz differentiation of this product has only three surviving terms. The right side contains xv, whose second and higher derivatives of x also vanish. This makes an n+1 derivative tractable rather than explosive.


STEP 2 — DIFFERENTIATE n+1 TIMES
Apply Dⁿ⁺¹ to both sides of (6.12).


For the left side, with u=x²−1,
Dⁿ⁺¹[u v′]
=u v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾ + C(n+1,1)u′v⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ + C(n+1,2)u″v⁽ⁿ⁾.
Because
u′=2x,
u″=2,
this becomes
(x²−1)v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾ + 2(n+1)x v⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ + n(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾.
The last coefficient follows from
C(n+1,2)·2 = [(n+1)n/2]·2 = n(n+1).


For the right side,
Dⁿ⁺¹[2nxv]
=2n Dⁿ⁺¹[xv]
=2n[xv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾+(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾],
because only x and x′=1 contribute.


Equating the two sides:
(x²−1)v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾ +2(n+1)xv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ +n(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾
=2nxv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ +2n(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾.


Collecting like derivative orders gives
(x²−1)v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾ +2xv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ −n(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾=0.              (6.13)


COEFFICIENT CHECK
For v⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾:
2(n+1)x−2nx=2x.
For v⁽ⁿ⁾:
n(n+1)−2n(n+1)=−n(n+1).
These are exactly the coefficients printed in the instructor’s equation (6.13).


STEP 3 — REDUCE TO A SECOND-ORDER ODE
Set
y=v⁽ⁿ⁾.
Then
y′=v⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾,
y″=v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾.
Substituting into (6.13),
(x²−1)y″+2xy′−n(n+1)y=0.
Multiply by −1:
(1−x²)y″−2xy′+n(n+1)y=0.


This is the Legendre differential equation.


WHY n+1 DIFFERENTIATIONS ARE NECESSARY
If equation (6.12) were differentiated only n times, the resulting highest derivative would be v⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ and the substitution y=v⁽ⁿ⁾ would produce only y′, not the required second derivative y″. Differentiating n+1 times is what produces v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾ and hence the second-order Legendre equation.


LOW-ORDER SANITY CHECKS
n=0 gives
(1−x²)y″−2xy′=0;
y=1 satisfies it.


n=1 gives
(1−x²)y″−2xy′+2y=0;
y=x satisfies it.


n=2 gives
(1−x²)y″−2xy′+6y=0;
y=(3x²−1)/2 satisfies it.


n=3 gives
(1−x²)y″−2xy′+12y=0;
y=(5x³−3x)/2 satisfies it.


These checks confirm the derived ODE for the first standard Legendre polynomials.


WHY THE MAJOR STEPS ARE NECESSARY
Choosing v=(x²−1)ⁿ provides the structured polynomial used by the instructor proof.
Multiplying v′ by x²−1 creates the simple identity (6.12).
Leibniz differentiation n+1 times generates the exact derivative-order coefficients.
Collecting derivative families exposes equation (6.13) rather than leaving a long product-rule expression.
Setting y=v⁽ⁿ⁾ turns the high-order identity into the requested second-order ODE.
Multiplying by −1 puts it in the conventional Legendre form printed in the question.


MATH QA
PASS — source equations (6.11)–(6.13) alignment.
PASS — Leibniz coefficient C(n+1,2)·2=n(n+1).
PASS — right-side derivative Dⁿ⁺¹[xv]=xv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾+(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾.
PASS — collected v⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ coefficient =2x.
PASS — collected v⁽ⁿ⁾ coefficient =−n(n+1).
PASS — y=v⁽ⁿ⁾ substitution produces the requested ODE exactly.
PASS — low-order n=0,1,2,3 polynomial substitutions satisfy the equation.


RELATED COURSE CONTEXT
NMA-Q-0174 in this Batch 02 uses the same source chain and continues beyond the ODE to determine the Rodrigues normalization constant.
NMA-Q-0175 in this Batch 02 starts from Legendre’s equation and develops the series/parity structure.
NMA-Q-0173 in Batch 01 covers the generating relation for Legendre polynomials.


COMMON MISTAKES
Differentiating (6.12) n times instead of n+1 times.
Forgetting the binomial coefficient C(n+1,2) in the Leibniz expansion.
Writing the coefficient of v⁽ⁿ⁾ as +n(n+1) after moving the right side to the left.
Setting y=v⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ instead of y=v⁽ⁿ⁾.
Stopping at equation (6.13) without translating it into y,y′,y″.
Losing the sign when converting x²−1 to 1−x².
Continuing into Rodrigues normalization even though this question asks only for the differential-equation derivation.


EXAM-READY ANSWER
Let
v=(x²−1)ⁿ.
Then
v′=2nx(x²−1)ⁿ⁻¹,
so
(x²−1)v′=2nxv.                                      (1)
Differentiate (1) n+1 times. By Leibniz theorem,
Dⁿ⁺¹[(x²−1)v′]
=(x²−1)v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾+2(n+1)xv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾+n(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾,
while
Dⁿ⁺¹[2nxv]
=2n[xv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾+(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾].
Hence
(x²−1)v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾+2xv⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾−n(n+1)v⁽ⁿ⁾=0.
Put y=v⁽ⁿ⁾. Then y′=v⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ and y″=v⁽ⁿ⁺²⁾, giving
(x²−1)y″+2xy′−n(n+1)y=0.
Multiplying by −1,
(1−x²)y″−2xy′+n(n+1)y=0,
which is the Legendre differential equation.

SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The frozen record is SOURCE_LOCK_VERIFIED. The broad prompt is therefore answered as a source-bounded short note.


PREREQUISITES
1. Recognize Legendre’s equation as a second-order differential equation.
2. Distinguish the first-kind polynomial Pₙ(x) from the second-kind branch Qₙ(x) as presented in the registered notes.
3. Use Rodrigues’ formula for the polynomial sequence Pₙ.


LEGENDRE’S EQUATION
The registered notes define Legendre’s equation as
(1−x²)y″−2xy′+n(n+1)y=0.

FIRST AND SECOND KIND
